Description_Botanical: A biennial or short-lived perennial native mustard serving as an important host plant for Julia's Orangetip and Sara's Orangetip butterflies, growing in sandy or rocky sites in full sun with winter moisture. Grows in sandy or rocky sites in full sun, especially with winter moisture. Biennial (occasionally perennial) from a taproot and a simple stem-base; stems stiff, erect, angled, branched, (10) 20-60 cm tall. Basal leaves are pinnately lobed, long-stalked, less than 12 cm long, with 1-5 pairs of lateral lobes and a largest terminal lobe that is egg-shaped and entire or irregularly toothed, with stalks and sometimes leaflets long-fringed or sparsely short-hairy.

Summary_Public: Evergreen tree 6 to 30 m tall; cinnamon red thin smooth bark peeling in papery flakes away from trunk; thick glossy dark green oval leaves; fragrant white-to-pink bell flowers; scarlet red mealy berries. Inhabiting woodlands, rocky slopes, dry open forests on coarse or shallow soils in the lowland and montane zones; common in extreme southern BC and extending south to Baja CA; found in wooded slopes and canyons within oak, redwood, mixed evergreen, and chaparral communities at elevations of 100-1500 m, ranging from southern CA to British Columbia.
Description_Botanical: Evergreen tree up to 30 m tall with characteristic peeling reddish bark; alternate dark waxy green oval leaves (15 cm); hanging clusters of white bell flowers; bright small red berries. Pacific madrone is an evergreen broadleaf tree of the Heath family (Ericaceae), native to the northwestern Coast Ranges of North America. Reaching heights of 6 to 30 m tall (6-30 m, or 6m to 30m or more depending on environmental conditions), trees feature single or multiple trunks from the base with rounded, spreading crowns, or a more shrublike habit. Young bark is chartreuse and smooth, aging to thin, smooth, deep brownish-red or cinnamon red bark that peels in large papery flakes away from the trunk and young branches to reveal an attractive, satiny green surface beneath that darkens with time to deep red. In midsummer, the exfoliated bark and shed leaves in shades of red to orange form a distinctive colorful carpet beneath the tree canopy (Saunders 1923).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Evergreen tree 6 to 30 m tall; cinnamon red thin smooth bark peeling in papery flakes away from trunk. Pacific madrone is an evergreen broadleaf tree of the Heath family (Ericaceae), native to the northwestern Coast Ranges of North America. Reaching heights of 6 to 30 m tall (6-30 m, or 6m to 30m or more depending on environmental conditions), trees feature single or multiple trunks from the base with rounded, spreading crowns, or a more shrublike habit.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, evergreen, leathery, egg-shaped to elliptic, glabrous, entire on mature older growth, fine-toothed on young shoots, 5-15 cm long, dark shiny green above, whitish-green below.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Borne in large drooping terminal clusters; corollas are white or pinkish, urn-shaped, 6-8 mm long, and fragrant.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berries, globe-shaped, orange to red, about 1 cm across; surface finely granular.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Long-lived perennial canopy tree establishing deeply within 2–3 growing seasons.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Arbutus is a somewhat unusual tree because of its bark, which naturally peels off and away from the trunk and branches. The leaves or inner bark of arbutus may be chewed for toothache and stomach problems.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Distinctive winter bark and stem colour provide strong cold-season architectural interest.
Spread_Behavior: Deep spreading root system with woody basal burl capable of post-fire resprouting
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Forms tight ericaceous root mats and phenolic leaf litter that gradually acidifies surface humus and slows annual weed invasion; compatible with acid-tolerant woodland companions.
Light_Tags: Full Sun; Part Shade; Full Shade
Moisture_Notes: Requires sharp drainage and winter precipitation followed by dry summers.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: These trees are adapted to humid coastal sites as well as dry foothill slopes and canyons in areas with dry summers and mild winters. They grow on soils with low nitrogen and low moisture content. Dry wooded slopes, canyons, oak savannas, and rocky coastal bluffs; prefers well-drained, low-nitrogen, moisture-deficient soils.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Arbutoid Mycorrhiza (Ectomycorrhizal & Ericoid forest fungal network)
Summer_Watering: Zero summer water once established; summer irrigation promotes fatal root rot.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting woodlands, rocky slopes, dry open forests on coarse or shallow soils in the lowland and montane zones; common in extreme southern BC and extending south to Baja CA; found in wooded slopes and canyons within oak, redwood, mixed evergreen, and chaparral communities at elevations of 100-1500 m, ranging from southern CA to British Columbia. Pacific madrone typically occurs in mixed stands and is native to the West Coast of North America, with occasional populations in the middle elevations of the Sierra Nevada Range.

Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Deer, Raccoons, Bears, Wild Sheep, Goats. Berries feed mammals; sprouts browsed by deer and sheep.
Seed_Collection_Harvest: Pacific madrone is a prolific seed producer, which produces seed every year from the age of three to five years. One pound of seeds will produce approximately 1,000 plants. Seedlings grow slowly and are highly susceptible to mortality. To start from seed, gather the fruits from the trees when they are ripe—generally from October to December.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: These trees should only be planted in very well drained soils in areas with non-alkaline water. Although generally started from seed, Pacific madrone may also be propagated from cuttings, grafting, or layers. For best germination, use seeds that have been stratified by pre-chilling for one to two months at 2 to 5°C. Propagated by seed (stratified 1–2 months at 2–5°C) or sprouting from underground burls after fire/cutting.
Pruning_Management: Within managed conifer stands, Pacific madrone has been considered a “weedy” tree species. This is because it can out-compete replanting of timber species because of its ability to resprout from its stump or burl after disturbance. Interestingly, there is some evidence that Pacific madrone can facilitate growth of Douglas fir at some sites. In natural areas, the situation is reversed from that of timber production areas.
Nursery_Availability: Listed by Satinflower Nurseries (Vancouver Island native plant nursery).
Nursery_Stock_Format: 1-gal to 5-gal Deepots / Containers; Stratified Nursery Seed
Edible_Parts_Flavor: Berries eaten fresh, cooked, dried, or cider.
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Edible fruit. The Salinan, Miwok, Pomo, and other California tribes have long used the berries of Pacific madrone for food and to make cider. Berries eaten fresh, made into unfermented cider, or cooked and dried for later use.
Ethno_Medicinal: Leaves or inner bark chewed for toothache and stomach problems. Bark boiled into tea for colds and sore throats. Leaves chewed to reduce stomach pain and cramps.
Ethno_Material_Tech: The dense, fine-grained, wood is heavy and brittle. Bark used for toys and wood carved into tools. Fine wood used for carving, utensils, and gunpowder charcoal.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Sacred tree featured in flood story.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Insect pests include aphids, caterpillars, woodborers, and Madrone psyllid. The trees are susceptible to several fungal infections, which cause leaf diseases, root rot, and crown rot. Pacific madrone is also affected by “sudden oak death” caused by the introduced fungus, Phytophthora.

Summary_Public: Deciduous Shrub up to 1.5 m height; small leaves, deep pink flowers, small oblong sweet bald hips without flower parts, soft prickles. Dry to moist open forests, forest edges, thickets and clearings in the lowland and montane zones; common in S BC south of about 53°N.
Description_Botanical: Flowers bloom May through July, are usually solitary and small, with deep pink to light-to-dark pink, broadly notched petals 10–15 mm long. A low to medium deciduous shrub, 0.3-1.5 m tall (up to 1.5 m / 0.3–1.2 m), spreading via extensive rhizomes and occasionally forming thickets, with spindly, erect to spreading stems. Low to medium shrub, 0.3-1.5 m tall; stems spindly, erect to spreading, usually bristly with numerous soft, straight prickles all about the same size, occasionally unarmed especially on younger stems, which are often stalked-glandular; mature stems greyish-brown. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, and odd-pinnately compound, with the leaf-stalk and axis somewhat stalked-glandular.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous Shrub up to 1.5 m height; small leaves, deep pink flowers, small oblong sweet bald hips without flower parts, soft prickles. A low to medium deciduous shrub, 0.3-1.5 m tall (up to 1.5 m / 0.3–1.2 m), spreading via extensive rhizomes and occasionally forming thickets, with spindly, erect to spreading stems.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, odd-pinnately compound, the leaf-stalk and axis somewhat stalked-glandular; leaflets 5, 7 or 9, elliptic, 1-4 cm long, double-toothed with gland-tipped teeth, otherwise smooth; stipules glandular and usually blunt-toothed.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of usually single, occasionally 2 to 3, stalked flowers at the ends of lateral branchlets, the stalks bristly-glandular; corollas pale pink to rose, bowl- to saucer-shaped, small (2-3.5 cm across), the petals 5, 10-15 mm long; calyces 5-lobed, the lobes 5-12 mm long, egg-shaped to triangular tapering to a tail-like sharp tip, smooth or occasionally glandular on the back, deciduous; ovaries superior but enclosed in the urn-shaped floral tube (hypanthium); stamens numerous.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 2-3.5 cm across; 10-15 mm long; 5-12 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes, few to about 12, smooth except for a few long hairs at the tip, enclosed by the fleshy hypanthium, which ripens into an orange to scarlet, pear-shaped to ellipsoid hip 6-10 mm long, the neck and calyx-lobes deciduous.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Xwiinlhp is the more subtle of the wild roses, with smaller leaves, thorns and hips. The thorns are much more numerous but are not as solid and as well established as qel’qulhp. Xwiinlhp is found in a wide range of habitats.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Dry to mesic; 5 - 7 pH; tolerates clay but prefers moist loamy soil. It is adapted to soils with medium texture, moderate fertility, and neutral pH (USDA NRCS, 2012). It can tolerate a moderate level of salinity.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Dry to moist open forests, forest edges, thickets and clearings in the lowland and montane zones; common in S BC south of about 53°N. It is common in southern British Columbia south of approximately 53°N and extends south to California, Montana, and Idaho. Rosa gymnocarpa grows as an understory plant in dry and moist forest communities, including Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), western white pine (Pinus monticola), mountain hemlock (Tsuga mertensiana), Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis), larch (Larix spp.), lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), redwood (Sequoia sempervirens), sagebrush (Artemisia spp.), pinyon pine (Pinus spp.), and juniper (Juniperus spp.) (Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture, 2012). It is often found in association with salal (Gaultheria shallon), oceanspray (Holodiscus discolor), Oregon grape (Mahonia nervosa), creeping Oregon grape (Mahonia repens), ninebark (Physocarpus malvaceus), big thimbleberry (Rubus parviflorus), and huckleberry (Vaccinium membranaceum) (Reed, 1993).

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Rosa gymnocarpa plants are sexually reproductive after 3 to 5 years of growth (Hungerford, 1957 as cited by Reed, 1993). Seed is obtained by collecting rose hips after they turn a bright red color. The seeds can be removed from the hip flesh by macerating the hips in water and allowing the debris to float to the surface.
Stratification_Dormancy: Dried seeds have a hard seed coat and require a cold moist stratification period of 90 days to improve germination (Mirov and Kraebel, 1939). Dried seed needs a cold stratification period of 90 days for optimal germination; stratification.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Freshly cleaned dwarf rose seed can be sown in the field by broadcasting or drilling ¼ to ¾ inch deep, and covering with firm soil and mulch. Dried seed needs a cold stratification period of 90 days for optimal germination.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: For propagating by seed: 3 mos. stratification; preceding this by 2-3 mos. warm stratification may improve germination (USDA Forest Service 1974).

Description_Botanical: Striking native carrot family species (20-80 cm) with globe-shaped yellow flowers on long petioles. This species has a wide range of habitats that it will thrive in, from seasonally wet meadows to coastal sand ecosystems. A striking native carrot family (Apiaceae) species possessing a strong pleasant smell, thriving in habitats ranging from seasonally wet meadows to coastal sand ecosystems, and serving as a prized caterpillar-feeding habitat for Anise Swallowtails. Barestem biscuitroot is a stout, glabrous, and strongly glaucous perennial forb arising from a stout taproot, reaching a mature height of 20 to 90 cm.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Barestem biscuitroot is a stout, glabrous, and strongly glaucous perennial forb arising from a stout taproot, reaching a mature height of 20 to 90 cm.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Mostly basal, large, compound, 1-3 times divided; ultimate segments 3-30, entire or shallowly toothed, 2-9 cm long, 10-60 (rarely 4) mm wide, veiny, often stalked.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: The inflorescence is a compound umbel bearing small yellow flowers on stalks of unequal length, completely lacking involucels.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Oblong to elliptic, 7-15 mm long, sometimes narrowed to a beaklike tip; ribs distinct with wings up to 1/2 the width of the body.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Indian consumption plant, usually known only by its Hul’q’umi’num’ name, is a small herb that grows in dry, open, often pebbly to sandy areas. It has yellow flowers that develop into small, flat fruits that resemble rolled oats and are usually thought of as “seeds”. These “seeds” often are used as medicine for respiratory conditions and are highly valued.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurring in dry open sites, meadows, beaches, and rocky slopes, as well as dry rocky or grassy slopes and open woods in the lowland and steppe zones. Locally common on southeastern Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, and rare eastward in southern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Alberta and south to Utah and California. Habitats further include bluffs and ocean frontage. Barestem biscuitroot is found in dry, open to sparsely wooded places in lowlands to middle elevations (Cronquist et al 1997), often growing in sagebrush, pinyon-juniper, ponderosa pine, and mountain brush communities in the Intermountain West (Welsh et al 2003).

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Flowering occurs from April to June and seed is typically harvested in mid July. Bartow (2003) achieved 90% germination from seed sown into conetainers, bagged in polyethylene and put in a cooler at (2–4°C) for 6 weeks.
Stratification_Dormancy: A cold-moist stratification is necessary for germination (Russell 2011). Cold stratification required; sow seeds in fall for spring germination with cold stratification.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Biscuitroot species can be broadcast or drill seeded. Optimal establishment results from dormant fall seedings into a firm, weed-free seed bed. Seed should be placed at a depth of 0.6 to 1.2 cm and packed to ensure good seed to soil contact.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: A cold-moist stratification is necessary for germination.
Nursery_Availability: Seed of barestem biscuitroot is available in limited quantities on the commercial market. Larger quantities of seed can be grown on a contract basis (Walker and Shaw 2005).

Ethno_Culinary_Food: Roots, young leaves, and flavorful seeds eaten. It was eaten raw and used like celery by the Okanagon, Atsugewi and Paiute tribes. Young leaves and shoots gathered in spring, eaten raw or cooked as a potherb, or stored (frozen, jarred, dried).
Ethno_Medicinal: It was used as a cold remedy or cough medicine by the Quw'utsun' (Cowichan), Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl), Ditidaht (Nitinaht), W̱SÁNEĆ (Saanich) and Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribes. Root, bark, fruit, or leaf poultices used for bruises, cuts, and boils (Salish). Seeds soaked and boiled into tea for sore throats, colds, stomach problems, and headaches (W̱SÁNEĆ (Saanich), Lekwungen (Songish), Quw'utsun' (Cowichan)).
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Embedded in traditions, narratives, ceremonies, dances, songs, and discourse. Spiritual and sacred role.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: No significant pest or disease problems are reported for barestem biscuitroot. Barestem biscuitroot is native to western North America and presents minimal weediness or ecological concern.

Summary_Public: Native, long-lived medium to large deciduous tree to 30 m tall; simple opposite leaves 10-30 cm wide; yellow fragrant flowers in nodding racemes; paired brown winged seeds with stiff hair. Thriving in forests, riparian areas, and woodlands, as well as moist to mesic forests and open slopes in the lowland and montane zones, this species is common in southwestern British Columbia west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains and extends south to California, with disjunct populations in ID.
Description_Botanical: This majestic deciduous tree can reach a towering height of 30 meters, its greenish bark smoothing with age and eventually giving way to a greyish-brown, textured surface often adorned with lichens and mosses. Its large, deeply lobed leaves, spanning 10-30 cm in width, create a lush canopy that transitions to a vibrant yellow in autumn. The tree produces an abundance of greenish-white flowers, followed by distinctive yellowish-brown, hairy winged fruits arranged in a V-shape. This magnificent tree is a commanding presence in any landscape, offering beauty and grandeur throughout the seasons.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: This majestic deciduous tree can reach a towering height of 30 meters, its greenish bark smoothing with age and eventually giving way to a greyish-brown, textured surface often adorned with lichens and mosses.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, 10-30 cm wide, deeply 5-lobed, tips abruptly sharp-pointed, dark green above and paler green below, turning yellow in fall, stalks with milky juice when cut.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: The inflorescence is racemose, bearing male and female flowers on the same plant in numerous short stalks that appear with or before the leaves; the petals are greenish-white.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Winged, in pairs, 3-6 cm long, yellowish-brown, hairy, pairs attached in a V-shape.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Long-lived perennial canopy tree establishing deeply within 2–3 growing seasons.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Ts’alhulhp (Bigleaf Maple) is among the first hardwood trees to sprout and grow in moist coastal forests and along streams. Two names are used: ts’alhulhp is the general name and q’um’-unulhp refers to straight, flexible trees ideal for carving paddles (sq’umul).
Spread_Behavior: Woody crown and lateral root system
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Deep lateral / Taproot / Woody burl); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Light_Tags: Full Sun; Part Shade; Full Shade
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Acer macrophyllum generally occurs in coarse, gravelly, dry to moist sites, often mixed with red alder, western redcedar, Douglas fir, and western hemlock. It attains its best development near borders of foothills, low mountain streams, and in alluvial river bottoms.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Thriving in forests, riparian areas, and woodlands, as well as moist to mesic forests and open slopes in the lowland and montane zones, this species is common in southwestern British Columbia west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains and extends south to California, with disjunct populations in ID. The Coast region spans from southeastern Alaska through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada to California, inhabiting coarse, gravelly dry or moist sites, foothills, streams, and river bottoms. Acer macrophyllum is distributed around the coast region of southeastern Alaska, on the west side of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada from British Columbia through most of California.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: Maple keys may be one of the most identifiable fruits in our region with each bearing two seeds and the winged fruits designed to travel through the air like a helicopter. The large seeds don't need to be extracted ahead of sowing, Instead, you can snap the "wing" off to plant the seed still wrapped in the protective coating. At our nursery, we sow them soon after they fall to the ground through fall, but many stay attached directly to the trees into winter.

Tree preparations used for sore throats and rubbed on young men's faces to stop thick whisker growth (W̱SÁNEĆ (Saanich)).
Ethno_Material_Tech: A fiber was obtained from the inner bark and used in making ropes, baskets, and crude dresses. Tough, hard wood carved into canoe paddles ("paddle tree"), spindle whorls, bowls, dishes, masks, and tools. Inner bark used for baskets, rope, and whisks.

Summary_Public: A large deciduous shrub up to 5 m tall featuring yellow tubular flowers, red involucral bracts, and shiny paired black fruits. Found in riparian areas, thickets, and woodlands, as well as moist forests and thickets in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common in British Columbia south of 58°N; north to the Yukon Territory, east to Quebec, and south to Michigan, Wisconsin, New Mexico, California, and Mexico; inhabiting riparian areas, thickets, and woodlands.
Description_Botanical: Yellow tubular flowers on this large deciduous shrub attract bees and hummingbirds. The involucral bracts are a showy red and have inspired the species name and shiny black fruits in pairs are savoured by waxwings and other birds, but not fit for human consumption. A large deciduous shrub up to 5 m tall featuring yellow tubular flowers, red involucral bracts, and shiny paired black fruits.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A large deciduous shrub up to 5 m tall featuring yellow tubular flowers, red involucral bracts, and shiny paired black fruits.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, short-stalked, elliptic to oblanceolate or broadly lanceolate, 3-16 cm long, 2-8 cm wide, entire, rounded or tapered at base, abruptly sharp-pointed at tip, pale and glabrous or somewhat hairy beneath.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of short-stalked flower pairs subtended by large involucres 2-4 cm across consisting of 2 pairs of fused bracts, borne on stalks 1-4 cm long in leaf axils; corollas tubular bell-shaped, yellow, 1-2 cm long, glandular-hairy externally, scarcely 2-lipped with 5 roughly equal lobes above; corolla tubes bearing short, thick spurs at the bases.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 2-4 cm across; 1-4 cm long; 1-2 cm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berries, shiny black, 0.8-1.2 cm across, paired, loosely surrounded while young by paired bracts, which darken and redden (to purplish-maroon) as they recurve from the maturing fruits.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Distinctive winter bark and stem colour provide strong cold-season architectural interest.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Twinberry honeysuckle is typically found in moist forests, clearings, riparian habitats, swamps and thickets (MacKinnon, Pojar & Coupe′ 1992). It prefers a good moist soil but can succeed in any fertile soil.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in riparian areas, thickets, and woodlands, as well as moist forests and thickets in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common in British Columbia south of 58°N; north to the Yukon Territory, east to Quebec, and south to Michigan, Wisconsin, New Mexico, California, and Mexico; inhabiting riparian areas, thickets, and woodlands. Lonicera involucrata is widely distributed across North America from Quebec westward to Alaska and British Columbia and southward into California, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona (McMinn 1939).

Birds_Interactions: Attracts hummingbirds, waxwings, and other birds.
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Black Bears. Berries eaten by bears (inedible/toxic to humans).
Stratification_Dormancy: Seed is obtained by collecting the ripe berries from July through September then macerating the fruit to separate the seed from the pulp. The seed should be cold moist stratified ( moist chilled at 1–2°C) for 30 to 90 days in order to overcome embryo dormancy and improve germination.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Sow the seeds as soon as they are ripe in a cold frame. When the seedlings are large enough, plant them directly into their permanent positions in late spring or early summer.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Lonicera involucrata seeds should be collected from isolated plants and extracted by maceration in water.
Nursery_Availability: Somewhat available from native plant nurseries.
Nursery_Stock_Format: 4-inch to 2-gal Container; Bare-root; Live Stakes; Forestry Plugs; Seed
Edible_Parts_Flavor: Inedible / Toxic.
Ethno_Medicinal: A decoction of the bark has been applied to a woman’s breasts to encourage milk flow. An infusion was used to treat chest and stomach complaints and to cleanse the body. The Dakelh (Carrier) boiled the leaves and used the liquid to bathe sore eyes, or applied the crushed leaves as a poultice to open sores.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Berries used as dye. The Quileute and Kwakwaka’wakw people used these berries as a black pigment. The Haida rubbed the berries on the scalp to prevent hair from turning gray.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Keep showy fruits out of reach of young children; mildly irritating if ingested in quantity.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Twinberry honeysuckle berries has been noted as poisonous. Since the European species of honeysuckle are regarded as emetic and cathartic, they are better avoided in favor of something less dubious. Berries regarded as inedible or toxic by humans ("raven's berry", "monster's fruit").

Summary_Public: Perennial Grass, 30-120 cm height, blueish-green foliage and spike-like flowers. Inhabiting meadows and woodlands, as well as moist to dry slopes and open forests in lowland, montane, and subalpine zones.
Description_Botanical: Blue wildrye is a large perennial bunchgrass with an upright growth habit, featuring bluish-green foliage, spike-like flowers, and reaching heights of 30-180 cm with just a few stems per plant. Perennial, bluish, tufted grass from fibrous roots or short rhizomes; stems 30-180 cm tall, erect or slightly decumbent at the base, the nodes exposed and often covered with dense short hairs. Sheaths are smooth to rough, white-hairy close to the base, and often purplish at the stem-base. Leaf blades are lax, flat or slightly in-rolled, bluish-green with a white waxy coating, measuring 4-13 mm wide (ranging from 4-12 mm or 5–13 mm), rough on the nerves, sometimes hairy, and feature ear-shaped lobes up to 2.5 mm long at the leaf-bases that are often purple.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Blue wildrye is a large perennial bunchgrass with an upright growth habit, featuring bluish-green foliage, spike-like flowers, and reaching heights of 30-180 cm with just a few stems per plant. The stems are erect or slightly decumbent at the base, displaying exposed nodes often covered with dense short hairs.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Sheaths smooth to rough, white-hairy close to the base, often purplish at the stem-base; blades 4-13 mm wide, lax, flat or slightly in-rolled, bluish-green, rough on the nerves, sometimes hairy, ear-shaped lobes at the leaf-bases up to 2.5 mm long, often purple; ligules up to 1 mm long, entire or ragged.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 4-13 mm wide; 2.5 mm long; 1 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a spike 5-21 cm long, 0.5-2 cm wide, erect to slightly nodding, rarely pendent, (1) 2 to 3 spikelets per node; spikelets 8-25 mm long, purplish, with bases often overlapping, with 2 to 4 (6) fertile florets; glumes 9-14 mm long, unawned or awned, the awns 1-5 mm long; lemmas 9-14 mm long, smooth to short-hairy at least on the nerves, the awns 1-25 mm long, straight to slightly curved; anthers 1.5-3.5 mm long. Spikelets measure 8-25 mm long, are purplish with bases frequently overlapping, and contain 2 to 4 (6) fertile florets.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 5-21 cm long; 0.5-2 cm wide; 8-25 mm long; 9-14 mm long; 1-5 mm long
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Seeds mature in late spring to summer; can be collected for 2-7 weeks depending on ecotype and growing conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Semi-deciduous
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic but vigorous clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); forms thickets that outcompete slow-establishing forbs—allow generous spacing or use root barriers in tight borders.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Clay; Rocky / Shallow
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: It tolerates wide variations in soil and weather conditions, though grows best in good soils. It prefers moisture but tolerates drought and is usually more drought-tolerant than meadow barley (Hordeum brachyantherum) and California brome (Bromus carinatus).
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting meadows and woodlands, as well as moist to dry slopes and open forests in lowland, montane, and subalpine zones. Subspecies glaucus is common in southern British Columbia and less frequent north of 55°N, while subspecies virescens is infrequent in coastal British Columbia and rare east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains. Geographically, ssp. glaucus ranges north to southeastern Alaska and Yukon Territory, east to Ontario, and south to New York, Illinois, Arkansas, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California; ssp. virescens ranges south to California. Thriving in meadows and woodlands at elevations of 0–2861 m in California, across clay, silt, loam, sand, bedrock, and rocky soils with a pH of 4.9-8.3, exhibiting moderate salinity tolerance.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Flowering occurs in the late spring typically April to May in California. Further north, flowering typically occurs in June and July. Adequate moisture will promote good seed set, but even under adverse conditions of low moisture, seed will be produced in most years.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Seed is up to 8mm long, germinates easily, and has good seedling vigor. There are approximately 134,000 seeds/lb, and if planted at a rate of 1 lb./acre, there would be approximately 3 seeds/square feet.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: ‘Mariposa’ (CA) - Collected from a native stand near Mariposa, California at an elevation of 183 m above sea level. ‘Mariposa’ has shown a preference for loam to clay loam soils. It can persist on moderately deep road cut slopes.
Pruning_Management: Forage quality can be excellent when cut before the boot stage. It will not survive if grazed too heavily. Likewise, it is generally tolerant of mowing if not cut too short.
Nursery_Availability: It is best grown for seed on well to moderately well drained, moist, medium textured soils. It establishes rapidly from seed but is short-lived. The species may also be less competitive with recently planted forest tree seedlings compared to certain introduced grasses. It establishes rapidly from seed but is relatively short-lived.

Ethno_Material_Tech: It is less desirable for basketry as the nodes are thick, but this does not exclude its use in some baskets.

Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Perennial Rush, 30-50 cm height with round leaves, bracts, and brown flowers. Found in meadows and wetlands, specifically wet meadows and lakeshores in the lowland zone; infrequent in southwestern British Columbia and rare in southeastern British Columbia, ranging south to California.
Description_Botanical: At first glance, you might mistakenly think you're looking at the equally distinctive Dagger-leaf Rush. At closer inspection, the round leaves and bracts are a giveaway that you are looking at Bolander's Rush. This rush prefers wet soils in full sun. A rhizomatous perennial rush forming loose tufts from short rhizomes, 30-50 cm in height, with erect stems 40-75 cm tall.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: This rush prefers wet soils in full sun. A rhizomatous perennial rush forming loose tufts from short rhizomes, 30-50 cm in height, with erect stems 40-75 cm tall.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Both basal and throughout the stem, nearly circular in cross-section, tapered, the early leaves stiff, with prominent complete cross-walls; sheaths long, open with prominent, cylindrical, ear-shaped lobes.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence terminal, consisting of 1 to 5 globe-shaped heads that are many-flowered; perianth segments deep brown, 3-3.5 mm long, pointed, narrowly short-awned, the inner about the same length as the outer; stamens 3; anthers 0.7 mm long, shorter than the filaments.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, egg-shaped to cylindrical, abruptly narrowed (almost rounded), pointed, slightly shorter than the perianth segments; seeds barrel-like, about 0.4 mm long, lacking tail-like appendages.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic but vigorous clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); forms thickets that outcompete slow-establishing forbs—allow generous spacing or use root barriers in tight borders.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Wet Soil. Wet meadows, marshes, and stream margins. Moist to wet; wet soils.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Typically Non-Mycorrhizal or facultatively weakly AM (specialized root hairs or wetland nutrient uptake)
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in meadows and wetlands, specifically wet meadows and lakeshores in the lowland zone; infrequent in southwestern British Columbia and rare in southeastern British Columbia, ranging south to California.

Summary_Public: A low, mat-forming succulent perennial herb from a fibrous root, growing up to 15 cm tall with prostrate, fleshy, subglobose to rounded stem segments 2-5 cm long that readily detach; areoles are coarsely white-woolly with a few yellowish, spiny bristles and 2-7 strongly barbed, straight, yellowish to brownish spines 1-3 cm long, and bear showy, tissue paper-like yellow flowers. Summary_Public: Tall, robust native perennial meadow grass (30-100 cm) with soft broad foliage often showing purple hues. Found in deeper soil meadows and woodlands, growing in open woods and forests, shrublands, grasslands, meadows, and waste places.
Description_Botanical: Tall, robust native perennial meadow grass (30-100 cm) with soft broad foliage often showing purple hues. California brome is a native, cool-season perennial bunchgrass that lives 3 to 5 years, growing 60 to 120 cm tall (overall foliage range 30-100 cm). It features deep, widespread, quickly growing fibrous roots. Young plants are erect, but older stems grow along the ground with only the apical tips remaining erect (decumbent).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: California brome is a native, cool-season perennial bunchgrass that lives 3 to 5 years, growing 60 to 120 cm tall (overall foliage range 30-100 cm).
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: California brome grows well in a variety of soils including poorly drained types. It is most abundant in moderately moist, well-developed, deep, medium-textured soils. It tolerates soils in the pH range of 5.5 to 8.0.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in deeper soil meadows and woodlands, growing in open woods and forests, shrublands, grasslands, meadows, and waste places. It is closely associated with pine dropseed, bracken fern, corn lily, dwarf purple monkey flower, mountain muhly, and Rocky Mountain iris, and shares dominance in plant communities such as coastal prairie, northern coastal scrub, sagebrush steppes, aspen forests, oak woodlands, and Douglas-fir forests. Its distribution extends from Alaska east to Ontario and south to Illinois, Texas, California, and northern Mexico, being native from the Pacific Coast to the Rocky Mountains and casually introduced in the Great Plains. California brome grows in open woods and forests, shrublands, grasslands, meadows, and waste places.

Pruning_Management: Although fair control of California brome by trifluralin and pronamide has been documented, it does not respond to most herbicides. Cattle are more likely to overgraze than trample the plants.

Stratification_Dormancy: Determine viability and then fall (Sept-Oct) sown or cold, moist stratified for 30-120 days. Dehulling or scarification may also be needed to break dormancy. As with sowing California oatgrass for revegetation and other uses, planting new fields for agronomic seed increase and producing container nursery stock from seed may be confounded by poor or delayed germination due to seed dormancy. If dormancy is known or suspected, seed should have a TZ test to determine viability and then fall (Sept-Oct) sown or cold, moist stratified for 30-120 days.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Establishment of California oatgrass from seed can be problematic as the result of delayed germination and variable seed dormancy, as well as moderately slow seedling development combined with early competition from other species. Difficulties with reseeding Danthonia species were reported in the early to mid 1900’s when interest grew in reintroducing native perennial grasses on depleted or weedy grazing lands in California. Seed dormancy and germination: Evidence suggests the variable seed dormancy in California oatgrass is the result of either single or double (combined) dormancy.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: In 2000, the NRCS Plant Materials Center at Corvallis, Oregon, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Oregon Agricultural Experiment Station released Baskett Slough Germplasm California oatgrass, a selected class pre-variety (Darris and Lambert, 2000). The origin of this “natural” germplasm is the Baskett Slough National Wildlife Refuge in Polk County, Oregon.
Pruning_Management: Swards of native perennial grasses or grass-forb meadows containing California oatgrass can be improved and maintained with properly timed mowing, grazing, burning, herbicide applications, or combinations thereof. In California, the Pacific Northwest, and possibly other regions, doing nothing is often not an option in the long run because of ongoing and sometimes increasing competition from weedy annuals or invasive perennials, and the spread of shrubs or trees previously controlled or excluded by fire (Stromberg and Kephart 2003). Mowing is a viable option for controlling certain annual and perennial weeds as well as undesirable woody plants. For example, invasive perennial grasses such as tall oatgrass (Arrhenatherum elatius) are replacing native species on grasslands targeted for habitat conservation.
Nursery_Availability: Seed is commercially available. Several other source identified populations of California oatgrass are periodically grown and sold as seed in Oregon and California. Native plant nurseries regularly produce plants of known origin in plugs and pots. Population genetics and seed transfer: Understanding patterns of genetic variation in California oatgrass across the landscape provides insight into adaptation and can help guide seed movement of populations within and among regions. In an analysis of data from a common garden study containing 66 populations (accessions) primarily from western Oregon and southwest Washington, plant vigor and seed abundance significantly correlated with winter precipitation, winter minimum temperature, and summer maximum temperature. However, for the subset of 33 Willamette Valley accessions, there were no significant correlations suggesting this region could be treated as a single seed zone for the species (Johnson undated). This makes it more likely for California oatgrass to have genetically distinct populations resulting in the need for smaller seed transfer zones compared to tree species. Knapp and Rice also noted seedlings from one population with narrower leaves came from a unique vernal pool location suggesting that restorationists should consider localized selection pressures when considering seed sources for a planting.

Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Few pest problems for California oatgrass have been recorded. The species can be infected by a nematode (Cynipanguina danthoniae) that causes leaf galls. Amme (1986) indicated that California oatgrass, along with other native grasses tested, appeared disease resistant during germination, transplanting, and growth in liners.

Summary_Public: Perennial Forb from bulb, 20-60 cm height with bell-shaped brownish-purple/yellowish-green mottled flowers; root bulblets look like rice; flowers smell like raw meat. Found in meadows and woodlands; inhabiting dry to mesic grassy bluffs, meadows, and open forests in the lowland and steppe to lower subalpine zones; common on southeastern Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, and inland to south-central British Columbia south of 52°N; ranging south to Idaho and California.
Description_Botanical: Belonging to the lily family (Liliaceae), the nodding flowers are bell-shaped to bowl-shaped, possessing a scent like raw meat and variable petals/six tepals ranging from brownish-purple mottled with greenish-yellow to yellowish-green mottled with purple (or brown-mottled with green or yellow). A perennial herb and forb growing from a bulb composed of a few larger, fleshy scales and numerous small, rice-grain bulblets (with root bulblets resembling rice), reaching 20-80 cm tall (or 20-60 cm height, and 20-50 cm in chocolate lily). Perennial herb from a bulb of a few larger, fleshy scales and numerous small, rice-grain bulblets; stems 20-80 cm tall, slender to sturdy, smooth. Leaves occur usually in 1 or 2 whorls of 3 to 5 (or 1-3 whorls of 5-11) on the stem, scattered and alternate above, narrowly lanceolate to lance-egg-shaped, measuring 5-10 (15) cm long and 0.5-3 cm wide, and smooth.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A perennial herb and forb growing from a bulb composed of a few larger, fleshy scales and numerous small, rice-grain bulblets (with root bulblets resembling rice), reaching 20-80 cm tall (or 20-60 cm height, and 20-50 cm in chocolate lily).
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Usually in 1 or 2 whorls of 3 to 5 on the stem, scattered and alternate above, narrowly lanceolate to lance-egg-shaped, 5-10 (15) cm long, 0.5-3 cm wide, smooth.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a single nodding flower, or 2 to 5 relatively long-stalked flowers in a terminal cluster; flowers variably brownish-purple mottled with greenish-yellow, to yellowish-green mottled purple, broadly bell-shaped, of 6 similar, distinct tepals, the tepals oblong to egg-shaped, 2-4 cm long, 1-2 cm wide, with a long, yellowish-green nectar gland on inner surface near the base; stamens 6; pistil 1, 3-chambered.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, erect, cylindric-egg-shaped, 6-angled, winged on the angles, 2 cm long; seeds numerous, flattened.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Emerges winter-to-spring before retreating into summer dormancy.
Spread_Behavior: Slowly multiplying clump from underground bulbs or corms
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Bulb / Corm / Tuber); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Moist in spring, dry in summer soils. Dry to mesic soil conditions.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in meadows and woodlands; inhabiting dry to mesic grassy bluffs, meadows, and open forests in the lowland and steppe to lower subalpine zones; common on southeastern Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, and inland to south-central British Columbia south of 52°N; ranging south to Idaho and California. Chocolate lily occurs in open dry woods and meadows from southern coastal British Columbia eastward to the Okanagan in eastern Washington and south to California. In California, chocolate lily occurs commonly in oak or pine scrub and grasslands below 1800 m in the Klamath Ranges, north Coast Ranges, Cascade, northern Sierra Nevada Foothills, San Francisco Bay area (Hickman 1993).

Description_Botanical: A rhizomatous perennial forb standing 50-150 cm in height, characterized by stems, woolly leaves, a branched inflorescence, shiny bracts, glabrous receptacles, and yellowish-green, shiny female (3 to 7) and disk (2 to 8) flowers. The plant arises from a short, stout rhizome with erect, stout, clustered stems 0.5-1.5 m tall. Numerous stem leaves are white- to grey-woolly beneath and green and glabrous or glabrate above, broadly lanceolate to oblanceolate or elliptic, entire, toothed, or coarsely lobed below, measuring 8-15 cm long and 1.5-5 cm wide, and become reduced upwards. Salt tolerant.

Summary_Public: Stoloniferous Perennial Forb (5-20 cm) with shiny evergreen foliage, mat-forming cover, white flowers, creeping runners, and small red or white sweet berries. Thriving on shorelines and beaches, as well as dry to mesic sand dunes and rocky coastal bluffs just above high tide in the lowland zone, this plant is frequent in coastal British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska and south to California, with disjunct populations in South America; additionally found in sunny dry sites below 200 m elevation in dune and grassland communities of coastal California, spanning from Alaska to coastal South America and Hawaii.
Description_Botanical: Shiny evergreen foliage for the salt-spray zone and tasty small red or white berries make this species desirable. Spreads by stolons, for mat-forming cover for coastal rocky slopes and meadows. A stoloniferous perennial forb 5-20 cm tall valued for its shiny evergreen foliage in salt-spray zones and its small, sweet red or white berries. It forms mat-like cover on coastal rocky slopes and meadows via creeping runners.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Spreads by stolons, for mat-forming cover for coastal rocky slopes and meadows.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal in rosettes, palmately compound, on stalks 4-20 cm long; leaflets 3, egg-shaped, short-stalked, 1.5-4 cm long, thick, leathery, the lower surface strongly net-veined, pale and somewhat hairy, the upper surface green, smooth and wrinkled, the margins coarsely toothed with the terminal tooth shorter than its neighbours.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an open cluster of 5 to 15 (20) stalked flowers atop axillary, leafless shoots 3-15 cm long, shorter than to slightly exceeding the leaves; corollas white, 2-4 cm across, the petals 5, egg-shaped to round, 8-16 mm long; calyces silky-hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes (sepals) lanceolate, 6-10 mm long, alternating with elliptic bractlets that are almost as long as the sepals; ovaries superior; stamens about 20.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 3-15 cm long; 2-4 cm across; 8-16 mm long; 6-10 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Strawberries, hemispheric, 1-1.5 cm in diameter, hairy, covered with achenes; achenes about 2 mm long, slightly immersed in the fleshy receptacle.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial groundcover establishing rapidly from runners in 1 growing season.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Year-round evergreen foliage anchors winter garden structure.
Spread_Behavior: Creeping mat spreading via aboveground stolons
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Stoloniferous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Dry to mesic; salt-spray zone. Sandy, well-drained coastal soils. Dry, well-drained soil.

Pruning_Management: Keep the runners pruned back because they can be invasive. It is necessary to divide the patch every three to four years and start a new patch for increased vigor. Younger plants are more vigorous and produce more berries.

Summary_Public: Perennial Forb, 20-60 cm height with purplish-blue (rarely light blue or white) flowers and edible bulb. Inhabiting mesic to vernally moist meadows and grasslands across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; locally frequent on southeastern Vancouver Island (with ssp. azurea rare in peatlands on western Vancouver Island), the Gulf Islands, and southeastern British Columbia; ranging east to Alberta and south to Montana, Idaho, and Washington.
Description_Botanical: A showy perennial wildflower in the Asparagus plant family with purplish-blue flowers (sometimes light blue and occasionally white) and an edible bulb. Yellow, pollen-packed stamens contrast against the colourful tepals and the large, open flowers draw in a rich diversity of pollinators.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Erect, leafless, smooth flowering scapes (20–70 cm tall) arising from an egg-shaped tunicated bulb.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves several to numerous, linear-lanceolate and grass-like, to 50 cm long, 1-3 cm wide, smooth, sheathing at the base, the margins entire; stem leaves lacking.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a terminal raceme of 5 to many, stalked flowers, the stalks 1-2 cm long, spreading in flower, ascending to erect in fruit; flowers pale to deep blue, rarely white, weakly bilaterally symmetric, of 6 similar, distinct tepals, the tepals 15-40 mm long, 2-8 mm wide; stamens 6, anthers yellow to violet; pistil 1, 3-chambered.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 1-2 cm long; 15-40 mm long; 2-8 mm wide
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, egg-shaped to oblong, cross-ridged, 1-2.5 cm long; fruiting stalks shorter than the bracts, ascending to erect, curved in towards stem; seeds several to many, shiny black, 2-4 mm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Bulbous perennial geophyte requiring 3–5 years from seed to reach flowering maturity.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Speenhw was at one time very common in open grasslands and p’hwulhp meadows. Today speenhw is not nearly as common and is found mainly on more remote mountain slopes, p’hwulhp meadows and small pockets of rocky grassland. There are two species: common camas (C. quamash) and giant camas (C. leichtlinii).
Fall_Winter_Interest: Emerges winter-to-spring before retreating into summer dormancy.
Spread_Behavior: Slowly multiplying clump from underground bulbs or corms
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Bulb / Corm / Tuber); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Dry to seasonally wet; shallow dry soils or winter-flooded clay soils. Heavy clay / Seasonally wet clay. Tolerates very dry shallow soils as well as winter flooding in clay soils.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting mesic to vernally moist meadows and grasslands across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; locally frequent on southeastern Vancouver Island (with ssp. azurea rare in peatlands on western Vancouver Island), the Gulf Islands, and southeastern British Columbia; ranging east to Alberta and south to Montana, Idaho, and Washington. Distributed across western North America from British Columbia to California, east to Alberta, Montana, Wyoming, and Utah, occupying mountain grasslands, prairies, wet meadows, and coastal forests from sea level to 2134 m, as well as coastal oak meadows. Rock outcrops. Great camas grows in wet meadows, woods, prairies, moist hillsides, and streamside areas.

Summary_Public: A deciduous, erect, slender shrub up to 1-2 m high, rhizomatous, bearing opposite oval wavy leaves, pink and white bell-shaped hairy flowers, and a dry waxy white spherical non-edible berry (6-12 mm) containing 2 seeds. Occurring in meadows, thickets, wetlands, and woodlands, as well as mesic to dry meadows, disturbed areas, grasslands, shrublands, and forests across the lowland, steppe, and montane zones.
Description_Botanical: A deciduous, erect, slender shrub up to 1-2 m high, rhizomatous, bearing opposite oval wavy leaves, pink and white bell-shaped hairy flowers, and a dry waxy white spherical non-edible berry (6-12 mm) containing 2 seeds. It is a much-branched shrub, often densely colonial from rhizomes, 0.5-3 m tall, with older stems dark greyish-brown with shredding bark, glabrous branchlets, and thin, wiry twigs. Leaves are opposite, on stalks 2-4 mm long, elliptic to oval, 1.5-5 cm long and 1-3.5 cm wide, obtuse at base and tip, with margins entire or occasionally bearing a few wavy teeth; leaves are often larger and irregularly lobed on sterile shoots, and are glabrous above, and glabrous or spreading-hairy beneath.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A deciduous, erect, slender shrub up to 1-2 m high, rhizomatous, bearing opposite oval wavy leaves, pink and white bell-shaped hairy flowers, and a dry waxy white spherical non-edible berry (6-12 mm) containing 2 seeds. It is a much-branched shrub, often densely colonial from rhizomes, 0.5-3 m tall, with older stems dark greyish-brown with shredding bark, glabrous branchlets, and thin, wiry twigs.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, on stalks 2-4 mm long, elliptic to oval, 1.5-5 cm long and 1-3.5 cm wide, obtuse at base and tip, margins entire or occasionally with a few wavy teeth; leaves often larger and irregularly lobed on sterile shoots; glabrous above, glabrous or spreading-hairy beneath.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 2-4 mm long; 1.5-5 cm long; 1-3.5 cm wide
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: The inflorescence consists of short, dense clusters (racemes) of few, short-stalked to nearly sessile flowers situated at the ends of twigs and often also in the upper leaf axils; corollas are widely bell-shaped, 5-7 mm long, and hairy within; petals are pink to whitish, fused at the bases into tubes that flare at the top into 5 lobes which are as long to half as long as the tubes; styles are 2-3 mm long and glabrous; stamens are shorter than the corolla lobes, with anthers 1-1.5 mm long, about as long as the filaments.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 5-7 mm long; 2-3 mm long; 1-1.5 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berrylike drupes, densely clustered, waxy white, ellipsoid or nearly globose, 5-15 mm long; nutlets 2, each enclosing a seed; some fruits persist through the winter.
Discovered_Drive_Details: P’up’q’uyas’ulhp (Common Snowberry) is a common deciduous shrub found in open forests, rocky slopes, and streambanks. Its white spongy berries persist on the bare twigs through winter; while toxic to eat in quantity, the berries and leaves were traditionally rubbed on the skin for sores and burns.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Light_Tags: Full Sun; Part Shade; Full Shade
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Clay; Rocky / Shallow
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Symphoricarpos albus is found along stream banks, in swampy thickets, moist clearings and open forests at sea level to middle elevations MacKinnon 1994. It tolerates soil types but grows best in heavy clay soils.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurring in meadows, thickets, wetlands, and woodlands, as well as mesic to dry meadows, disturbed areas, grasslands, shrublands, and forests across the lowland, steppe, and montane zones. Extremely common in southern British Columbia, common in central British Columbia, and infrequent northward; extending north to the Northwest Territories, east to Quebec, and south to Nebraska, Virginia, Colorado, and California. Habitat includes bushy areas, open woodland, valley slopes, grasslands, ravines, and disturbed ground in rocky or coarse soils under wet to dry conditions, mild acid to alkaline pH, and moderate salinity (Alberta, southeastern Alaska to Quebec, south to California, Virginia). Snowberry inhabits slopes and valley bottoms of the foothills of the Coast Ranges, the Sierra Nevada, and the mountains of southern California (McMinn 1939), extending northward to British Columbia and eastward to Pennsylvania and the New England states.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: Symphoricarpos albus seeds are best sown in the fall after maturity. When the seedlings are large enough to handle, place them into individual pots and grow them in the greenhouse for their first winter.

Ethno_Medicinal: One or two of the berries were eaten by the Stl’atl’imx to settle the stomach after too much fatty food. An infusion of the fruit was used as eyewash for sore eyes and the berries were rubbed on the skin as treatment for burns, rashes, and sores. Fruits crushed or boiled to make a wash for sore eyes. A tea made from the roots of this species was used to clear up afterbirth. Wash used for skin rashes or mixed with other plants for venereal disease tea.

Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Saponin is much more toxic to some creatures, such as fish, if eaten in large quantities. Snowberry fruit contains low concentrations of a bitter principle, saponin, which foams in water. It is very poorly absorbed by the body and can be broken down by thoroughly cooking the fruit.

Summary_Public: Large robust hairy perennial 1-2 m tall with hollow single stem from stout roots; strong pungent odor; large compound leaves up to 40 cm across (immature form single-leaved); flat umbel of small white flowers; heart-shaped winged seeds. Large Perennial Forb, 1-2 m height with a large umbel of small white flowers, hollow stems, and solid leaf stalks.
Description_Botanical: Large, striking plant with a large umbel of small white flowers that pollinators enjoy in both full sun and partial shade. Heracleum maximum, commonly known as cow parsnip or hogweed, is a member of the carrot family (Apiaceae). It is a large, striking, biennial or short-lived perennial herb native to North America, growing 1-2 m (or 1-3 m / 0.9–3 m) tall from a fleshy taproot or stout cluster of fibrous roots. Stems are single, hollow, deeply ridged, light green, moderately to very pubescent (lanate or woolly) with spreading white hairs (trichomes), and produce a strong, pungent odor.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Large robust hairy perennial 1-2 m tall with hollow single stem from stout roots. Large Perennial Forb, 1-2 m height with a large umbel of small white flowers, hollow stems, and solid leaf stalks.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Leaves with widely sheathing petioles 10-40 cm long, upper sheaths enlarged, bladeless, blade 20-50 cm wide, round to kidney-shaped, leaflets 3, 10-40 cm wide, ovate to round, lobed or toothed, usually hairy.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 10-40 cm long; 20-50 cm wide; 10-40 cm wide
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence usually 10-20 cm in diameter, woolly or long-hairy, peduncle 5-20 cm long, involucre bracts 5-10, deciduous, narrow, 5-20 mm long, involucel bractlets similar to involucre bracts, rays 15-30, 5-10 cm long. Petals obovate, white.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 10-20 cm; 5-20 cm long; 5-20 mm long; 5-10 cm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Fruit 8-12 mm long, obovate to heart-shaped, narrowed toward base, flat, winged, glabrous or hairy.
Discovered_Drive_Details: It establishes quickly by seed and readily reseeds, making it a good choice for short and long-term revegetation projects (Esser, 1995).
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water. (Wetland status: FAC.)
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Clay; Rich / Organic
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Cow parsnip is found in a variety of moist soils. It often grows in loamy to sandy loam soils but also occurs in clay and gravelly soil. It grows best in partly shady locations but can withstand full sun provided soil conditions are moist and loamy.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabits meadows, thickets, and woodlands, as well as wet to moist areas from the lowland to the alpine zone. It is common throughout British Columbia, exhibiting an amphiberingian distribution extending east to Newfoundland and south to Georgia, New Mexico, and California, with occurrences also in East Asia. Habitats include stream banks, moist slopes, clearings, marshes, meadows, thickets, roadsides, and shaded riparian zones. Cow parsnip grows in partially shaded, wet to somewhat moist environments including forest edges, openings, floodplains, wet meadows, thickets, and streambanks (Reznicek et al., 2011).

Erosion_Slope_Control: Erosion Control: The fleshy roots of cow parsnip can be used for erosion control in areas that are gently sloped (Dittberner & Olson, 1983). It establishes quickly by seed and readily reseeds, making it a good choice for short and long-term revegetation projects (Esser, 1995; Dittberner & Olson, 1983).
Foot_Traffic_Lawn_Use: Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.
Pollinators: Bumblebees; Native Bees; Butterflies; Moths; Flies; Wasps
Common_Bee_Visitors: Bumblebees (Bombus occidentalis, B. vosnesenskii, B. mixtus); Mason & Orchard Bees (Osmia lignaria, Osmia spp.); Mining & Digger Bees (Andrena spp., Colletes spp.)

Host_Moths_Scientific: Papaipema insulidens; Agrotis vetusta; Anagrapha falcifera
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Elk, Black Bears, Deer-resistant. Succulent stems and flower heads eaten by elk and bears; deer-resistant.
Seed_Collection_Harvest: Cow parsnip seed is hand-collected when the fruit turns brown. Dried seed is estimated to be viable for up to three years when stored at 1–3°C (Luna et al., 2008).
Stratification_Dormancy: The water should be changed daily and followed by a 100-day cold-moist stratification period (Luna et al., 2008; moisture should be maintained), before undergoing a second 100-day cold-moist stratification; germination will not take place between the first and second cold moist stratification period. Cow parsnip will not germinate unless its double dormancy is broken.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Cow parsnip can be broadcast or drilled at 1.1–2.2 kg/ha in the fall (Esser, 1995; Horton, 1994). Sow in fall for spring germination.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are currently no named or improved cultivars.
Pruning_Management: Cow parsnip needs little care. If plants begin to grow in areas where it is not wanted, it is removable by hand.
Nursery_Availability: Cow parsnip seed is available for purchase through many native seed companies.
Nursery_Stock_Format: Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS)
Edible_Parts_Flavor: Young stalks/leaf stems (ya:la') peeled and eaten raw/cooked ('native rhubarb') (caution: juice causes UV-amplified skin blistering); Hollow stems and leaf stalks (ya:la') peeled and eaten (caution: juice causes skin blistering).
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Young (peeled) stems and leaves edible. Strongly flavored root edible. Emerging leaf and flower buds were cooked and used in stews.
Ethno_Medicinal: Cow parsnip is still used for food and traditional medicine by American Indians. Leaves, stems, and roots were used in teas, poultices, and powders to treat boils, warts, swelling, and bruising. Ground into a poultice for bruises and cuts.
Ethno_Material_Tech: The roots were used to dye fibers yellow. Root yellow dye. Americans Indians used cow parsnip for food, medicine, and tools.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Skin-blistering sap hazard for children and pets brushing foliage in sunlight.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Sap contains furanocoumarins causing severe phytophotodermatitis blisters on sun-exposed skin; wear gloves and wash exposed skin promptly. Peeling outer skin required before cooking young stems. If skin is exposed to the sap of cow parsnip, wash the area with soap and water immediately (NYDEC, n.d.)

Description_Botanical: Drought-tolerant evergreen canopy tree up to 70 (occasionally to 90) m tall and 4.4 m wide, featuring thick, rough, dark brown, fire-resistant furrowed bark and a rounded to flattened crown when older (young trees with a pyramidal to conic crown). Needles flat, (1.5) 2-3 (3.5) cm long (or 2-4 cm in length), tapering to a short petiole, spreading around the twig or turned upward, with an obtuse to abruptly sharp-pointed tip; color varying from yellow-green to dark-green in var. menziesii to blue-green in var. glauca, the lower surface bearing two longitudinal bands of white stomata. Seed cones drooping, yellowish- to purplish-green when young, turning reddish-brown, soon deciduous, maturing the first season, 6-10 cm long in var. menziesii, 4-7 cm in var. glauca (overall range 5-9 cm); scales with a 3-lobed tip, the centre one the longest; seeds with wings less than 25 mm; pollen cones yellow to reddish, 6-10 mm long. Pine Family (Pinaceae).

Ethno_Medicinal: Douglas-fir resin was used by the Shasta in northern California to poultice cuts and the Yuki along the California coast used a decoction from spring buds to treat venereal diseases. The Sinkyone of California made Douglas-fir bark tea which eased colds and stomach ailments. Sap used as disinfectant for wounds. Douglas-fir needles were made into a tea and drank by Isleta Puebloans in New Mexico to cure rheumatism.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Wood used as fuel, timber, and carved into spear handles, harpoon shafts/barbs, dip-net poles, spoons, hooks, caskets, and fire tongs. Pitch/resin used as glue for harpoon heads, fishhooks, caulking canoes, perfumes, and candles. Bark tannins used for dye.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Prayer sticks made of Douglas-fir wood were excavated from archeological sites in New Mexico dating back to the Anasazi.

Description_Botanical: Evergreen Shrub, 0.25 - 0.8 m height with purple-green/long slender veined holly-like foliage, yellow blossoms, and blue/purple fruits with white waxy coating. Summary_Public: Coarse coastal perennial grass, 50-150 cm tall, forming large clumps from thick, ascending rhizomes, featuring blueish-green blades and yellow flowers; stems erect, stout, 50-150 cm tall, usually finely but copiously hairy or sometimes smooth above. Moist to mesic sandy or gravelly beaches and shoreline forests in the lowland zone; common in coastal BC; amphiberingian, N to AK, YT and N, E to NF and S to NH, PA, MI, IL and CA.
Description_Botanical: Coarse coastal perennial grass, 50-150 cm tall, forming large clumps from thick, ascending rhizomes, featuring blueish-green blades and yellow flowers; stems erect, stout, 50-150 cm tall, usually finely but copiously hairy or sometimes smooth above. Sheaths open, smooth; blades tough, flat to in-rolled, 6-15 mm wide, with numerous prominent nerves, very finely minutely rough appressed-hairy on the upper surfaces and smooth underneath; ear-shaped lobes usually developed at some leaf-bases; ligules more or less fringed with fine hairs, scarcely 1 mm long. Coarse, blue-green perennial grass (50–150 cm tall) with thick creeping rhizomes and heavy terminal spikes. Coarse coastal dune grass.

Summary_Public: A sun-loving, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant perennial forb 30-80 cm (or 15-80 cm) in height, well-suited for well-drained rocky sites and tending toward a fuller stature in deeper, richer soils; it produces cheerful yellow flowers over a long, late-season bloom period, attracting an abundant diversity of native pollinators. Inhabiting mesic to dry beaches, coastal bluffs, waste places, and roadsides in the lowland zone, this plant is common in coastal British Columbia and ranges south to northern California.
Description_Botanical: This plant blooms over a long period of time and late into the season, attracting a large diversity and abundance of native pollinators. Tends to be a full-statured plant that will get larger in deeper and richer soils. Perennial herb from a taproot and a stout branched stem-base; stems erect or ascending, several, usually branched, nearly glabrous or with long, soft hairs, 15-80 cm tall.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Perennial herb from a taproot and a stout branched stem-base; stems erect or ascending, several, usually branched, nearly glabrous or with long, soft hairs, 15-80 cm tall.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves alternate, toothed or entire, lower ones oblanceolate, up to 40 cm long and 4 cm wide; stem leaves unstalked, sometimes clasping.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of solitary heads or a flat-topped cluster of heads; disk 1-3 cm wide; yellow rays 10-35 or more; involucral bracts slightly or moderately sticky, outer ones long slender, green-tipped, loose or spreading but not regularly reflexed.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes compressed, scarcely nerved, featuring a pappus of 2 to several deciduous, firm bristles.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Year-round evergreen foliage anchors winter garden structure.

Summary_Public: Stems 1.3 to 3 m tall, unbranched with creeping rhizome, forming clonal colonies; alternate lance-shaped leaves; terminal racemes of pink to light purple/magenta flowers; 4-sided capsule fruit with silky hairy seeds. Rhizomatous Perennial Forb with pink to magenta flowers.
Description_Botanical: Forms tall striking clusters of vegetation through summer by rhizome. Fireweed (Onagraceae) is a native, herbaceous rhizomatous perennial herb developing from widespread rootstocks and spreading roots typically within the top few inches of the ground surface, forming clonal colonies that bloom from June to September and attract native bees and leafcutter bees. Fireweed plants are protandrous (male reproductive organs mature before the female reproductive organs) and self-compatible (capable of self-fertilization) (Mosquin 1966). Flower anthers open, and disperse pollen, within 24 hours of the flower opening while the stigmas remain closed and the style strongly reflexed away from the anthers for 2 to 3 days, a process that promotes cross-pollination (Mosquin 1966).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Stems 1.3 to 3 m tall, unbranched with creeping rhizome, forming clonal colonies. Tall rhizomatous perennial forb with showy pink-to-magenta flower spires.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, narrowly lanceolate, (5) 10-15 (20) cm long, entire or finely toothed, green, veiny below; nearly stalkless.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a many-flowered, terminal raceme that elongates in fruit, with flowers nodding in bud; hypanthium practically lacking; petals 8-20 mm long, the upper 2 wider than the lower 2, deep pink to magenta, rarely white; sepals narrowly lanceolate, 7-16 mm long; anthers 1.5-2.2 mm long; ovaries 0.8-1.8 cm long, densely short-hairy; styles longer than the stamens, hairy on the lower portion; stigmas 4-lobed. Flowers protandrous (anthers shed pollen within 24 hours while stigmas remain closed for 2–3 days).

Circumboreal, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and the Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to California and Virginia; also in Eurasia. Occurs in open forests, riverbanks, gravel bars, waste ground, roadsides, burned areas, logged sites, and meadows on soils ranging from clays to sandy loams (pH 4.8-7). Circumpolar, distributed throughout Alberta south to California, New Mexico, and North Carolina.

Summary_Public: Perennial Forb from corm, 30-60 cm height with umbel-shaped white flowers. Occurs in meadows, rocky slopes, and woodlands, specifically on dry to mesic grassy coastal bluffs, rocky slopes, and meadows in the lowland zone; frequent on southern Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, and the adjacent mainland; ranging south to Idaho, Nevada, and California.
Description_Botanical: Perennial forb (30-60 cm) from corm with umbel-shaped white flowers. Leaves wither during flowering to form a unique tower of flower heads when planted in larger clusters; this drought-tolerant species is suited to both full sun and part shade. Plants arise from a deep, straw-coloured, fibrous-scaly, nearly globose, bulb-like corm (additionally propagating vegetatively from tan, fibrous-coated corms).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Perennial forb (30-60 cm) from corm with umbel-shaped white flowers.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves 1 or 2, linear, keeled, 20-40 cm long, 3-10 mm wide, smooth, sheathing at the base, the margins entire; stem leaves lacking.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a compact, terminal umbel of several to many, erect to ascending, more or less equally stalked flowers, above several membranous bracts, the stalks 1-4 cm long; flowers white often tinged with blue, to light blue, with green mid-veins, broadly bell-shaped to bowl-shaped, of 6 fused segments, 1-1.5 cm long; corolla lobes in 2 petal-like whorls, much longer than the tube, spreading, the 2 series much alike, broadly lanceolate to oblong-egg-shaped; stamens 6, attached to the petal-like tube at the same level and about the same length, the filaments flattened and joined toward the base; pistil 1, 3-chambered.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, egg-shaped, stalked; seeds rounded, black.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Spread_Behavior: Slowly multiplying clump from underground bulbs or corms
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Bulb / Corm / Tuber); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Seasonally wet meadows, Garry oak savannas, and rocky slopes. Dry to mesic. Heavy clay / Seasonally wet clay.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: If possible, obtain the seed and corms from local sources to maintain genetic diversity of white brodiaea and for the best adaptation to local conditions. Some nurseries may label their corms and seeds according to geographic source. If planting flowering-size corms, they can be directly planted outside.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: This plant is not readily available from commercial nurseries.
Pruning_Management: The area of white brodiaea will require regular weeding and the use of a very weak solution of fertilizer twice only during the active growth in the spring. The corms can be kept from overcrowding by thinning them every three years. This involves picking off the cormlets and replanting them elsewhere in the garden. There are five major types of indigenous management activities conducted in California that were designed to ensure future corm production at traditional gathering sites: (1) conscious breaking off cormlets from the harvested parent corms and replanting them; (2) sparing whole plants; (3) harvesting the corms after plants have gone to seed and dumping the seeds on the ground; (4) burning areas; and (5) irrigation.

Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Perennial Forb, 40-80 cm height with broad heart-to-kidney-shaped fuzzy leaves and greenish-white to rose fringed flower spires. Inhabiting forests and woodlands, specifically moist forests, streambanks, and thickets in the lowland and montane zones; common in W and E BC south of 57°N, mostly absent from central BC north of 51°N; ranging north to the Aleutian Islands and S AK, east to AB, and south to MT, N ID, and CA; recorded in forests and woodlands, and the understory/herb layer of Littlewood Forest.
Description_Botanical: Broadheart-to-kidney-shaped deep green leaves with spike-like inflorescence with many greenish-white to rose fringed petals. A rhizomatous perennial forb standing 40-80 cm tall, featuring scaly rhizomes and flowering stems that are strongly long-hairy below and increasingly glandular-hairy above, bearing 1 to 3 reduced stem leaves. Basal leaves are broad heart- to kidney-shaped, 3-8 cm wide and about as long, shallowly 5- to 7-lobed, and irregularly toothed; stalks are 5-20 cm long and strongly long-hairy. Stipules are about 5 mm long, membranous, and fringed to toothed.
