Summary_Public: Deciduous tree up to 15-25 m tall with thick furrowed light grey bark; deeply round-lobed shiny leathery green leaves; host for lichens; acorn fruits in shallow cups. Inhabiting meadows, woodlands, and rocky slopes, as well as mesic to dry grasslands and rock outcrops in the lowland zone, this species is locally common on southeastern Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, and rare in the lower Fraser Valley, extending south to California.
Description_Botanical: A characteristic deciduous tree of full sun meadow habitat in our region, where it grows up to 25 m tall in deeper soils. Deciduous tree characteristic of full sun meadows, growing up to 25 m tall in deeper soils, whereas in shallow, dry, rocky habitats it can be long-lived yet remain small, shrubby, and as short as 1 m with trunks up to 1 m wide and light grey bark with thick scaly ridges.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous tree up to 15-25 m tall with thick furrowed light grey bark. A characteristic deciduous tree of full sun meadow habitat in our region, where it grows up to 25 m tall in deeper soils.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, blades oblong to egg-shaped in outline with 3-7 lobes per side, the lobes entire or 2-3 toothed, up to 12 cm long with stalks 1-2 cm long, the largest sinuses extending more than halfway to the midrib, bright shiny green and glabrous above, paler below with reddish to yellow hairs, turning yellowish-brown in the fall.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of tiny inconspicuous male and female flowers, these separate but on the same tree; female flowers clustered or single surrounded by a scaly cuplike involucre; male flowers numerous in catkins.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Acorns 1-seeded, maturing in one season, unstalked, egg-shaped to nearly round, 2-3 cm long, subtended by shallow, bumpy cups that are hairy within.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Long-lived perennial canopy tree establishing deeply within 2–3 growing seasons.
Discovered_Drive_Details: P’hwulhp (Garry Oak) is the only native oak in British Columbia, forming open savanna meadows on sunny, rocky lowland sites in the rainshadow of Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands. Its acorns were traditionally steamed or roasted as food, and controlled burning maintained rich camas and spring-wildflower meadows beneath its canopy.

Summary_Public: Perennial Forb, 30-80 cm height with lemon-yellow flowers. Found in dry to moist meadows, grasslands, rocky slopes, open forests, roadsides, and waste places from the lowland to montane zones; common in southern British Columbia except rare on the coast (var. gracilis), and rare in British Columbia north of 55°N; ranging north to Alaska, east to Saskatchewan, and south to California and Mexico.
Description_Botanical: Early summer lemon-yellow blooms and distinctive foliage. Plant in a full sun area. Soils can be dry, but it also is very tolerant of wet winter meadows that dry in summer. A perennial forb and native wildflower of the rose family (Rosaceae), also known as slender cinquefoil, characterized by early summer lemon-yellow blooms, a height of 30-80 cm (stems 20.3–101.6 cm), and a thick, scaly, branched stem-base/rhizome.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A perennial forb and native wildflower of the rose family (Rosaceae), also known as slender cinquefoil, characterized by early summer lemon-yellow blooms, a height of 30-80 cm (stems 20.3–101.6 cm), and a thick, scaly, branched stem-base/rhizome.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves long-stalked, palmately compound; leaflets 5 to 7 (9), lanceolate to oblong-elliptic, (2) 3-8 (10) cm long, coarsely saw-toothed to deeply lobed, greenish and variously hairy (most often spreading-hairy to woolly-hairy, sometimes also glandular, sometimes nearly smooth) above, usually paler and hairier, often white-woolly beneath; stem leaves alternate, reduced, 1 or 2.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an open, somewhat flat-topped, terminal cluster of several to many stalked flowers; corollas yellow, bowl-shaped, the petals 5, heart-shaped, 6-10 mm long, shallowly notched at the tip; calyces hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes broadly lanceolate, 4-7 mm long, alternating with 5 shorter, narrowly lanceolate bractlets; ovaries superior; stamens 20.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes, numerous, clustered, lopsided-egg-shaped, 1-2 mm long, greenish, smooth to faintly net-veined.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic but vigorous clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); forms thickets that outcompete slow-establishing forbs—allow generous spacing or use root barriers in tight borders.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Wet to dry meadows and open woods.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in dry to moist meadows, grasslands, rocky slopes, open forests, roadsides, and waste places from the lowland to montane zones; common in southern British Columbia except rare on the coast (var. gracilis), and rare in British Columbia north of 55°N; ranging north to Alaska, east to Saskatchewan, and south to California and Mexico. Slender cinquefoil is frequently encountered in meadows, grasslands, roadsides, subalpine meadows, open forests, and moist areas within deserts and arid shrub-steppe regions at elevations up to 3505 m, and is widely distributed throughout North America from Alaska to Baja California, extending east through the northern Great Plains to the Great Lakes Basin and Quebec.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Seeds are typically mature by late summer early fall. Transplants will flower and produce seed one year after transplanting.
Stratification_Dormancy: Seeds exhibit physiological dormancy which requires 60 to 120 days cold-moist stratification or fall sowing to break dormancy, depending on the latitude and elevation of the source population.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Seeds should be lightly covered, and usually germinate within one to two weeks after appropriate stratification. Cinquefoil may easily be established as a transplant from container stock in the fall or spring. For seed production fields, seeds are usually started as large plugs in the greenhouse during the winter and planted out in the spring on 30.5 cm within row spacing and 18-to 61 cm between row spacing.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are no developed cultivars of slender cinquefoil, but both non-certified and certified source identified seed is widely available from commercial sources. Container plants are also sometimes available from native plant nurseries.
Pruning_Management: Slender cinquefoil requires little maintenance once established and will generally persist for 3 to 10 years. For seed production fields, seeds are usually started as large plugs in the greenhouse during the winter and planted out in the spring on 30.5 cm within row spacing and 18-to 61 cm between row spacing. Transplants will flower and produce seed one year after transplanting. Large seed production fields can be direct combined, while plants in small fields are generally swathed and collected to dry under cover on tarps or in bags.
Nursery_Availability: Listed by Satinflower Nurseries (Vancouver Island native plant nursery).
Nursery_Stock_Format: Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS); Rooted Divisions
Ethno_Medicinal: Slender cinquefoil was used by tribes of the Pacific Northwest for various medicinal purposes. The Syilx (Okanagan) / Colville tribe made an infusion of pounded roots as a tonic for the blood, general aches and pains, diarrhea, gonorrhea, and for washing sores. The Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribe used a poultice of mashed leaves and roots on wounds to draw out the pain.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: This species has little potential to become weedy or invasive. There is, however, a similar looking, related Eurasian species, sulfur cinquefoil (Potentilla recta), that is considered a noxious weed in Colorado, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Washington, and British Colombia.

Description_Botanical: This prominent perennial emerges from a substantial bulb to reach heights of up to 100 cm. Its grass-like basal leaves create a lush foundation for the showy display of pale to deep blue flowers. These large, distinctive blooms, reaching up to 4 cm in length, form an elegant terminal raceme. As the flowers mature, their tepals twist together, adding a unique visual element.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: This prominent perennial emerges from a substantial bulb to reach heights of up to 100 cm. Its grass-like basal leaves create a lush foundation for the showy display of pale to deep blue flowers.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves several to numerous, linear-lanceolate and grass-like, to 60 cm long, 1-2 cm wide, smooth, sheathing at the base, the margins entire; stem leaves lacking.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a terminal raceme of 5 to many, stalked flowers, the stalks 1-4 cm long, spreading in flower, spreading to ascending in fruit; flowers pale to deep blue, rarely white, of 6 similar, distinct tepals, the tepals 20-40 mm long, 5-10 mm wide, twisting together over the ovaries when withered; stamens 6; pistil 1, 3-chambered. Stamens number 6; the pistil is 1 and 3-chambered.

Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, egg-shaped to oblong, cross-ridged, 1-2.5 cm long; fruiting stalks often longer than bracts, spreading to ascending, curved in towards stem; seeds several to many, shiny black, 2-4 mm long.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Camas bulbs may be roasted and eaten, and are said to be sweet and chewy. They have been gathered from island bluffs and baked, steamed or roasted in hot ashes, or mashed and formed into patties and then roasted on special flat rocks at the edge of the fire.

Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Great camas is frequently found in areas with soil moisture persisting throughout most of the growing season. Bulb depth appears limited by shallow water tables, anoxic conditions, or restrictive layers. Dry to seasonally wet; 5.6 to 6.8 pH; tolerates clay soils; 0% CaCO3 tolerance.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting vernally moist meadows in the lowland zone; locally frequent on southeastern Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, with a single report from the adjacent mainland (Sechelt Peninsula); ranging south to California. Great camas occurs in coastal oak meadows from southern British Columbia to California, west of the Cascades, as well as in moist savannahs, ditches, and seepages in the CDF zone, Salish Sea meadows, and the Willamette Valley, inhabiting dry and moist meadows from southern Vancouver Island to northern California, coast to the Cascades and Sierra Nevada below 3292 m, alongside wet meadows, woods, prairies, moist hillsides, streamsides, and riparian zones. Great camas grows in wet meadows, woods, prairies, moist hillsides, and streamside areas, often in ephemeral habitats that dry up by late spring. In western Oregon, its preferred habitat includes shady environments such as riparian zones or under moderately dense deciduous forest canopies, though it can inhabit more open areas elsewhere in its range.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Great camas propagates easily from seed. It can be collected as soon as the pods mature (turn light brown) or split open to reveal the mature black seeds. Pods ripen from late May to July.
Stratification_Dormancy: Camas seed is dormant and typically requires 60-100 days of cold moist stratification (moist chilling at 1–4°C) for maximum germination (Bartow, 2015). Fall-sown seedbeds should be kept weed-free during early spring establishment.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Great camas can be propagated from seeds or bulbs; shade tolerance, moisture requirements, and preferred planting depth may differ among specific phenotypes. Plants require irrigation or moist soil conditions to become established. Great camas can be difficult to establish in California.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Cultivars of Leichtlin’s camas are widely available in the flower bulb industry. One cultivar, ‘Alba’, is white (or bluish-white), while ‘Caerulea’ has light blue flowers, and ‘Plena’ has double greenish yellow blooms (Brenzel, 1995). ‘Blauwe Donau’ is described as having sea-lavender-violet flowers and lilac anthers. ‘Lady Eve Price’ has campanula-violet flowers with each segment having a darker colored methyl-violet central stripe (Royal General Bulbgrower’s Association, 1991). ‘Semiplena’ has large, semi-double, creamy-white flowers.
Pruning_Management: Consistent soil moisture is required every spring, but the soil can be allowed to dry out soon after the pods mature or the leaves senesce (dry up and turn brown). Moderate soil nutrient levels are beneficial. In natural settings, minor soil disturbance (loosening, surface scarification) adjacent to existing specimens may enhance natural regeneration by seed; seedling recruitment is highest in areas that are bare when the seeds germinate in February.

Edible_Parts_Flavor: Bulb; Extensively cultivated staple food and trade item; bulbs steamed/roasted in pit-ovens for 24-48 hrs to convert inulin to fructose; dried, stored, eaten at feasts/potlatches; Important root food cooked in pits/stovetops, sun-dried, in cakes, or soaked; sweetener, flavoring; stalks/leaves for mattresses; Bulbs.
Ethno_Culinary_Food: According to Dr. Nancy Turner, TRM included the following: Ownership, demarcation, and inheritance of beds or patches, Clearing of rock, brush, and weedy vegetation, Harvesting bulbs after seeds were produced, during specific times of the year, Periodic field burning in summer after digging, Digging or “cultivation” to keep the soil loose, Sustainable harvest techniques, including partial, selective harvests and incidental or planned promotion of camas In some cases, sod removal then bulb removal followed by sod replacement, “Selective breeding” by transplanting “better” bulbs to the beds, colonization and reproduction, and Death camas bulbs (Zigadenus venenosus) were removed, so they wouldn’t accidentally be mistaken for the edible camas bulbs. Starchy bulb used as a staple food and trade item for Indigenous Peoples in the region for generations. Important root food cooked in pits/stovetops, sun-dried, in cakes, or soaked. The bulbs were dug with a pointed digging stick.
Ethno_Medicinal: Nez Perce used boiled root juice mixed with honey as cough medicine. Prepared as cough medicine (boiled, juice strained and mixed with honey).
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Camas is favored as forage by deer, so fencing or repellents may be useful, particularly during the first growing season. Bulb predation by pocket gophers can be a substantial threat to stands if left unchecked.

Summary_Public: A tufted, sun-loving, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and pollinator-friendly perennial forb suited for well-drained rocky sites, reaching 20-60 cm (or 20-80 cm) in height and bearing cheerful yellow flowers. Inhabiting dry rock outcrops and meadows within the lowland zone, this species is rare on the Gulf Islands—known only from Lasqueti Island—and is disjunct south to California.
Description_Botanical: Growing from a taproot and a stout, branched stem-base, it produces erect stems that are few-branched above, densely glandular, and interspersed with stiff, translucent hairs; basal leaves are toothed, while stem leaves are alternate, oblong to lanceolate, stiff-hairy, and toothed with regular teeth 1-2.5 mm long. Tufted perennial forb (20–60 cm tall) with sticky gummy heads and bright yellow flowers. Perennial herb from a taproot and a stout, branched stem-base; stems erect, few branched above, densely glandular, also with some stiff, translucent hairs; 20-80 cm tall.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Growing from a taproot and a stout, branched stem-base, it produces erect stems that are few-branched above, densely glandular, and interspersed with stiff, translucent hairs.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves toothed; stem leaves alternate, oblong to lanceolate, stiff-hairy, toothed, the teeth regular and 1-2.5 mm long.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of solitary or a flat-topped cluster of heads, the heads 12-23 mm wide; rays yellow, 20-60; involucral bracts erect to reflexed, outer ones long, slender.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes compressed, smooth to ridged, 4.5-5 mm long; pappus awns flat.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Dry rock outcrops and gravelly meadows. Dry; well-drained rocky sites.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting dry rock outcrops and meadows within the lowland zone, this species is rare on the Gulf Islands—known only from Lasqueti Island—and is disjunct south to California. This plant may be found in sandy or saline bottomlands, dry banks, rocky fields, plains, and roadsides (Munz, 1968). The plant may also be found to the east, across the North Coast Ranges and around the San Francisco Bay, north to the Cascade Range foothills, west along the Sierra Nevadas, and south along the outer Southern Coast Ranges into Baja California (Moore, 2012). Great Valley gumweed is native to central California.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: Sow in fall or early spring for germination in the same season. Propagation is easiest from seed, and germination rates are generally high. Achenes placed under a thin layer of soil on wet filter paper at ambient temperature and diffuse light germinate at around 70%, but an 8-day cool pretreatment at 8°C can raise these rates slightly (McLaughlin, 1987).
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Sow seeds in fall or early spring. There are no developed cultivars of Great Valley gumweed, but seed is generally available from commercial sources both individually and in pollinator mixes.

Ethno_Medicinal: Steeped for respiratory ailments. Native Americans regarded Great Valley gumweed as a useful medicinal plant for a variety of treatments, including respiratory and dermatological afflictions. The Costanoan Indians boiled leaves and flower heads of gumweed for healing dermatitis caused by poison oak, and for wounds, burns, boils, and sores.

Summary_Public: Deciduous Woody Vine with purple tubular flowers, red fruit, and hairy vines. Forests and woodland.
Description_Botanical: A deciduous woody vine featuring purple tubular flowers, red fruit, and hairy vines. It is a partially evergreen, woody vine or sprawling shrub, 1-6 m long/tall, with hollow twigs that are usually short-hairy and glaucous when young. Foliage is opposite, on stalks 3-5 mm long (some with paired, fused stipules between the leaf stalks), oblong to egg-shaped, 2-8 cm long, 1.5-5 cm wide, often somewhat heart-shaped at the base, obtuse at the tip, usually stiffly hairy (sometimes glabrous), and glaucous beneath, with upper pairs joined to form disks around the stem. Deciduous trailing or climbing woody vine with hairy stems, pinkish-purple tubular flowers, and red berries.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A deciduous woody vine featuring purple tubular flowers, red fruit, and hairy vines. It is a partially evergreen, woody vine or sprawling shrub, 1-6 m long/tall, with hollow twigs that are usually short-hairy and glaucous when young.

Summary_Public: Mediterranean-climate shrub similar to arbutus; pink flowers (6-7 mm), fruit persisting in August. Inhabits rocky outcrops and rocky slopes, as well as dry open forests in the lowland and montane zones; infrequent in extreme southwestern British Columbia, extending south along the coast to California.
Description_Botanical: An erect or spreading Mediterranean-climate shrub 1-3 m tall with old branches possessing purplish-red bark and young twigs and stalks that are greyish-hairy and typically distinctly bristly with longer, scattered, glandular hairs. Leaves are alternate, evergreen, egg- or lance-shaped to elliptic, 2-5 cm long, 1-2.5 cm wide, narrowed at the tip, finely greyish-hairy particularly beneath, on stalks about 5 mm long. Belonging to the Heath Family (Ericaceae), hairy manzanita functions as an erect, much-branched evergreen shrub or small tree 1-3 m high with a broad, rounded, dense canopy, lacking a basal burl and thus unable to crown sprout after fire. Young twig bark is densely white-hirsute, while mature bark is smooth and dark red-brown.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: An erect or spreading Mediterranean-climate shrub 1-3 m tall with old branches possessing purplish-red bark and young twigs and stalks that are greyish-hairy and typically distinctly bristly with longer, scattered, glandular hairs.

Summary_Public: Deciduous shrub up to 2 m in height with dense pinkish-purple flower spikes forming impenetrable thickets (alternatively characterized as a low to medium shrub, 0.5-2.5 m tall, from a creeping rhizome often forming thickets). Occurring in thickets, wetlands, riparian areas, fens, swamps, bogs, streambanks, lake margins, and moist to wet thickets and open forests in lowland and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia south of about 56° N, ranging south to California and Idaho, as well as sunny moist lake margins and wet meadows.
Description_Botanical: Deciduous shrub up to 2 m in height with dense pinkish-purple flower spikes forming impenetrable thickets (alternatively characterized as a low to medium shrub, 0.5-2.5 m tall, from a creeping rhizome often forming thickets). Low to medium shrub, 0.5-2.5 m tall, from creeping rhizome, often forming thickets; stems erect, much-branched, the slender branchlets usually somewhat woolly, later becoming smooth. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, short-stalked, oblong to egg-shaped, 3-10 cm long, and coarsely toothed mostly above the middle, featuring a dark green and smooth upper surface and a paler, woolly-hairy to smooth lower surface. Thicket-forming shrub with pink/purple plume-like flower clusters and long, limber, curved stems.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous shrub up to 2 m in height with dense pinkish-purple flower spikes forming impenetrable thickets (alternatively characterized as a low to medium shrub, 0.5-2.5 m tall, from a creeping rhizome often forming thickets). Stems are erect and much-branched, featuring slender branchlets that are usually somewhat woolly and later become smooth.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, short-stalked, oblong to egg-shaped, 3-10 cm long, coarsely toothed mostly above the middle, dark green and smooth above, paler and woolly-hairy to smooth beneath.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a branched, narrowly conic to cylindric, dense terminal cluster of numerous small flowers, the cluster several times longer than broad, the branches often woolly; corollas deep to pale pink, the petals 5, egg-shaped to round-elliptic, about 2 mm long; calyces fine-hairy to nearly smooth on the outside, 5-lobed, the lobes triangular, bent back, about 1 mm long; ovaries superior; stamens numerous.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Follicles are usually 5, short-beaked, 2-3 mm long, somewhat leathery, shining, and smooth except for occasional long hairs along the suture; seeds are several and spindle-shaped.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: With spring cuttings, some suggest making a slice cut at the basal end, soaking in water for several weeks in a cooler, and dipping in a rooting hormone (1000 ppm IBA - talc or solution) before planting into a light rooting medium. If installed properly in fall or winter, a fair percentage of untreated hard wood cuttings (18 in or longer) can root and establish directly on suitable, moist revegetation sites.
Discovered_Drive_Details: T’eets’ulhp (Hardhack) grows in sunny moist areas along lake margins, stream banks, swamps, bogs and wet meadows, forming dense thickets with plumes of tiny pink flowers. The straight strong stems were traditionally used to make fish spreaders for drying or smoking fish.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Shallower organic or humus horizons.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.

Pruning_Management: The area planted in harvest brodiaea will require regular weeding and the use of a very weak solution of fertilizer twice only during the active growth in the spring. The corms can be kept from overcrowding by thinning them every three years. This involves picking off the cormlets and replanting them elsewhere in the garden. There are five major types of indigenous management activities conducted in California that were designed to ensure future corm production at traditional gathering sites: (1) conscious breaking off cormlets from the harvested parent corms and replanting them; (2) sparing whole plants; (3) harvesting the corms after plants have gone to seed and dumping the seeds in the hole; (4) burning areas; and (5) irrigation.

Summary_Public: Deciduous shrub 1.5 to 5 m tall; oblong-elliptical green leaves smelling like cucumber when crushed; early 5-petaled white flowers in pendulous clusters; bluish-black/orange-pink drooping drupe fruits. Occurs in woodlands, thickets, and riparian areas, as well as moist to dry open forests, forest edges, streambanks, clearings, and roadsides in the lowland zone; frequent on southern Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, and the adjacent mainland, extending south to northern California under moist conditions in sun or shade west of the Cascades, ranging from British Columbia to California in dry-shaded soils.
Description_Botanical: Fruits are large-pitted and vividly coloured fluorescent orange before ripening and turning to deep blue-purplish/black when ripe. A deciduous shrub standing 1.5 to 5 m tall featuring clumped, arching stems with chambered pith and bitter, purplish-brown bark. Crushed leaves emit a cucumber scent and are alternate, short-stalked with stalks 5-10 mm long, lanceolate to oblong-egg-shaped or elliptic, measuring 5-12 cm long, with entire margins, pale green and smooth above, and paler and often sparsely hairy below.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A deciduous shrub standing 1.5 to 5 m tall featuring clumped, arching stems with chambered pith and bitter, purplish-brown bark.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, lanceolate to oblong-egg-shaped or elliptic, short-stalked, the stalks 5-10 mm long, the blades 5-12 cm long, not toothed, pale green and smooth above, paler and often sparsely hairy below; crushed leaves smell like cucumber.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences loose, drooping, bracted, 5- to 10-cm long clusters, at the ends of short axillary branchlets, of several (5 to 10) stalked flowers; flowers mostly unisexual, the male and female flowers on separate plants, appearing very early in the year, as the leaves develop; corollas greenish-white, saucer- to cup-shaped, about 1 cm across, the petals 5, egg-shaped, 5-6 mm long, spreading (shorter, narrower and erect on female flowers); calyces 6-7 mm long, 5-lobed, the lobes about equalling the top-shaped hypanthium; ovaries (female plants) usually 5, superior; stamens 15.

Summary_Public: Native cool-season tufted perennial bunchgrass, 30-60 cm tall; soft blue-green flat/in-rolled basal leaves; dense narrow contracted panicle seedheads with pale green/purplish spikelets. Dry rocky or grassy slopes and forest openings in the steppe to subalpine zones; common in SC and SE BC, less frequent in SW and N BC; circumpolar, N to AK, YT and SW NT, E to Labr. And S to ME, NY, OH, AL, MS, TX, NM, AZ, CA and MX.
Description_Botanical: Native cool-season tufted perennial bunchgrass, 30-60 cm tall; soft blue-green flat/in-rolled basal leaves; dense narrow contracted panicle seedheads with pale green/purplish spikelets. Plant in dry soils for best results. A strong, tufted perennial bunchgrass arising from fibrous roots with smooth to soft-hairy stems measuring (20) 30-60 cm tall. Sheath margins are typically non-overlapping above, with collars frequently bearing long, straight hairs 1-1.5 mm long.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Native cool-season tufted perennial bunchgrass, 30-60 cm tall.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Sheath margins usually not overlapping above, the collars often with long, straight hairs 1-1.5 mm long; blades 1-2 (4.5) mm wide, 2-6 (20) cm long, sometimes flat, but usually folded to in-rolled, usually rough to densely hairy or short stiff-hairy or both, rarely smooth, often greyish, the margins at the insertions often with long, straight hairs 1-1.5 mm long, the tips strongly prowlike; ligules 0.5-2 mm long, strongly hairy, jagged to nearly entire, more or less fringed with fine hairs.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 1-1.5 mm long; 1-2 mm wide; 2-6 cm long; 0.5-2 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a spikelike panicle, 4-13 cm long, the short branches spreading at flowering; spikelets 2- (3- or 4-) flowered; glumes unawned or rarely awn-tipped, the lower ones 3.5 mm long, the upper ones 4-6 mm long, somewhat wider than the lower ones and about equalling or slightly exceeding the lower florets, sparsely to copiously rough short-hairy; lemmas 3.5-5 mm long, minutely rough to short-hairy, unawned or awn-tipped; anthers about 2 (2.5) mm long. The inflorescence is a spikelike panicle measuring 4-13 cm long, featuring short branches that spread at flowering.

Circumpolar, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and southwestern Northwest Territories, east to Labrador, and south to Maine, New York, Ohio, Alabama, Mississippi, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, and Mexico; also found in Eurasia. Found in rich swamps, woodlands, and forests, as well as mesic to wet alluvial forests, glades, streambanks, gullies, slidetracks, meadows, swamps, and rock outcrops from the lowland and steppe to alpine zones; common throughout British Columbia; amphiberingian, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to South Dakota, New Mexico, Arizona, and California; also in eastern Asia.
Description_Botanical: Lime green deciduous fern (up to 1 m) unfurling fiddleheads in spring. Summary_Public: Taprooted Perennial Forb, 20-40 cm height with rare orange flowers. Inhabiting rock outcrops, mesic to dry grassy slopes, meadows, and forest openings from lowland to lower montane zones, Bigflower agoseris is infrequent in extreme southern British Columbia and ranges south to Utah, Nevada, and California.
Description_Botanical: Orange flowers are rare in our native plant community of southern Vancouver Island so these are a unique treat for full sun to partial shade in a very dry spot. A distinctive taprooted perennial wildflower rising 20–70 cm on hollow, milky-sapped scapes. The basal leaves (10–25 cm long, 1–3 cm wide) are oblanceolate and pinnately lobed. Large solitary dandelion-like flower heads bloom in spring, giving rise to prominently beaked achenes (4–7 mm body with a beak more than twice its length) bearing fuzzy dispersal pappi.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A distinctive taprooted perennial wildflower rising 20–70 cm on hollow, milky-sapped scapes.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: All basal, oblanceolate to lance-elliptic or broadly linear, entire to deeply pinnately cut with broad or narrow lobes which are widely spreading or pointed towards the base, 10-25 cm long, 1-3 cm wide.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Heads with strap-shaped flowers, solitary, large; involucres broadly bell-shaped to rounded, 1.5-4 cm tall; involucral bracts in 4-5 series, the outer relatively broad and short, conspicuously fringed with small hairs; receptacles naked; flowers yellow, often turning pinkish or purplish upon drying.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes smooth, spindle-shaped, the body about 4-7 mm long, tapering to a smooth, slender beak 2-4 times as long as the body; pappus of numerous hairlike bristles, 8-14 mm long, white. Vol1_3.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: This plant is adapted to a broad range of soil types.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting rock outcrops, mesic to dry grassy slopes, meadows, and forest openings from lowland to lower montane zones, Bigflower agoseris is infrequent in extreme southern British Columbia and ranges south to Utah, Nevada, and California. It occurs in small numbers in grassland, sagebrush, and mountain brush communities below 2,000 m, spanning western North America from British Columbia south to California and east to Montana and Utah. Bigflower agoseris is found in small numbers in grassland, sagebrush and mountain brush communities below 2,000 m (Hickman 1993; Welsh et al. 2003).

The pappus can be removed with a hammer mill or brush machine, but pappus removal is not necessary for greenhouse propagation (Skinner 2004).
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Bigflower agoseris can be seeded in spring or fall. It should be planted into a firm, weed-free seed bed at a depth of 3–6 mm. The recommended full stand seeding rate is 4 lbs pure live seed (PLS) per acre.
Pruning_Management: Bigflower agoseris should be used as a minor component of seed mixtures. Management strategies should be based on the key species in the established plant community. Grazing should be deferred on seeded lands for at least two growing seasons to allow for full stand establishment.
Nursery_Availability: Seed of bigflower agoseris is available in limited quantities on the commercial market. Larger quantities of seed may be grown on a contract basis.

Description_Botanical: A perennial forb 20-60 cm in height (also characterized as a perennial herb 30-100 cm tall), arising from a short rhizome and stout stem-base, featuring 1 to several erect, simple, coarse-spreading-hairy stems. The basal leaves are several, long-stalked, 10-40 cm long, interruptedly pinnately cleft, and hairy along the veins beneath, consisting of mostly 5 to 9 egg-shaped, blunt-toothed main segments interspersed with several much smaller segments; the terminal segment is heart- to kidney-shaped, 3-10 cm long by 3-15 cm wide, coarsely blunt-toothed, often deeply 3-lobed, rounded or squared-off to heart-shaped at the base, and substantially larger than the lateral leaflets below. The cauline leaves are alternate, numbering 2 to 5, reduced, unstalked or nearly so, and deeply 3-lobed or 3-parted. Perennial forb (20–60 cm tall) with hooked sticky burs and broad basal leaves.

Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Perennial Forb up to 1.5 m height with large purple-blue flowers and whorled leaves. Found in moist to mesic meadows, riverbars, streambanks, seashores, clearings, roadsides, glades, and open forests in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; frequent in southwestern, south-central, and west-central British Columbia, and less frequent northward; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to Idaho and California.
Description_Botanical: An extremely striking rhizomatous perennial forb up to 1.5 m in height with large purple-blue flowers and whorled leaves, developing from a branched, somewhat rhizomatous stem-base with erect stems up to 1.5 m tall, generally unbranched, cylindric-hollow at the base, usually nearly glabrous but sometimes soft- or stiff-hairy, and a few basal and alternate stem leaves that are palmately compound, the stalks of the basal leaves often much longer than those of the stem leaves, bearing 9 to 17 elliptic-oblanceolate leaflets pointed at the tip, 3-12 cm long, glabrous above, and sparsely stiff-hairy below. Prefers soils that are relatively wet through winter.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: An extremely striking rhizomatous perennial forb up to 1.5 m in height with large purple-blue flowers and whorled leaves, developing from a branched, somewhat rhizomatous stem-base with erect stems up to 1.5 m tall, generally unbranched, cylindric-hollow at the base, usually nearly glabrous but sometimes soft- or stiff-hairy, and a few basal and alternate stem leaves that are palmately compound, the stalks of the basal leaves often much longer than those of the stem leaves, bearing 9 to 17 elliptic-oblanceolate leaflets pointed at the tip, 3-12 cm long, glabrous above, and sparsely stiff-hairy below.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal (a few) and alternate along the stem, palmately compound, the stalks of the basal leaves often much longer than those of the stem leaves; leaflets 9 to 17, elliptic-oblanceolate, pointed at the tip, 3-12 cm long, glabrous above, sparsely stiff-hairy below.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a dense, stalked, terminal raceme, up to 40 cm long, of whorled or somewhat scattered, pea-like flowers; corollas bluish to violet, glabrous, 11-16 mm long, the banner nearly circular and slightly shorter than the wings; calyces about equally 2-lipped, both lips entire or minutely toothed.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Pods, curved, densely long-soft-hairy, 3-5 cm long; seeds 6 to 10, greyish with dark mottling.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Plants may be used for prairie or wetland restoration as an important component of the native flora. They are deep rooted and suitable for erosion control and soil stabilization. Also, as a native legume, they can be used in revegetation of logging roads or clear cuts as nitrogen fixers (Pojar and MacKinnon, 1994).
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixer that elevates site fertility and accelerates canopy closure; in low-nutrient Garry oak or alpine meadows, space carefully so vigorous nitrogen responders do not crowd slow forbs.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Although bigleaf lupine prefers cool, subalpine climates and damp to wet soils, it can also tolerate full sun and seasonally drier soils (Robson et al., 2008). Observations indicate it can even prefer acidic, nutrient-poor mineral soils, giving it a competitive advantage over other plants in the community (Fremstad, 2010).
Mycorrhizal_Association: Arbuscular Mycorrhizal (AM) & Rhizobial Nitrogen-Fixing (Bradyrhizobium / Rhizobium nodules)
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in moist to mesic meadows, riverbars, streambanks, seashores, clearings, roadsides, glades, and open forests in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; frequent in southwestern, south-central, and west-central British Columbia, and less frequent northward; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to Idaho and California. This species prefers moist habitats and seasonally wet soils, but will tolerate seasonal dryness (Robson et al., 2008). It is commonly found in a variety of habitat types including seasonally dry to marshy meadows, wetlands and damp forests, along stream banks and ditches, and in disturbed areas (Turner and Gustafson, 2006). Bigleaf lupine is native to western North America, from British Columbia and Alberta south to California and east to Montana, Idaho, and Nevada.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Bigleaf lupine can be hard-seeded, so physical or chemical scarification can improve uniformity of germination.
Stratification_Dormancy: Prior to planting, reduction of the weed seed bank on site and proper field preparation is important. Bigleaf lupine, like many legumes, has hard - coated seeds, so will germinate unevenly if not scarified prior to sowing.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Scarified seeds or plugs should be started in moist to wet soils. The preferred planting method for seed production fields of this species is to plant plugs on wide row spacing (61–91.4 cm) to accommodate plant size and weed management strategies. Direct seeding is not recommended because weeds can out-compete seedlings in the spring.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are a number of horticultural cultivars available commercially that are sometimes called bigleaf lupines but are actually crosses of L. polyphyllus with L. arboreus and possibly L. nootkatensis. These Russell Hybrids (named for British horticulturist George Russell) are sold under hybrid names such as Rainbow Lupins, Lupin Tutti Fruitti, and Band of Nobles (mixed), Chandelier (yellow), My Castle (red), Noble Maiden (white), The Chatelaine (pink), and The Governor (blue).
Pruning_Management: Planting in late fall, near a water source, or with irrigation is ideal for emerging L. polyphyllus seedlings. As they mature, however, the established plants are often very prolific and hearty and will not necessarily require irrigation throughout the dry season.

Ethno_Medicinal: Tribes throughout the range of bigleaf lupine reportedly used different parts of the plant for medicinal or tonic purposes. Although the Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribes of British Columbia considered it poisonous, they used it medicinally for themselves and their horses. The Salishan used it to make tonics and the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) ate the roots, fresh or steamed.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Seeds toxic to livestock (particularly sheep/cattle) and pets when ingested raw.

Summary_Public: Low-growing Perennial Sedge (10-30 cm) with brown-yellow flowers (spreads by rhizomes). Description_Botanical: One of the few dryland sedges of our region and a valued for people who are trying to plant or restore realistic Garry Oak meadow and woodlands. A low-growing perennial sedge (10-30 cm) with brown-yellow flowers that spreads by rhizomes rather than stolons.

Summary_Public: A perennial forb and herb arising from tuberous roots, bearing deep-blue, bilaterally symmetric flowers on plants 20-60 cm in height. Inhabiting meadows, rocky slopes, and woodlands, as well as mesic to dry grassy bluffs, meadows, and forest openings in the lowland and lower montane zones, this species is common in southwestern British Columbia and extends south to Oregon, with a habitat presence also noted in meadows, rocky slopes, and woodlands.
Description_Botanical: A perennial forb and herb arising from tuberous roots, bearing deep-blue, bilaterally symmetric flowers on plants 20-60 cm in height. Perennial herb from tuberous roots; stems slender, erect, simple or branched above, 35-70 cm tall, minutely-hairy, sometimes glandular, bases often reddish. At flowering time, there are none to 4 basal leaves and 3 to 7 alternate stem leaves with stalks 0.5-11 cm long. Leaf blades are round, 1.5-5 cm long and 3-9 cm wide, reduced upward, and palmately divided, with leaflets incised into narrowly oblong to linear segments.

Summary_Public: Fast-growing, adaptable, broad upright Deciduous Shrub up to 3-4 m height with large white early fragrant flowers. Found in thickets, woodlands, moist to dry talus slopes, shrublands, streamsides, and open forests across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; frequent in southern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Alberta and south to Montana, Idaho, and northern California.
Description_Botanical: A showy fast-growing fragrant shrub with large white flowers that are sure to attract Western Tiger Swallowtail, Pale Swallowtail, Anna's Hummingbird, and a plethora of native bees. A fast-growing, adaptable, broad upright deciduous shrub, erect and loosely branched, reaching 1.5-3 m tall (or 3-4 m height, and 0.9–3 m tall). Deciduous shrub, erect, loosely branched, 1.5-3 m tall; bark reddish-brown, turning grey and flaking off in patches; twigs glabrous to hairy.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous shrub, erect, loosely branched, 1.5-3 m tall; bark reddish-brown, turning grey and flaking off in patches; twigs glabrous to hairy.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, short-stalked, widely egg-shaped to rounded, 3-5 cm long, margins entire to toothed, flat with 3 major veins from the leaf base, slightly sand-papery to touch.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of 3-15 flowers in a raceme; petals 4, white, 5-20 mm long, oblong; calyces top-shaped or bell-shaped, 4-6 mm long, 4-lobed, the lobes egg-shaped, 5-6 mm long; stamens yellow, numerous, unequal. The inflorescence is a raceme composed of 3-15 flowers.

Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Woody, 4-chambered capsules measuring 1 cm long, containing many brown, spindle-shaped seeds 2.5-3 mm long.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Seed propagation is ordinarily used where uniformity of plant characteristics is not an issue, such as in conservation plantings.
Stratification_Dormancy: Dried capsules are collected in late summer and crushed to release the seed. Seeds that were cold stratified in coarse moist sand for 8 weeks at cold stratification temperatures and placed in coarse sand medium at warm greenhouse temperatures germinated at 64 to 72 percent.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Three samples of seed averaged 5,300,000 seeds per pound. Fall sowing is an alternative to cold stratification.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: The Pullman Plant Materials Center, NRCS, Pullman, Washington released two mockoranges in 2002 as selected class releases. These were St. Maries Germplasm (St. Maries, Idaho) and Colfax Germplasm (Colfax, Washington). Lewis' mockorange is propagated via seeds, hardwood and softwood cuttings. Vegetative propagation of cultivar material is recommended to maintain uniformity of desired characteristics. Lewis mockorange is readily propagated by seed, stem cuttings, layering, root suckers, or division.
Pruning_Management: Native and Conservation Stands: Mockorange is moderately tolerant of browsing but heavy grazing by wild ungulates and livestock has a negative impact.
Nursery_Availability: These materials both produced seed in the third year after being planted.

Summary_Public: Perennial Forb from elongated bulb, 15 – 40 cm height with nodding bell-shaped pink to rose-purple or whitish flowers; bulbs multiply quickly. Inhabiting rock outcrops, woodlands, and shorelines, as well as dry to mesic rocky bluffs, grassy slopes, meadows, and open forests in the lowland and steppe to subalpine zones, this species is common in British Columbia south of 56°N, extending east to Ontario and south to New York, North Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi, Texas, Wyoming, Utah, Idaho, and Oregon, also occurring on dry poor gravelly or sandy soils and exposed meadows.
Description_Botanical: This slender perennial arises from a cluster of unique, elongated bulbs. Its slender stems, often gently curved, reach a height of 10-50 cm and are adorned with linear basal leaves. The plant culminates in a nodding cluster of compact bell-shaped flowers, ranging in color from delicate pink to rose-purple or whitish.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Its slender stems, often gently curved, reach a height of 10-50 cm and are adorned with linear basal leaves.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves several per bulb, linear, flat to channeled, shorter than the flowering stem, about 3 mm wide, smooth, the margins entire or minutely toothed; stem leaves lacking.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a compact, terminal, nodding umbel of several to many stalked flowers, subtended by 2 membranous bracts, the stalks 1-3 cm long, the bracts soon deciduous; flowers pink to rose-purple or whitish, bell-shaped, comprising 6 distinct tepals, the tepals 4-6 mm long, elliptic-egg-shaped, blunt; stamens 6, exserted; pistil 1, 3-chambered.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, more or less egg-shaped, 3-lobed, with 6 crests, 2 on each lobe; seeds 6 or fewer, dull-black.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Spread_Behavior: Slowly multiplying clump from underground bulbs or corms
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Bulb / Corm / Tuber); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.

Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Deciduous Shrub up to 0.5-3 m height with large open aromatic pink/lilac-pink flowers, thorny stems, and large reddish-orange rose hips high in Vit C. Inhabiting meadows, riparian areas, mesic to moist thickets, forest edges, river terraces, shorelines, streambanks, clearings, and roadsides in lowland and montane zones.
Description_Botanical: Large open pink flowers that are aromatic and pollinator-friendly. Rosa nutkana is a rhizomatous deciduous shrub reaching 0.5 to 3 m in height (0.3–2.7 m tall), characterized by large, open, aromatic pink to lilac-pink flowers and stout to spindly, erect to arching stems that become blackish at maturity.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Rosa nutkana is a rhizomatous deciduous shrub reaching 0.5 to 3 m in height (0.3–2.7 m tall), characterized by large, open, aromatic pink to lilac-pink flowers and stout to spindly, erect to arching stems that become blackish at maturity.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, odd-pinnately compound, the leaf-stalk and axis glandular-hairy or short-hairy; leaflets 5 or 7 (9), elliptic to egg-shaped, 1-7 cm long, coarsely single- or double-toothed, somewhat glandular-short-hairy beneath; stipules usually glandular-blunt-toothed.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences comprise typically single, sometimes 2 or 3, stalked flowers borne on lateral branchlets; corollas pink, saucer-shaped, large, 4-8 cm across, consisting of 5 petals (2) 2.5-4 cm long; calyces smooth or glandular-bristly, 5-lobed, the lobes lanceolate, 1.5-4 cm long, long-tapering and narrowing before flaring below the tip, persistent; ovaries superior yet enclosed within the urn-shaped floral tube (hypanthium); stamens numerous.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 4-8 cm across; 2.5-4 cm long; 1.5-4 cm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes, numerous, stiffly long-hairy on one side, enclosed by the fleshy hypanthium, which ripens into a purplish-red, globe- to pear-shaped hip 1-2 cm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Rosa nutkana plants are sexually reproductive after 2 to 5 years of growth (Reed, 1993).
Fall_Winter_Interest: Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Light_Tags: Full Sun; Part Shade; Full Shade
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: It is adapted to medium and fine textured soils with neutral pH (USDA NRCS, 2012). It can tolerate low levels of fertility but does not tolerate drought (USDA NRCS, 2012).
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting meadows, riparian areas, mesic to moist thickets, forest edges, river terraces, shorelines, streambanks, clearings, and roadsides in lowland and montane zones. Common throughout British Columbia south of 55°N (except in the Chilcotin area), infrequent northward, and absent in northeastern British Columbia; ranging north to Alaska and south to California, Colorado, and Utah. Rosa nutkana is an understory plant in dry and moist forest communities, including Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa), mountain hemlock (Tsuga mertensiana), Sitka spruce (Picea sitchensis), lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and western hardwoods (Reed, 1993). It is often found in association with red-osier dogwood (Cornus sericea), quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides), black cottonwood (Populus trichocarpa) and snowberry (Symphoricarpos albus) (Aller et al., 1981).

Summary_Public: Medium to tall deciduous shrub up to 4 m tall with multiple upright, arching stems, pithy/ridged stems, grayish-green shallowly-toothed leaves, and sweet-scented creamy-white lilac-like flower plumes; extremely hard wood. Thriving in forests, woodlands, thickets, and rocky slopes—as well as dry to mesic bluffs, clearings, forest edges, and open forests spanning the lowland to montane zones—this plant is common in southern British Columbia with a disjunct population in the Bella Coola valley, and ranges south to Idaho, Montana, and California.
Description_Botanical: Drought-tolerant deciduous shrub up to 4 m with showy cascading white flowers. A drought-tolerant, medium to tall deciduous flowering shrub reaching 1–4 m in height, featuring extremely hard wood, multiple upright, arching, pithy/ridged, and hairy stems; young stems are ridged, while older stems bear reddish-grey, peeling bark. The cascading, showy, sweet-scented creamy-white lilac-like flower plumes bloom from June through July, supporting wildlife including nesting Bushtits, seed-foraging birds, and butterflies ovipositing on buds and leaves.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Medium to tall deciduous shrub up to 4 m tall with multiple upright, arching stems, pithy/ridged stems, grayish-green shallowly-toothed leaves, and sweet-scented creamy-white lilac-like flower plumes; extremely hard wood. Summary_Public: Deciduous Woody Vine up to 10 m tall with trumpet-shaped orange-yellow tubular flowers followed by red berries. Description_Botanical: A deciduous woody vine featuring orange tubular flowers and orange-coloured fruit. This deciduous woody vine grows up to 10 m tall, twining, trailing, or climbing, sometimes reaching 6 m high, with widely branching, hollow, glabrous twigs that are glaucous when young. Foliage is opposite, short-stalked to nearly stalked, elliptic to oval, 4-10 cm long, 2.5-5 cm wide, entire, rounded to pointed at the tip, and glabrous except for a fringe of long hairs along the edges and glaucous beneath, with the end pair on each flowering twig joined to form a disk around the stem below the inflorescence. Deciduous Woody Vine up to 10 m tall with trumpet-shaped orange-yellow tubular flowers followed by red berries.

Found in riparian areas, thickets, woodlands, moist to wet open forests, streambanks, upper beaches, shoreline thickets, estuary fringes, swamps, and bogs in the lowland zone; common on coastal islands and the adjacent mainland, ranging north to Alaska and south to California.
Description_Botanical: A deciduous tree or tall shrub up to 5-12 m (or 2-8 m) tall with tight intertwined wood grain, armed with short, sharp, thorn-like spur-shoots.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: The plant is armed with short, sharp spines.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, lance- to egg-shaped, long-stalked, the blades 3-9 cm long, sharp-pointed at the tip, saw-toothed and often irregularly lobed, green and smooth or hairy above, paler and hairy below. L, H, Ah, Ae, Bhg+Btj, Cg1, Cg2 / LF, H, Ahe, Aeg, Btg, Cg1, Cg2.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences flat-topped clusters of 5 to 12 long-stalked flowers on short spur-shoots; corollas white to pink, fragrant, about 2 cm across, the petals 5, egg-shaped, 8-14 mm long; calyces hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes lanceolate, bent back, 3-5 mm long, deciduous; ovaries inferior; styles usually 3, smooth; stamens about 20. Calyces are pubescent, 5-lobed, with lanceolate, reflexed lobes measuring 3-5 mm long that are deciduous.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 2 cm across; 8-14 mm long; 3-5 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Fleshy pomes (small apples), ellipsoid to egg-shaped, 1-1.5 cm long, green becoming yellow to reddish or purplish, 3- to 4-chambered; seeds 1 or 2 per chamber.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Long-lived perennial understory tree establishing deeply within 2–3 growing seasons.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Qwa’up-ulhp grows in moist, open woodlands, and near marshes, the ocean and water courses. Although qwa’up-ulhp has many uses, one of the important ones is as a club. Its very tightly intertwined (sqaytth’ulus) grain means that it wouldn’t fall apart upon impact.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Yellow-orange autumn foliage and persistent small pomes add late-season interest.
Spread_Behavior: Woody crown and lateral root system
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Deep lateral / Taproot / Woody burl); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.

It also occupies riparian areas, thickets, woodlands, moist forests, swamps, streams, ponds, beaches, and estuaries (noted in regions; and Tl'ches, San Juan, and Gulf Islands 14).

Summary_Public: Deciduous shrub up to 4 m tall with reddish peeling papery/attractive bark; 3-5 lobed serrated leaves; small white 5-petaled flowers with pink stamens in clusters ('Snowball bush'). Summary_Public: Deciduous monecious tree up to 25 m tall with smooth grey lichened bark; inner bark turns rusty red when cut; soft, spongy orange cambium; male/female catkins; small winged nutlets in brown cone-like fruits (t’um’ekw’un). Found in woodlands, forests, floodplains, streambanks, clearcuts, slides, creeks, beaches, and riparian zones across lowland and montane zones, this taxon is common in coastal British Columbia, extending north to southeast Alaska and south to California.
Description_Botanical: This versatile deciduous shrub or tree can reach a prominent height of 25 meters. Its bark, often adorned with lichens, presents a distinctive tapestry of yellowish-brown and grey-white splotches. The smooth leaves, with their unique outward-pointing teeth and rolled-under margins, add a touch of distinction. Before the leaves fully emerge, the tree unveils a compact display of male and female catkins.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous monecious tree up to 25 m tall with smooth grey lichened bark; inner bark turns rusty red when cut. This versatile deciduous shrub or tree can reach a prominent height of 25 meters.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, smooth, coarsely to irregularly toothed, the teeth pointing outwards, leaf margins rolled under, brownish in the fall.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of male and female catkins which open before the leaves enlarge; male catkins with stalks. Inflorescence composed of staminate and pistillate catkins expanding prior to leaf expansion; staminate catkins pedunculate.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Small nutlets, with narrow-winged margins; female cones 1.5-2.5 cm long, egg-shaped.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Mature seeds can be collected beginning in May.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Red alder bark may be boiled to yield a dye or to be used as medicine. The wood may be used for smoking fish.
Spread_Behavior: Woody crown and lateral root system
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixer that elevates site fertility and accelerates canopy closure; in low-nutrient Garry oak or alpine meadows, space carefully so vigorous nitrogen responders do not crowd slow forbs.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Clay; Rocky / Shallow; Rich / Organic
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Red alder has two adaptations that allow the trees to colonize bare infertile substrates: (1) the roots have nodules that house symbiotic bacteria which fix nitrogen from the air contained in the pores of the soil, and (2) the seeds need sunlight to germinate. Actinomycetes (filamentous bacteria) in the genus Frankia invade alders through their root hairs and stimulate cell division, forming nodules on the roots Species of Frankia remove nitrogen from the air and ‘fix’ it in a form useful to plants. Red alder provides a home for the actinomycete, which in turn ‘leaks’ some of the nitrogen, making it available for the alder.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Dual Ectomycorrhizal (EcM) & Actinorhizal Nitrogen-Fixing (Frankia root nodules)
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in woodlands, forests, floodplains, streambanks, clearcuts, slides, creeks, beaches, and riparian zones across lowland and montane zones, this taxon is common in coastal British Columbia, extending north to southeast Alaska and south to California. It is frequently associated with mixed evergreen and redwood forests, often forming communities with red alder trees. Red alder itself is primarily observed in moist areas within 200 kilometers of the Pacific Coast from Alaska to southern California at elevations below 762 meters, and ranges along streams and lakes from the Yukon Territory and British Columbia south through the Rocky Mountain region to Colorado and New Mexico, and along the Sierra Nevada to Lower California. Due to increased human disturbance such as logging, it has also successfully colonized upland areas.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: Red Alder has female cones and male catkins on the same tree (monecious). The female cones are what produce the winged nutlets that fall to the ground in winter. You can collect the cones and dry them just a little to release the seeds or collect the seeds directly off the ground.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Red alder prefers moist, well-drained, deep sandy loams and full sun.
Pruning_Management: If desired, red alder trees can be pruned for shape when young. Follow up pruning is minimal and consists of removing any suckers that may form as well as removing dead wood or crossing branches.

Description_Botanical: Taprooted perennial (25-100 cm) with characteristic reddish-orange flowers with spurred petals and delicate, distinctive foliage. It grows best in medium moisture in partial shade, but in deeper soils can be planted with more sunlight.

Summary_Public: Fast-growing Deciduous Shrub up to 2-6 m height with conical clusters of small white/creamy flowers, pithy hollow stems, and small shiny red berry clusters (leaves/stems/roots poisonous). Large shrub bearing clusters of red, waxy, pulpy berries.
Description_Botanical: A fast-growing, large, deciduous shrub inhabiting moist to wet sites in nutrient-rich soils, reaching 2-6 m in height. Conical clusters of small white flowers turn to an array of small red berries in early summer that are a favourite of many local birds. It features thick, soft, pithy, usually somewhat glaucous twigs, dark reddish-brown warty bark, and conical clusters of small white to creamy flowers that develop into clusters of small, shiny, red, waxy, pulpy berries (leaves, stems, and roots are poisonous) which are favored by local birds. Foliage is opposite, stalked, large, and compound, pinnately divided into 5-7 elliptic to lanceolate leaflets that are often asymmetric at the base, abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip, saw-toothed on the margins, and usually somewhat hairy beneath.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Fast-growing Deciduous Shrub up to 2-6 m height with conical clusters of small white/creamy flowers, pithy hollow stems, and small shiny red berry clusters (leaves/stems/roots poisonous).
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, stalked, large, compound, pinnately divided into 5-7 elliptic to lanceolate leaflets, often asymmetric at the base, abruptly sharp-pointed at the tip, saw-toothed on the margins, and usually somewhat hairy beneath.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence consists of numerous small flowers arranged in an egg-shaped to conical cluster 4-10 cm long with short lateral branches along a prominent central axis; corollas are white or cream, wheel-shaped, featuring petals fused at the base into a short, flat tube that spreads 3-6 mm across at the apex into 5 lobes that are longer than the tubes and ultimately become reflexed.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Fruit berrylike, globose, 5-6 mm across, shiny red or purplish-black, occasionally brown, yellow, or whitish, but not glaucous, containing 3 small, smooth to wrinkled or pebbled stones, each enclosing a single seed.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Red elderberry is a large shrub that produces creamy white flowers and large clusters of small red berries. The fruits are edible, but are cooked before eating. Kwulala’ulhp is a very fast-growing tree that thrives on logged sites, slides, creeks, rivers, beaches, and often dominating riparian areas.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.

Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurs in rich forests, woodlands, riparian areas, thickets, moist to mesic meadows, ditches, streambanks, grasslands, shrublands, disturbed areas, and forests in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones. Variety arborescens is common in and west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, variety melanocarpa is common east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains and less frequent to the west, and variety leucocarpa is infrequent in south-central and southeastern British Columbia. Variety arborescens ranges north to Alaska and Yukon and south to California; variety melanocarpa ranges east to Alberta and south to New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and northern California; variety leucocarpa ranges east to Quebec and New Brunswick and south to Tennessee and Georgia. Also found in rich forests, woodlands, and partially shaded riparian wet areas.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: Redmaid seeds and greens were an important food source for many tribes in California including those whose territory neighbored the Salinan. The shiny black seeds were a major ingredient in pinole (from the Aztec word for seed flour, pinolli) and were valued for their high oil content. Small black oil-rich seeds gathered, parched, and ground into nutritious meal.
Ethno_Material_Tech: The seeds were separated by shaking or hitting the plants over the cleaned area or into a basket. Then they were placed into a tightly woven winnowing basket where they were tossed, allowing the moving air to remove any chaff. The seeds were then dried for storage or parched in a cooking basket along with hot coals.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Not only were the seeds used as ceremonial offerings, as evidenced by these burial sites, but also they are often mentioned in Chumash myths.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Dense stands can spread aggressively and crowd out surrounding vegetation if unmanaged.

Summary_Public: Upright, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub, 1 to 6 m tall; young branches reddish-green in summer, bright red in winter; simple, opposite ovate leaves turning rich red in fall; greenish-white flowers in flat cymes; white to bluish-white drupe fruits. Deciduous upright shrub, 1 to 3 m high, with spreading rhizomes/prostrate lower branches; deep-red finely hairy twigs with white pith; oval to ovate-lanceolate leaves; flat terminal clusters of white flowers; white round succulent drupe fruit.
Description_Botanical: An upright, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub 1 to 6 m (or 1.4-6 m) tall, spreading by rhizomes, prostrate lower branches, or layering of prostrate stems that simulate stolons. Young branches are reddish-green in summer, bright red in winter, maturing to reddish-purple or greyish-green, with deep-red pubescent twigs possessing white pith. Leaves are simple, opposite, oval to ovate-lanceolate, 4-12 cm (or 5-10 cm) long, dark green above and hairy, lighter-colored or whitish below, turning rich red in autumn, featuring smooth margins, rounded bases, pointed tips, and 5-7 prominent parallel or falsely parallel veins converging at the leaf tips with white threads running through them. Inflorescences are flat cymes or terminal clusters of 2-3 mm white to cream-colored flowers blooming from June to August.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Upright, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub, 1 to 6 m tall; young branches reddish-green in summer, bright red in winter. Deciduous, perennial, upright shrub, 1 to 3 m high, with spreading rhizomes; lower branches often prostrate; deep-red (green-purple) pubescent twigs.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, deciduous, oval, pointed, 4-12 cm long, greenish above, whitish below, turning reddish in the autumn, 5-7 prominent parallel veins converging at the leaf tips, white threads running through the veins.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence takes the form of flat-topped terminal clusters, 2-4 cm wide; flowers are white to greenish-white, possessing 4 petals and stamens, with inconspicuous bracts.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Drupes are berrylike, 7-9 mm long, white and sometimes blue-tinged, each containing a flattened stone.

Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic but vigorous clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); forms thickets that outcompete slow-establishing forbs—allow generous spacing or use root barriers in tight borders.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Rocky / Shallow; Rich / Organic
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Redosier dogwood grows in soils that are saturated for at least a portion of the growing season. Not as tolerant of long-term root saturation as are some other shrubs, dogwood seems to prefer wetland margins where soils are nitrogen-rich, saturated, and shallowly inundated in the spring, and may be completely dry by late summer.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabits swamps, thickets, riparian areas, and woodlands, thriving in wet to mesic streamsides, lakesides, swamps, and forests across lowland, steppe, and montane zones. Common throughout British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to West Virginia, Ohio, Nebraska, New Mexico, California, and Mexico. Found along bottomland streambanks and floodplains with fluctuating water tables, nutrient-rich soils, ditches, swamps, and thickets; dry to moist soils (2); the understory of Littlewood Forest (7); moist woods, ponds, riverbanks, thickets, clearings, coulees, and flood plains throughout the Canadian prairies; widespread across Alberta, ranging from Alaska to California, New Mexico, and Ohio (26); and from Ohio to Maine south to Virginia and New Jersey, preferring moist, moderately acidic to neutral medium or coarse soils (43).

Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: ‘Alman’s Compacta’, ‘Allamans’, ‘Bailey’, ‘Cardinal’, ‘Coloradensis’, ‘Flaviromea’, ‘Isanti’, ‘Kelseyi’, ‘Lutea’, ‘Ruby’, ‘Silver’ and ‘Gold’, and ‘White Gold’ have been planted in the growing range of redosier dogwood. Consult your local nurseries to choose the right cultivar for your specific landscape.
Pruning_Management: Redosier dogwood is often coppiced in late fall after the leaves turn brown and fall off the stem. Cut all stems to approximately 2-3 in (5-8 cm) from the base before growth begins in spring. Apply fertilizer around the shrub to promote new growth, then apply mulch around the base. Coppicing stimulates the growth of new, vigorous stems whose deep burgundy color is especially vivid.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: Tea from roots treats dizziness. Fruit bitter, eaten fresh/dried/mixed in cakes. Root tea for dizziness.
Ethno_Medicinal: Tea from stems relieves chest trouble, coughs, fevers, or used as an emetic. Bark decoction as laxative. Peeled bark mixed with other plants treats sore eyes.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Some tribes ate the white, sour berries, while others used the branches for arrow-making, stakes, or other tools. Stems used for spruce bark canoe ribs. Dream catchers, dye, baskets, tanning hides, arrows, tools, toothbrushes.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Native Americans smoke the inner bark of redosier dogwood in tobacco mixtures used in the sacred pipe ceremony. Dream catchers, originating with the Potawotami, are made with the stems of the sacred redosier dogwood.

Summary_Public: Deciduous rhizomatous shrub, 1-4 m tall, erect or arching; new stems densely prickly; large deep pink/magenta flowers; pinnately compound leaves; round yellow/orange/deep red aggregate berries. Thriving in forests, riparian areas, swamps, thickets, woodlands, and moist to wet wetland habitats below 1400 m, including streambanks in lowland and montane zones (notably within the CWHvh2 subzone), this taxon is common in coastal British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska and south to California from the coast to the Cascades.
Description_Botanical: A moisture-loving spring-blooming deciduous shrub, preferring rich soils and part shade to shade. Hummingbirds are attracted to the fuschia-coloured flowers and multi-coloured berries are savoured by local birds. Salmonberry (Rose Family, Rosaceae) is a moisture-loving, spring-blooming deciduous rhizomatous shrub, 1-4 m tall, often thicket-forming, with erect or arching stems. Stems vary from unarmed to strongly bristly, especially below with short, straight bristles, while new stems may be densely prickly on upper portions, with twigs in winter showing a distinctive golden-brown to rust-red color and shredding yellowish-brown bark.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous rhizomatous shrub, 1-4 m tall, erect or arching; new stems densely prickly. A moisture-loving spring-blooming deciduous shrub, preferring rich soils and part shade to shade.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, pinnately compound, 7-22 cm long; leaflets 3, egg-shaped, 3-15 cm long, shallowly lobed and double-saw-toothed, sharply long-pointed at the tip, greenish on both surfaces, smooth to sparsely hairy above, paler and hairy on the veins beneath; stipules linear, 5-10 mm long.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 7-22 cm long; 3-15 cm long; 5-10 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of mostly 1 or 2 stalked, nodding flowers on short, leafy, lateral branchlets; corollas rosy red to reddish-purple, bowl-shaped, the petals 5, spreading, elliptic to egg-shaped, 10-25 mm long; calyces hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes lance-egg-shaped, spreading, 7-15 mm long; ovaries superior; stamens 75 to 100. Inflorescences consist of mostly 1 or 2 stalked, nodding flowers borne on short, leafy, lateral branchlets.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Drupelets, smooth, more or less coherent in a yellow or salmon to dark red cluster that falls intact from the semi-fleshy receptacle (raspberry-like), the berries 1.5-2 cm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Salmonberry shrubs produce pink to reddish - purple flowers and edible fruits that range in color from yellow to red to purple. Lila’ is a common small shrub on the West Coast. It occurs in riparian areas near rivers, lakes, creeks and by the ocean.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Light_Tags: Full Sun; Part Shade; Full Shade
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: River valleys, moist coastal rainforests, streamsides, riparian zones, and disturbed forest sites (below 1,400 m elevation).
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Stratification_Dormancy: Salmonberry grows well in full or partial shade. Cultivars are available in the horticultural trade.
Pruning_Management: This plant grows very rapidly in moist, shady conditions; if summer drought occurs, water so roots remain fairly moist. Traditional resource management includes pruning branches after berry harvest to stimulate new growth and fruit production under family-tended patches.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: Edible fruit. Salmonberry fruits are edible, but are considered too soft to dry. Both the large, raspberry-like fruit and the young shoots were widely eaten by coastal peoples of British Columbia and western Washington.
Ethno_Medicinal: Quileute chewed leaves (or bark in winter) and spat on burns. Bark pounded and laid on aching tooth or festering wound. The Quinault boil the bark in seawater, and the brew is drank to lessen labor pains and to clean infected wounds, especially burns. The Quileute chew the leaves and apply them to burns, using the bark in winter when leaves are unavailable.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Branches used for tools/implements. Leaves boiled with fish as flavoring, used to line baskets, wipe fish, and cover food in steaming pits.
