Summary_Public: Functioning as a perennial bunchgrass with a height of 15-80 cm, it forms a more or less densely tufted habit from fibrous roots, producing stems 15-120 cm tall. Found in meadows and rocky slopes, specifically inhabiting dry to moist meadows and grasslands from the steppe to lower alpine zones.
Description_Botanical: Tolerates some trampling. Functioning as a perennial bunchgrass with a height of 15-80 cm, it forms a more or less densely tufted habit from fibrous roots, producing stems 15-120 cm tall. Sheath margins are open 3/4-9/10 their length, and sterile shoots emerge inside sheaths while breaking through the sheath bases.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Functioning as a perennial bunchgrass with a height of 15-80 cm, it forms a more or less densely tufted habit from fibrous roots, producing stems 15-120 cm tall.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Sheath margins open 3/4-9/10 their length; sterile shoots emerging inside sheaths and breaking through the sheath bases; blades 0.4-3 (5) mm wide, often glaucous (ssp. juncifolia), flat, folded, or in-rolled, thin or thick, smooth or rough; ligules 0.5-10 mm long, the tips blunt to long-pointed, the backs smooth or rough.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an erect, somewhat lax panicle, 2-25 cm long, usually moderately green or purplish, narrowly lanceolate to egg-shaped, congested, more or less open in flower and contracted at maturity, infrequently permanently open, some glaucous, the branches usually 1 to 3 per node, usually appressed or ascending, usually sparsely to distinctly rough on and between weakly developed angles, with spikelets in the terminal 1/2; spikelets weakly laterally compressed to nearly round, usually narrowly lanceolate, green or strongly purplish, 4-8 mm long, some glaucous, (2-) 3- to 10-flowered; glumes broadly lanceolate, the keels indistinct, the lower glumes 3-nerved; rachilla internodes usually exceeding 1 mm long, smooth or rough; lemmas lanceolate to narrowly lanceolate or slightly oblanceolate, weakly keeled, 3.5-5 mm long, the tips rounded to broadly sharp-pointed (with broad thin margins), hairless or minutely soft- to short silky-hairy on the keels and marginal nerves, hairless or hairy between the nerves; calluses hairless or with a crown of hairs up to 0.5 (2) mm long; palea keels rough, medially some minutely soft- or short silky-hairy; flowers bisexual; anthers 1.5-3 mm long.

The species ranges north to extreme southern Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Mexico, Michigan, Minnesota, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Plants occur throughout Western North America with disjunct populations in Quebec and Chile.

Sowing_Protocol_Time: For best results, seed should be planted into a firm, weed-free seedbed, preferably with a drill that will ensure a uniform seed placement of about 6 mm. The small seed can be broadcast seeded, harrowed, and packed for good seed-soil contact; however, in dryland situations good precipitation at the time of germination is critical for emergence and establishment. The full seeding rate is 1.7 kg/ha PLS (2.0 lb/ac PLS), but this species would seldom be seeded in a pure stand. Seed of Sandberg bluegrass should be drilled at 6–19 mm deep depending upon soil type: 6 mm for fine, moist soils, 13 mm for medium textures, and 1.9 cm for coarse or dry soils. On semiarid lands, 3 pounds pure live seed (PLS) per acre is adequate.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Various "ecotypes" should be utilized within a reasonable geographic range from the original source, since available releases are primarily source identified or selected germplasm releases and have not been progeny tested to determine their range of adaptation and performance. Service big bluegrass (Poa ampla) comes from a collection made east of Whitehorse, Yukon Territory, Canada.
Pruning_Management: Sandberg bluegrass will withstand heavy grazing and trampling, in part, because of its early maturity and apparent dormancy during the summer and fall grazing period. When planted in a native reclamation mix, it will be a minor component of the establishing plant community; therefore management should be based on other key species in the mixture. Any new planting should be deferred from livestock grazing until it is well established which may require 1 to 3 years.
Nursery_Availability: Breeder seed is available through the Alaska Plant Materials Center, Palmer, Alaska. It is intended for use in range reseeding, cropland retirement plantings, and revegetation of disturbed lands in mountain brush communities and openings in aspen and conifer forests. Foundation seed is available through Washington State Crop Improvement Association, and breeder seed is maintained by the Pullman, Washington Plant Materials Center. Foundation seed is available through the Washington State Crop Improvement Association. This is the first release of the Nevada bluegrass type to the commercial seed industry. The original collection of this seed came from a site near Wisdom Junction along Highway 1 east of Anaconda, Montana. G1 (equivalent to Foundation) seed is available to commercial growers through the Foundation Seed Program at Montana State University and the University of Wyoming. Seed production field of High Plains Sandberg bluegrass at the Bridger, MT PMC. This is the first release of the Poa sandbergii type to the commercial seed industry. G1 and G2 seed is maintained by the USDA-ARS Forage and Range Research Laboratory, Logan, UT. G3 seed is available through the Utah Crop Improvement Association.

Summary_Public: Deciduous Shrub or tree, 1-7 m height with white flowers and edible purple-black berries; smooth grey/brown branches 9; flexible, strong wood. Inhabiting woodlands, thickets, meadows, dry to mesic open rocky slopes, bluffs, gullies, forest margins, and open forests from the lowland to subalpine zones, this species is common throughout British Columbia, particularly in central and southern regions east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains.
Description_Botanical: A large white-flowering shrub with edible blue berries. Flowers attract pollinators.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A large white-flowering shrub with edible blue berries.

Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences short, drooping to erect, leafy or bracted, terminal racemes at the ends of branches; flowers 3 to 20, on slender ascending stalks; corollas white, the petals 5, linear to lanceolate, 6-25 mm long; calyces 5-lobed, the lobes lance-triangular, 1-5 mm long, the hypanthium 1-2 mm long; ovaries inferior, smooth or hairy on top; stamens about 20. Entry 1 data is missing or not provided.

Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berry-like pomes (like miniature apples), crowned with the persistent calyx, globe- to egg-shaped, 5-14 mm long, dull red initially, becoming purple to nearly black, with a white bloom.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Flowers are produced almost every year, but good seed crops may be produced only every 3-5 years because of drought, spring frost, and/or juniper rust.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting woodlands, thickets, meadows, dry to mesic open rocky slopes, bluffs, gullies, forest margins, and open forests from the lowland to subalpine zones, this species is common throughout British Columbia, particularly in central and southern regions east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains. Its broader distribution extends north to Alaska, east to Alberta, and south to California, Nebraska, North Dakota, Colorado, and Arizona. It ranges from lower-elevation coniferous forests up to timberline, riparian zones, open or shaded disturbed sites, open woodlands, mountain shrublands, coulees, dry bluffs, and oak meadows, and is distributed along the Pacific coast from Alaska to California, eastward to Utah, Colorado, Iowa, Minnesota, Ontario, and Quebec, and north through the plains and prairies into the Northwest Territories of Canada.

Stratification_Dormancy: Seedlings can take up to 5 years before they start to produce fruit, but other starts may begin at 2-4 years old and with proper management can yield 8-10 tons of fruit per hectare. Seeds require cold stratification to break dormancy and may remain viable for 10 or more years.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Saskatoon has been artificially crossed with other species of serviceberry, and similar hybridization and intergradation also occurs in the field, particularly between saskatoon and low serviceberry (Amelanchier humilis Wieg.) Cultivars sold as Amelanchier alnifolia may actually be hybrids between A. alnifolia and other species of Amelanchier. Saskatoon reproduces from seed but more commonly by sprouting from the root crown and rhizomes and by layering.
Pruning_Management: Saskatoon in forests is fire-dependent, occurring in forests with fire regimes varying from frequent, low-severity fire (low-elevation forests) to infrequent, severe fire. It may persist in the understory for decades but eventually dies out with fire exclusion and canopy closure. After top-kill by light-to moderate-severity fire, saskatoon sprouts usually arise from the root crown or from shallowly buried rhizomes; sprouts arise from deeply buried rhizomes after even the most intense fire. Sasktoon cover and biomass production in western Montana may generally increase after fires in Douglas-fir/ninebark habitats, but browsing pressure from big game may slow the recovery.

Summary_Public: Inhabits wet to dry bogs, lower slopes, and high river terraces across lowland, montane, and subalpine zones. Description_Botanical: Tree, mostly to 30 m tall, but up to 40 m; var. latifolia mostly straight and columnar with narrow rounded crown, var. contorta often somewhat contorted and even bonsai-like; bark reddish-brown to blackish, cracked at the base and somewhat flaky above, furrowed and thicker in var. contorta. Var. latifolia is mostly straight and columnar with a narrow rounded crown and yellowish-green needles in groups of two, usually curved and slightly twisted, 2-7 cm long, with seed cones pointing outward. Var. contorta is often somewhat contorted and even bonsai-like, with deep green needles, seed cones pointing backwards on the twig, furrowed and thicker bark, and reddish-brown to blackish bark that is cracked at the base and somewhat flaky above. Seed cones are egg-shaped, lopsided, 3-6 cm long, serotinous, with stiff bracts and armed tips.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A tree growing mostly to 30 m tall, but up to 40 m. Var. latifolia is mostly straight and columnar with a narrow rounded crown and yellowish-green needles in groups of two, usually curved and slightly twisted, 2-7 cm long, with seed cones pointing outward.

Summary_Public: Deciduous Shrub up to 8 m height. Inhabits wetlands and riparian areas, including moist to mesic thickets, floodplains, lakeshores, avalanche tracks, clearings, and forest margins within lowland and montane zones.
Description_Botanical: Deciduous Shrub up to 8 m height. Dioecious shrubs or trees, 1-8 m tall, non-colonial; branches erect with flexible bases; twigs yellow- to red-brown and densely hairy. Leaves alternate, simple, elliptic to lance- or egg-shaped, 3-12 cm long, 1.7-5 cm wide; lower surface very densely silky, satiny, or woolly with white hairs; upper surface dull, sparsely long soft-hairy to nearly smooth; margins entire or toothed; bases pointed; tips rounded to pointed. Leaf stalks lack glandular dots at the top; stipules leaflike or rudimentary.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous Shrub up to 8 m height. Branches erect with flexible bases; twigs yellow- to red-brown and densely hairy.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, simple, elliptic to lance- or egg-shaped, 3-12 cm long, 1.7-5 cm wide, lower surface very densely silky, satiny, or woolly, hairs white, upper surface dull, sparsely long soft-hairy to nearly smooth, margins entire or toothed, bases pointed, tips rounded to pointed; leaf stalks without glandular dots at top; stipules leaflike or rudimentary.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Flowers are unisexual, lacking sepals and petals, and are borne in slender to stout catkins on leafy twigs that flower as the leaves emerge or just before them; floral bracts are pale or dark with straight or wavy hairs; stamens number 1; ovaries number 1 and are hairy, with styles measuring 0.4-0.8 mm long.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules which split open to release the seeds, each of which is surrounded by a tuft of hairs; stalks 0.4-1.4 mm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Seeds are viable for only a few days and the maximum storage period is four to six weeks with germination rates dropping off fast after ten days at room temperature (Dirr & Heuser 1987).
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Sitka willow is found on or near lake shores, wetland margins, forest edges, wet openings, and clearings at low to middle elevations. This species prefers damp, heavy soil but will succeed in most soils.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabits wetlands and riparian areas, including moist to mesic thickets, floodplains, lakeshores, avalanche tracks, clearings, and forest margins within lowland and montane zones. It is common in southern British Columbia south of 56°N, particularly west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, and infrequent northward; ranging north to southern Alaska, east to Alberta, and south to Montana, Idaho, and California. Salix sitchensis is native to stream banks from southern Alaska to southwestern Oregon (Viereck & Little 1972).

Birds_Interactions: Small seeds eaten by birds; Nesting cover for birds. Birds known to eat sedge seeds include coots, ducks (such as wood ducks, canvasbacks, mallards, pintails, teal, shoveler), marsh birds and shorebirds (dowichers, rails, and sandpipers), upland gamebirds (grouse, pheasant, and wild turkey), and songbirds (house finch, junco, sparrow, and towhee). Waterfowl and ducks eat sedge seeds frequently in small to fair amounts.
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: River Otters, Beavers, Deer-resistant. Wetland shelter for otters and beavers; deer-resistant.
Pruning_Management: The leaves of slough sedge are cut in late summer (August). A knife was used to cut the plant at the base, as low to the ground as possible. The best plants were said to be those growing in 10 cm (4 in) of water. The cluster of leaves are cut off or pulled from the tender white bases, where they break off at or just below the ground level.

Ethno_Material_Tech: The leaves of Carex obnupta, are used for both wrapping and twining in the "grass" baskets that are well known and widely marketed by Ditidaht (Nitinaht) and Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) women even today. "Grass" baskets are created using "three-cornered grass" (Scirpus pungens) for the basket bottom and ribs, slough sedge for the wrapping, and the top rim is made of the inner bark of western red cedar (Thuja plicata). Leaves used as basket-making twine (horizontal weave) to create fine, regular, tightly sealed baskets.

Description_Botanical: Perennial Forb, 15-60 cm height. Perennial herb from well-developed, horizontal to ascending rhizomes, clothed with old, brown leaf-bases and stipules; stems 1 to several, erect, 15-60 cm tall, long soft-hairy below, strongly glandular-hairy in the inflorescence. Basal leaves kidney- to heart-egg-shaped, 3–8 cm wide, either shorter than wide with 5 to 7 rounded, shallow lobes, or longer than wide with pointy lobes cleft 1/3 their length, stiff-hairy below and sometimes also above, borne on long stalks that are sparsely to densely hairy or rarely smooth; stem leaves 1 or 2, greatly reduced, the upper bract-like; stipules membranous, fused to the leaf-stalks. Description_Botanical: A rhizomatous perennial forb standing 10-30 cm in height, characterized by pinkish-white flowers with uniquely divided petals. Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Evergreen Shrub 1 to 3 m height with tough glossy spiny holly-like leaves, creeping rhizomes, bright yellow flower clusters, and blue/purple edible berries. Found in meadows, woodlands, thickets, dry slopes, mixed coniferous woods, and the understory of Littlewood Forest, as well as mesic to dry open or closed forests in lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common in southern British Columbia; extending east to Alberta and south to Idaho and Oregon.
Description_Botanical: Evergreen perennial shrub with glossy, prominently toothed leaves that have variable colouration depending on the season (red, yellow, green). Clusters of bright yellow flowers attract bees in early spring, turning to large light blue berries in summer for birds. This plant is sun-loving, but also grows well in partial shade sites. An evergreen perennial shrub 1 to 3 m in height with creeping rhizomes, yellowish bark and wood, and branched, stoloniferous to stiffly erect stems 0.5-2.5 (4.5) m tall.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Evergreen perennial shrub with glossy, prominently toothed leaves that have variable colouration depending on the season (red, yellow, green).
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Evergreen, hollylike, alternate, pinnate; leaflets usually 5-11, pinnately nerved, more than twice as long as broad, mostly with 12-29 prominent spiny teeth, shiny above but less so beneath.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of clustered racemes 3-8 cm long; flowers yellow, the segments in 6's.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Clustered berries 7-14 mm in diameter, blue, glaucous, with a few large seeds.

Summary_Public: Tufted perennial sedge belonging to the species-rich Ovales Tribe, growing 20-50 cm tall with fine foliage, robust brown clustered heads, and green/brown dry single-seeded fruits. Occurs in mesic to wet sites in meadows and woodlands across all vegetation zones; common throughout all but northeastern British Columbia; amphiberingian, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Saskatchewan, and south to Colorado, Utah, Nevada, and California; also in northeastern Asia.
Description_Botanical: This is one of our local sedges in the species-rich Ovales Tribe that grows commonly in fairly moist to wet sites from full sun meadows to partial shade woodlands. Tufted perennial sedge belonging to the species-rich Ovales Tribe, growing 20-50 cm tall with fine foliage, robust brown clustered heads, and green/brown achenes.

Summary_Public: Annual forb, 10-30 cm in height with white and purple-red spotted flowers; annual herb from a taproot with stems 1 to several, spreading to erect, smooth and hairless, 10-70 cm long/tall. Inhabiting mesic to dry meadows and grassy slopes in the lowland zone, as well as rock outcrops, this species is locally frequent on southeastern Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands, and the adjacent mainland, ranging south to California.
Description_Botanical: The most common of the native clovers, this distinctive species thrives on moss-covered rocks and makes a showy addition to a spring wildflower assemblage. It serves as a host plant for the Grey Hairstreak butterfly and is suspected to have been a host for the Island Blue butterfly, which is thought to be extinct. Annual forb, 10-30 cm in height with white and purple-red spotted flowers; annual herb from a taproot with stems 1 to several, spreading to erect, glabrous, 10-70 cm long/tall. Leaves alternate, palmately compound; leaflets 3, linear to lance-oblong or elliptic, 1-4 cm long, the margins usually finely bristle-toothed; stipules egg-shaped, bristle-tipped, the upper jaggedly toothed, 1/3-1/2 as long as the leaflets.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Annual herb from a taproot with stems 1 to several, spreading to erect, glabrous, 10-70 cm long/tall.

Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a head-like, stalked, axillary cluster of 6 to 60 pea-like flowers, the heads 1-3 cm wide, set in wheel-like, irregularly and jaggedly toothed involucres; corollas lavender to purple, 10-13 mm long; calyces 6-10 mm long, shiny and often purplish, the tube 15- to 25-veined, the lanceolate teeth slightly shorter than the tube, bristle-tipped, entire or with 2 teeth flanking the base of the bristle.

Summary_Public: A dioecious deciduous trailing shrub/vine (or trailing shrub), 2-5 m or more long (0.6–1.8 m tall and 1.8 m spread) with 3 dark green serrated leaflets, curved prickly thorns, large white/pink flowers, and soft highly flavourful black aggregate fruit. Native trailing blackberry with smaller fruits than Himalayan variety.
Description_Botanical: Three leaflets, large white flowers and delicious fruits that go from red to purple-black when ripe. A dioecious deciduous trailing shrub/vine (or trailing shrub), 2-5 m or more long (0.6–1.8 m tall and 1.8 m spread) with 3 dark green serrated leaflets, curved prickly thorns, large white/pink flowers, and soft highly flavourful black aggregate fruit. Stems barely woody, 2-10 mm in diameter, arching, sprawling and trailing along the ground, some rooting at the tip, with slender, straight to slightly recurved prickles, somewhat hairy when young becoming smooth and glaucous; flowering branches ascending, to 50 cm tall. Leaves alternate, deciduous, pinnately compound, 5-15 cm long; leaflets 3 (rarely 5), narrowly to broadly egg-shaped, 3-10 cm long, coarsely double-saw-toothed, green and smooth or nearly so on both surfaces, the terminal leaflet largest and often deeply 3-lobed to divided, the leaf-stalks and midveins beneath fine-prickly; stipules linear, 8-11 mm long.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A dioecious deciduous trailing shrub/vine (or trailing shrub), 2-5 m or more long (0.6–1.8 m tall and 1.8 m spread) with 3 dark green serrated leaflets, curved prickly thorns, large white/pink flowers, and soft highly flavourful black aggregate fruit. Native trailing blackberry with smaller fruits than Himalayan variety.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, pinnately compound, 5-15 cm long; leaflets 3 (rarely 5), narrowly to broadly egg-shaped, 3-10 cm long, coarsely double-saw-toothed, green and smooth or nearly so on both surfaces, the terminal leaflet largest and often deeply 3-lobed to divided, the leaf-stalks and midveins beneath fine-prickly; stipules linear, 8-11 mm long.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 5-15 cm long; 3-10 cm long; 8-11 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of few stalked flowers in small, open, flat-topped terminal clusters, the stalks often purplish stalked-glandular; male and female flowers on separate plants; corollas white, the petals 5, spreading, elliptic and 8-11 mm long in female flowers, lanceolate and 12-17 mm long in male flowers; calyces woolly and usually stalked-glandular, sometimes fine-prickly, 5-lobed, the lobes lanceolate, spreading to bent back, 7-11 mm long; ovaries superior; stamens 75 to 100. Plants are dioecious with male and female flowers on separate individuals.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 8-11 mm long; 12-17 mm long; 7-11 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berries consisting of generally smooth drupelets, coherent in a black oblong to nearly globe-shaped cluster that falls with the fleshy receptacle (a blackberry), the berries 1-1.5 cm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Sqw’iil’muhw is a long thin vine that likes to crawl through underbrush in shaded areas of mixed and coniferous forests. The thorns are small and generally much less prevalent than the introduced blackberry that is more common in populated areas. Sqw’iil’muhw berries are often the preferred berries even though they are smaller than and not as plentiful as the introduced blackberries.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Year-round evergreen foliage anchors winter garden structure.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Fibrous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.

Summary_Public: Cool-season robust tufted perennial bunchgrass, 20 to 150 cm tall; shallow roots; rigid linear leaves (1.5-4 mm wide); loose open nodding panicle (10-25 cm); pale purplish sparkling spikelets; 2.5-3.5 mm grain. Saltmarshes, meadows, and shorelines.
Description_Botanical: Long panicles of small flowers sparkle on elongated stalks in summer. Well-suited to, and characteristic of, saline environments, but can be incorporated into wetland plantings and even coastal slopes.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Sheaths open, smooth to rough; blades matted at the base, rather stiff, sometimes flat but most folded or in-rolled, smooth to rough below, rough above, with a few, prominent, raised nerves, 1.5-3 (4) mm wide; ligules entire but often split, hairy, sharp-pointed or rounded, 4-8 mm long.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a loose and open to narrow panicle, 8-30 cm long, the branches spreading or drooping to erect (even at maturity); spikelets usually glistening, purplish to tawny, 2-flowered, rarely 3-flowered, glumes rather narrow, the lower ones 1-nerved, 2.5-5 (6) mm long, the upper ones 3-nerved, often somewhat jagged, 3-6 (7) mm long; lemmas 5-nerved, 2.5-4 mm long, the tips jagged and 4-toothed, awned from the base, the awns 3-5 mm long, straight or bent, the callus hairs about 1 mm long; lodicules egg-shaped to lanceolate, 0.7-1 mm long, anthers 1.2-2.2 mm long.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 8-30 cm long; 2.5-5 mm long; 3-6 mm long; 2.5-4 mm long; 3-5 mm long
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: The species is slow to establish the first year but can dominate a site by the third year if seeding rates are heavy (2.2–3.4 kg/ha).
Discovered_Drive_Details: Restoration and reclamation: It is used for restoration of moist to seasonally wet meadows and freshwater wetlands, and for stabilizing disturbed streambanks, canals, shorelines and upper tidal marshes. It is also used for acid and heavy metal mine spoil reclamation, alpine and boreal revegetation, grassed waterways, turf, and ornamental applications. (Darris and Gonzalves, 2009).
Fall_Winter_Interest: Semi-evergreen
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Moist open areas, salt marshes, high-elevation bogs, and rocky shores; wide soil pH tolerance (3.7–8.3). Moist to wet, seasonally flooded; saline tolerant. A wide range of soil conditions with pH 3.7 to 8.3; adapts to colonize calcareous mine waste, acidified soils, heavy metal contaminated soils, and low nutrient soils.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Saltmarshes, meadows, and shorelines. Saline meadows, beaches and tidal marshes in the lowland zone and moist meadows in the montane to alpine zones (ssp. beringensis ) and moist to mesic meadows, lakes shores, rocky ridges, shrub-carrs and talus slopes in the montane to alpine zones (ssp. cespitosa ); ssp. beringensis - common along the coast, ssp. cespitosa - common in and E of the Coast-Cascade Mountains in BC; ssp. beringensis - amphiberingian, N to AK and S to N WA; ssp. cespitosa - circumpolar, N to AK, YT and NT, E to NF and S to ME, MA, PA, NC, KY, IL, MN, SD, NM, AZ, and CA. Subspecies beringensis is common along the coast, whereas ssp. cespitosa is common in and east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains in British Columbia. Subspecies beringensis is amphiberingian, ranging north to Alaska and south to northern Washington; ssp. cespitosa is circumpolar, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Maine, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Kentucky, Illinois, Minnesota, South Dakota, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, with occurrences in Greenland and Eurasia.

Summary_Public: Annual Forb, 5-30 cm height with small hispid foliage and light pink flowers with yellow/white centres. Occurring in woodlands and forests, specifically in mesic forest openings, sandy or gravelly clearings, and along streambanks in the lowland zone; locally frequent on southern Vancouver Island, and infrequent on the adjacent coast and lower Fraser Valley.
Description_Botanical: Annual forb (5-30 cm) with small hispid foliage and light pink flowers with yellow/white centers. One of the few representatives of the Polemoniaceae (Jacob's Ladder) plant family in the Victoria region.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, mostly stalked, usually hairy and slightly glandular; lower leaves 1-2 times pinnately cleft, the blades to 3.5 cm long and 2 cm wide; middle and upper leaves progressively less divided upwards, the uppermost leaves (below the flower clusters) smaller than the others, nearly unstalked, elliptic, merely toothed or entire.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of dense, head-like, terminal (and sometimes axillary) clusters; corollas pink, lavender or white, the slightly flaring tube 8-17 mm long, spreading to five, 3-4 mm long lobes; calyces 5-8 mm long, the five lobes narrowly lanceolate. Inflorescences form dense, head-like clusters at branch terminals and occasionally in the axils.

Summary_Public: A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. Found in meadows and woodlands, specifically occupying moist to mesic meadows, grassy slopes, coastal bluffs, shores, clearings, and open forests from lowland to subalpine zones; common in coastal and northern British Columbia, infrequent elsewhere, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and Northwest Territories, east to Alberta, and south to California.
Description_Botanical: A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. Perennial herb from a cluster of fibrous roots; stems 1 to several, erect or nearly so, 15-40 (60) cm tall, more or less hollow; plants variously hairy. Basal leaves are broadly egg-shaped, semi-circular, or kidney-shaped, measuring ¾ to 5.1 cm long by ¾ to 7.6 cm wide (specifically blades 1.5-5.5 cm long, 2-8 cm wide), deeply 3-lobed or -parted, with segments 1- to 2-times incised and ultimate segments oblong, elliptic, oblanceolate, or lanceolate, toothed, and tips pointed to rounded; leaf stalks are long, measuring 1 to several times the blade length. Stem leaves are alternate, fewer, stay low to the base, are more deeply dissected, shorter-stalked, and transition to 3- to 7-parted lower bracts and entire upper bracts.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A perennial forb and native member of the Ranunculaceae family, standing 15-50 cm tall (or stems measuring 15-40 (60) cm tall, extending from 15.2 cm to 0.8 m tall) with yellow flowers bearing 5 to 14 petals. The plant arises from a cluster of fibrous roots with 1 to several erect or nearly erect, more or less hollow stems that are variously hairy.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal broadly egg-shaped or semi-circular to kidney-shaped, the blades deeply 3-lobed or -parted, 1.5-5.5 cm long, 2-8 cm wide, the segments 1- to 2-times incised, the ultimate segments oblong or elliptic to oblanceolate or lanceolate, toothed, tips pointed to rounded, the stalks long, 1 to several times the length of blade; stem leaves alternate, more deeply dissected, shorter-stalked, transitional to the 3- to 7-parted lower bracts and entire upper bracts.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences few- to many-flowered cymes terminal on main stem and branches; flower stalks to 10 cm long; receptacle smooth; petals 5 (6-14), distinct, yellow, oblong to narrowly egg-shaped, 5-13 mm long, 1.5-8 mm wide, nectary on upper surface, the nectary scale smooth, almost 1 mm long; sepals 5, bent back 2-3 mm from base, early deciduous, greenish or pinkish-tinged, 4-7 mm long, 2-4 mm wide, long stiff-hairy; stamens 30-60; pistils 5-20. Stamens total 30-60, with 5-20 pistils.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 10 cm long; 5-13 mm long; 1.5-8 mm wide; 1 mm long; 2-3 mm
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes several to many, aggregated in a hemispheric head 3-7 mm long and 5-9 mm wide; individual achenes egg-shaped, 2.6-3.6 mm long, 1.8-3 mm wide, smooth or rarely stiff-hairy, with prominent margins and lacking keels, bearing persistent, somewhat flattened, lanceolate- to awl-shaped, straight or curved beaks 0.4-2.2 mm long.
Discovered_Drive_Details: This native taxon grows as a great choice for wetland prairie restoration throughout its range.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: While western buttercup prefers vernal pools and wetland sites, it will also tolerate drier upland sites away from the coast that retain seasonally moist soils. It also does quite well in plant and seed production fields, tolerating all soil types and a range of pH values.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in meadows and woodlands, specifically occupying moist to mesic meadows, grassy slopes, coastal bluffs, shores, clearings, and open forests from lowland to subalpine zones; common in coastal and northern British Columbia, infrequent elsewhere, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon, and Northwest Territories, east to Alberta, and south to California. This species prefers seasonally moist soils across diverse habitats ranging from coastal prairies and bluffs to disturbed areas, meadows, and forested zones (Turner and Gustafson, 2006), generally associating with wetlands while tolerating seasonal drought and inhabiting non-wetland sites. It occurs from sea level to 2134 m elevations in western North America, extending from California and western Nevada north through western Canada and into Alaska. It is generally associated with wetland areas, although it will tolerate seasonal drought and is also found in non-wetland sites.

Erosion_Slope_Control: Restoration: This plant is a great choice for wetland prairie restoration throughout its range. Its versatility enables it to thrive in moist upland or lowland sites as a quickly establishing native (Stanley et al., 2010).
Foot_Traffic_Lawn_Use: Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.
Common_Bee_Visitors: Bumblebees (Bombus occidentalis, B. vosnesenskii, B. mixtus); Mason & Orchard Bees (Osmia lignaria, Osmia spp.); Mining & Digger Bees (Andrena spp., Colletes spp.); Leafcutter & Resin Bees (Megachile spp.); Sweat Bees (Halictus & Lasioglossum spp.)
Host_Moths_Scientific: Papaipema sauzalitae
Stratification_Dormancy: Seeds germinate best at cool temperatures (10–16°C) and stands are best established by directly sowing in the fall; alternately, plugs can be transplanted in the fall.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Broadcast at a single species application rate of 6 to 7 pounds pure live seed (pls) per acre. Western buttercup has approximately 200,000 seeds per pound, so applying seed at a rate of one pound per acre will result in about 5 seeds per square foot. Field Establishment & Management: There are limited labeled herbicides appropriate for forb species in seed production; therefore, a weed free seedbed is very important. Germination begins 5 to 6 weeks after fall sowing. At the Corvallis PMC, fields are drill planted at a rate of 6 to 7 lb pls/acre at a depth of 3–6 mm with row spacing of 25.4–35.6 cm. When establishing a field with transplants, plugs can be planted as close as 0.3 m centers as plants do not take up much space, but row spacing should be planned to accommodate cultivation and harvest equipment.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are no improved cultivars of western buttercup, but seed is sometimes available from commercial growers in the Pacific Northwest.
Pruning_Management: Once established in an appropriate environment, this species is relatively low-maintenance. On a restoration site, it is not aggressive and unlikely to dominate and become weedy like some other Ranunculus species. It can tolerate herbicide application during its late summer dormancy, and would likely benefit from mowing in late summer to reduce non-native competition on a restoration site.
Nursery_Stock_Format: Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS)
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Seeds eaten. Avoided as raw food. Many tribes ground the seeds of the buttercup and mixed them with other seeds to make pinole (a flour-like staple).
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: This is a hardy plant with few, if any, susceptibilities to disease or pests. The fresh leaves, stems, and flower sap of other members of the Ranunculus genus have been found to cause digestive or nervous system problems for livestock grazing in quantity.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: This is a hardy plant with few, if any, susceptibilities to disease or pests. The fresh leaves, stems, and flower sap of other members of the Ranunculus genus have been found to cause digestive or nervous system problems for livestock grazing in buttercup-dominated areas. Fresh leaves, stems, and flower sap contain protoanemonin and are toxic if ingested raw; the Aleut noted that juices of its blooms are poisonous.

Description_Botanical: Perennial forb, 15-50 cm height; perennial herb arising from a woody root and often an unbranched, short stem-base. Description_Botanical: A stoloniferous perennial forb with a trailing habit, developing from a fibrous root and short rhizome typically originating from a single crown, accompanied by several leafless runners. Perennial herb from a fibrous root and short rhizome usually from a single crown, with several leafless runners; stems trailing, rooting at the nodes; runners, leaf stalks and flower shoots with long spreading to appressed hairs and usually greenish not reddish-tinged. Basal leaves are borne in rosettes, are palmately compound on stalks 2-15 cm long, and consist of 3 short-stalked, egg-shaped leaflets measuring 2-7 cm long. The lower leaf surface ranges from smooth to silky-hairy, while the upper surface is smooth and glaucous bluish-green, with coarsely toothed margins where the terminal tooth is less than 1/2 as wide as and shorter than the adjacent teeth.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A stoloniferous perennial forb with a trailing habit, developing from a fibrous root and short rhizome typically originating from a single crown, accompanied by several leafless runners. The trailing stems root at the nodes, and the runners, leaf stalks, and flower shoots exhibit long spreading to appressed hairs and are usually greenish rather than reddish-tinged.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal in rosettes, palmately compound, on stalks 2-15 cm long; leaflets 3, egg-shaped, short-stalked, 2-7 cm long, the lower surface smooth to silky-hairy, the upper surface smooth and glaucous bluish-green, the margins coarsely toothed, the terminal tooth less than 1/2 as wide as and shorter than the adjacent teeth.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an open cluster of 2 to 15 stalked flowers atop axillary, leafless shoots that are usually shorter than the surrounding leaves at maturity; corollas white, the petals 5, egg-shaped to round, 4-9 (12) mm long; calyces long-silky-hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes (sepals) lance-elliptic, 3-7 mm long, alternating with lanceolate bractlets that are shorter than the sepals; ovaries superior; stamens about 20.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Strawberries, hemispheric, about 1 cm wide, covered with achenes; achenes about 1.5 mm long, partly sunken in the fleshy receptacle.

Summary_Public: A stoloniferous perennial forb with a low trailing habit, trifoliate ovate toothed green leaves, white 5-petaled flowers, and small aromatic red strawberries (with beach plants bearing waxy leaves). Found in woodlands and forests, specifically in dry to moist open forests, sandy fields, clearings, and meadows from the lowland to subalpine zones; common in southern British Columbia south of 53°N, rare northward; ranging north to Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to California, New Mexico, Missouri, and Virginia, as well as shrubby areas, seashores, and sandy or rocky seashores.
Description_Botanical: A stoloniferous perennial forb with a low trailing habit, trifoliate ovate toothed green leaves, white 5-petaled flowers, and small aromatic red strawberries (with beach plants bearing waxy leaves). Perennial herb from a fibrous root and short, thick rhizome, with long, leafless runners; stems trailing, rooting at the nodes; runners, leaf stalks and flower shoots greenish or very lightly tinged with reddish purple, lightly to densely hairy. The runners, leaf stalks, and flower shoots are greenish or very lightly tinged with reddish-purple, and are lightly to densely hairy. Basal leaves are arranged in rosettes, are palmately compound on stalks 3-12 cm long, and bear 3 elliptic to egg-shaped, more or less unstalked leaflets measuring 1-3 cm long.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A stoloniferous perennial forb with a low trailing habit, trifoliate ovate toothed green leaves, white 5-petaled flowers, and small aromatic red strawberries (with beach plants bearing waxy leaves). This perennial herb arises from a fibrous root and short, thick rhizome, producing long leafless runners and trailing stems that root at the nodes.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal in rosettes, palmately compound, on stalks 3-12 cm long; leaflets 3, elliptic to egg-shaped, more or less unstalked, 1-3 cm long, the lower surface pale and fine-hairy underneath, the upper surface yellow-green and nearly smooth, the margins strongly toothed with the terminal tooth projecting beyond the adjacent lateral ones.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an open cluster of 3 to 15 stalked flowers borne atop axillary, leafless shoots that typically exceed the leaves at maturity; corollas white, featuring 5 egg-shaped petals 5-10 mm long; calyces silky-hairy, 5-lobed, the lobes (sepals) 4-5 mm long, alternating with narrowly elliptic bractlets approximately equal in length to the sepals; ovaries superior; stamens about 20.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Strawberries, hemispheric, about 1 cm wide, covered with achenes; achenes 1.3 mm long, partly sunken in the fleshy receptacle.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Spread_Behavior: Creeping mat spreading via aboveground stolons
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Stoloniferous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in woodlands and forests, specifically in dry to moist open forests, sandy fields, clearings, and meadows from the lowland to subalpine zones; common in southern British Columbia south of 53°N, rare northward; ranging north to Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to California, New Mexico, Missouri, and Virginia, as well as shrubby areas, seashores, and sandy or rocky seashores. Found below 2000 m in partial shade of closed-cone pine, evergreen, mixed conifer forests, and chaparral across a very wide distribution.

Summary_Public: Native forb or subshrub, 10 to 60 cm tall, multi-branched erect to spreading; white hairs on stems/leaves; leaves 2.5-7.5 cm, irregularly lobed; solitary heads with golden yellow disk flowers and 8-12 yellow ray flowers; light green velvety foliage. Thriving in meadows, rocky slopes, banks, and rockeries from lowland to montane zones, this plant grows in dry, rocky, or sandy soils requiring a minimum of 25 cm of precipitation at elevations from sea level to 3,050 m.
Description_Botanical: A native forb or subshrub, annual, biennial, or short- to long-lived perennial depending on site conditions, with a multi-branched, erect to spreading form and a fibrous root system, growing 10 to 60 cm tall. Native woolly forb or subshrub (10–60 cm tall) with multi-branched stems covered in white felty hairs. Leaves measure 2.5-7.5 cm long, irregularly divided into narrow lobes. Flowers are solitary on long peduncles with golden yellow disk flowers and 8-12 yellow ray flowers measuring 1.5-2 cm long, forming a flower head 4 to 6.5 cm wide.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Native forb or subshrub, 10 to 60 cm tall, multi-branched erect to spreading; white hairs on stems/leaves. A native forb or subshrub, annual, biennial, or short- to long-lived perennial depending on site conditions, with a multi-branched, erect to spreading form and a fibrous root system, growing 10 to 60 cm tall.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves few, soon deciduous; stem leaves alternate to opposite, entire to narrowly lobed, 1-8 cm long.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Heads comprising both ray and disk flowers, solitary on long stems; ray flowers 8 to 13, yellow, 1-2 cm long; involucres 9-12 mm tall; involucral bracts firm, erect, and embracing the ray achenes.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes slender, 4-angled, glabrous to hairy; pappus composed of 6-12 translucent scales, or forming a toothed crown.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: The seed requires a cold and moist period of about 90 days for optimal germination (Skinner 2007).
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Clay; Rocky / Shallow
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Dry, rocky, or sandy soils, coulees, bluffs, canyons, grasslands, and open pine forests (sea level to 3,000 m elevation); highly drought-tolerant.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Thriving in meadows, rocky slopes, banks, and rockeries from lowland to montane zones, this plant grows in dry, rocky, or sandy soils requiring a minimum of 25 cm of precipitation at elevations from sea level to 3,050 m. Habitats include roadsides, coulees, bluffs, canyons, dry grasslands, thickets, and forests. It is common on Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland, and rare in south-central and southeastern British Columbia, with a regional range extending from British Columbia south to California and east to Nevada, Utah, Wyoming, and Montana. The species exhibits extensive genetic and phenotypic variation driven by polyploidy, encompassing diploid, tetraploid, hexaploid, and octoploid populations, with California serving as the geographic center of diversity containing 10 of the 12 recognized varieties.

Seed_Collection_Harvest: These species are readily managed in standard nesting substrates for Osmia bees, and have been studied for decades, most recently as pollinators of balsamroot., Most Eriophyllum lanatum plants will flower and produce seed in their first year of growth. Stratification_Dormancy: Plants can be established by seed or seedlings.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Seeds should be drilled into a weed-free seed bed in the fall at a rate of 3.4 kg PLS per ha (3 lbs PLS per acre) and at a depth of 0.6 to 1.25 cm. When planted in a mix, the seeding rate should be adjusted according to the proportion of the mix.
Pruning_Management: Eriophyllum lanatum is a prolific seed producer and will rapidly spread to any surrounding open ground. If plant spread is not desired, flower heads should be removed prior to seed ripening. The Forest Service J. Herbert Stone Nursery in Medford, OR, reports the biggest challenge to production of E. lanatum seed is weed control.

Description_Botanical: Delicate perennial forb (40-90 cm) growing from a tuberous-thickened edible root with white terminal umbels. Summary_Public: Aromatic rhizomatous perennial herb to 30-100 cm tall; dense rosette of fern-like leaves; terminal flat-topped clusters of 5 white to pink ray flowers and cream/yellow disk flowers. Moderately rhizomatous, long-lived perennial forb, 30-100 cm tall; unbranched erect lanate stems; alternate pinnately dissected semi-evergreen aromatic leaves; flat compound corymb flower cluster; 3-12 white to cream ray flowers, 10-75 yellow disk flowers; flattened smooth and hairless dry single-seeded fruit.
Description_Botanical: This aromatic perennial herb bears fern-like leaves and a profusion of compact flower heads in a flat-topped cluster. The flowers, ranging from white to pink or reddish, surround a center of creamy disk flowers. Adaptable to various environments, this versatile plant thrives in coastal regions, montane zones, and even alpine areas. Its unique varieties offer diverse foliage and flower characteristics.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Aromatic rhizomatous perennial herb to 30-100 cm tall. Moderately rhizomatous, long-lived perennial forb, 30-100 cm tall; unbranched erect lanate stems.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Fernlike, alternate, stalked below and unstalked above, pinnately dissected, the divisions again dissected.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Heads are numerous, arranged in a short, flat- or round-topped cluster; involucral bracts are dry, overlapping in several series, and frequently dark-margined; ray flowers typically number 3-8, measure 2-3.5 mm long, and range from white to sometimes pink or reddish; disk flowers number 15-40 and are cream-colored.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes are glabrous, flattened, and measure 1-2 mm long, with the pappus lacking.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Year-round evergreen foliage anchors winter garden structure.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.

Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in meadows, rocky slopes, and beaches, as well as mesic to dry coastal bluffs, grasslands, and open forests across all vegetation zones, this species is common throughout British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Florida, Texas, California, and Mexico. It occupies dry to moist open sites at low to high elevations, disturbed poor soils, roadsides, hills, canyons, pastures, sagebrush areas, and beaches, spanning natural and disturbed habitats throughout the western United States and exhibiting a circumboreal distribution from Alaska to Mexico. It thrives in full sun on roadsides, hills, canyons, pastures, sagebrush, open timber, and subalpine zones, preferring droughty gravelly loams and shallow silty steep sites. Common yarrow can be found in pastures, grasslands, woodlands, waste grounds, open forests, prairies, fallow fields, pathway edges, subalpine zones, and exposed ridges (Chandler et al., 1982).

Erosion_Slope_Control: Conservation Practices: Common yarrow has been used in the United States for land restoration of disturbed sites, installation of low maintenance sites, and erosion control of steep slopes (Johnson & Whitwell, 1997). Fast-germinating, low-growing rhizomatous cover; controls erosion due to basal leaves and extensive rhizomes; quick ground cover on degraded soil, roadsides, mined lands; drought and acid soil tolerant; holds soil on slopes.
Foot_Traffic_Lawn_Use: Tolerates light, occasional foot traffic once established; suitable for turf alternatives and path edges.

Birds_Interactions: Food source for sage-grouse (chicks eat foliage and insects) and upland birds.
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Bighorn Sheep, Pronghorn, Deer, Snowshoe Hares. Flower heads eaten by deer; browsed by sheep, goats, pronghorn.
Seed_Collection_Harvest: Common yarrow has high seed production from late summer to early fall, producing approximately 2.2 to 4.1 million seeds per pound (Noller, 2001). Seeds are viable for 5 to 7 years when stored in a cool, dry place around 4–10°C (Noller, 2001; Jensen, 2019).
Stratification_Dormancy: Seed of western yarrow is non-dormant and readily germinates when spring planted at a very shallow depth. It tends to be less competitive in early development and becomes more so with age.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Common yarrow is a drought tolerant species of which there are several different ornamental cultivars. Plant the seeds no more than ¼ inch deep due to the need of light for germination. Prepare soil by tilling or loosening the top 30.5–38.1 cm of soil and plant from September to April indoors or outdoors (USDA-NRCS, 2014).
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are many ornamental cultivars of common yarrow with a variety of flower colors such as white, cream, pink, yellow, red, and more (Schalau, 2009).
Pruning_Management: Common yarrow can be slow to grow in diverse environments and prefers well drained soils. It is fairly drought tolerant and requires little to no irrigation.

Edible_Parts_Flavor: Leaves (Tea); mosquito repellant; seed heads in tea calm nerves/muscles; Tea for stomach ailments; teas, oils, salves for healing.
Ethno_Culinary_Food: The Cherokee drank a tea. Food (tea from leaves). Seed heads in tea calm nerves/muscles.
Ethno_Medicinal: The Pawnee used the stalk in a treatment for pain relief. The Chippewa used the leaves in a steam inhalant for headaches. Historically, common yarrow has been used by Native American tribes and Greeks for its medicinal properties since the Trojan War. Blood purifier, for colds and coughs, stomach/digestive ailments, and during labour. Prepared as tonic and blood purifier.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Common yarrow does not usually appear in wetlands but can occasionally be found in riparian habitats. Common yarrow may suffer from mildew or root rot if not planted in well-drained soil. Common yarrow is susceptible to gray mold, root rot in poorly drained soils, and powdery mildew. Pests include common leaf bugs, flea beetles, and spittlebugs found mostly in the Great Plains region and the Midwest (Schuster, n.d; Warwick & Black, 1982); Common yarrow can be considered weedy or invasive in some regions.

Summary_Public: A spreading streamside non-spiny shrub, 1.5-3 m tall (or medium to tall shrub, 1-2.5 m tall), from extensive rhizomes, often thicket-forming, deciduous with large soft leaves, large fragrant white/pink flowers, and sweet red aggregate berries. Found in riparian areas, thickets, woodlands, and moist to mesic open forests, streambanks, clearings, and roadsides in the lowland to subalpine zones; common throughout southern British Columbia, south of approximately 56°N; ranging north to southern Alaska, east to Ontario, and south to Michigan, Minnesota, northern Mexico, New Mexico, and Colorado.
Description_Botanical: Deciduous rhizomatous shrub (up to 2 m) with large soft leaves, large white flowers, and red hemispheric aggregate fruits. Height 1.5-3m. A spreading streamside non-spiny shrub, 1.5-3 m tall (or medium to tall shrub, 1-2.5 m tall), from extensive rhizomes, often thicket-forming, deciduous with large soft leaves, large fragrant white/pink flowers, and sweet red aggregate berries. Stems erect to ascending, unarmed, young growth fine-hairy and stalked-glandular, becoming smooth eventually; bark grey, flaking-off.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Deciduous rhizomatous shrub (up to 2 m) with large soft leaves, large white flowers, and red hemispheric aggregate fruits.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, long-stalked, mapleleaf-shaped, 10-20 cm across, palmately 3- to 7-lobed, double-saw-toothed, green and smooth to finely glandular-fuzzy on both surfaces, the stalks with reddish glandular hairs; stipules lanceolate, 6-13 mm long.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of 2 to 10 stalked flowers in small, flat-topped, long-stalked, terminal clusters, the flower-stalks glandular-hairy; corollas white, bowl-shaped, the petals 5, spreading, egg-shaped, 10-30 mm long; calyces densely hairy and usually stalked-glandular, 5-lobed, the lobes egg-shaped with long tail-like tips, spreading, 10-20 mm long; ovaries superior; stamens numerous.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Drupelets, velvety-hairy, coherent in a red, hemispheric cluster that falls intact from the dry receptacle (raspberry-like), the berries 1-1.5 cm wide. Vol4_8. Aggregate.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Thimbleberries are red and very sweet. Because they are not particularly juicy, they are easy to preserve. They may be eaten fresh or preserved by drying or canning, or made into jam.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Strong clonal colony competitor (Rhizomatous); moderate allelopathic/litter suppression combined with dense rhizome or sucker expansion—give clear spacing from delicate spring ephemerals.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.

Summary_Public: Perennial, erect, aromatic shrub, 30 to 80 cm high; rhizomatous; alternate oblong to elliptic evergreen leaves, densely rusty-tomentose beneath; terminal umbel of white flowers; oval/oblong capsule fruit. Occurring in bogs and moist to wet forests in the lowland and montane zones; common throughout most of British Columbia, infrequent in south-central British Columbia; north to Alaska, east to Newfoundland, and south to Oregon, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey.
Description_Botanical: Erect shrub, 0.5-1.5 m tall, with rusty soft-hairy stems. Leaves are alternate, evergreen, leathery, oblong to lance-oblong or elliptic, (1.2) 2-6 cm long, 3-15 mm wide, with margins strongly to slightly rolled under, blunt tips, upper surface deep green, appearing somewhat wrinkled, glabrous to slightly reddish soft-hairy, and copiously rusty or yellowish soft-hairy beneath; stalks are 1-5 mm long. Fragrant leaves. Low evergreen aromatic shrub (30–80 cm tall) with linear-elliptic leaves featuring revolute margins and dense rusty wool (tomentum) underneath.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Erect shrub, 0.5-1.5 m tall, with rusty soft-hairy stems.

Flower_Inflorescence_Type: In terminal umbrella-like clusters; flower stalks (0.6) 1.2-2.5 cm long, with short, white hairs (rarely with a few contorted, reddish hairs), often glandular, curved in fruit; corollas white, wheel-shaped, 10-12 mm across, the 5 distinct petals spreading, oblong, and 5-8 mm long; calyces less than 1 mm long, minutely white-hairy on margins, sometimes glandular; stamens 5-8, slightly exceeding the styles, filaments glabrous or sometimes hairy at the base. Flowers are arranged in terminal umbrella-like clusters on stalks measuring (0.6) 1.2-2.5 cm long, which feature short white hairs (rarely with a few contorted reddish hairs), are often glandular, and curve in fruit.

Summary_Public: Annual Forb, 15 – 50 cm height with fibrous roots and yellow sunflower-like capitulum flowers. Inhabiting marshes, ponds, wet ditches, and lakeshores in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this taxon is common throughout British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains and less frequent on Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland; circumboreal, extending east to Quebec, south to North Carolina, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, and also occurring in Eurasia.
Description_Botanical: Annual Forb, 15 – 50 cm height with fibrous roots and yellow sunflower-like capitulum flowers. Plants reach 0.1-1.0 m tall (15 – 50 cm height) from fibrous roots, with erect, simple or branched stems that are sparsely spreading-hairy to glabrous. Basal leaves are lacking. Stem leaves are opposite, simple, unstalked, linear-lanceolate to lanceolate, 1.5-20 cm long, 0.5-4.5 cm wide, sometimes joining at the stems, coarsely saw-toothed to nearly entire, and glabrous.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Plants reach 0.1-1.0 m tall (15 – 50 cm height) from fibrous roots, with erect, simple or branched stems that are sparsely spreading-hairy to glabrous.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves lacking; stem leaves simple, unstalked, opposite, linear-lanceolate to lanceolate, 1.5-20 cm long, 0.5-4.5 cm wide, sometimes joining at the stems, coarsely saw-toothed to nearly entire, glabrous.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Capitulum; heads with ray and disk flowers, occasionally discoid, hemispheric to nearly so, numerous in well-developed specimens, becoming nodding with age; involucres 12-25 mm wide; involucral bracts in 2 dissimilar series, the outer ones 5-8, green, leafy, unequal, spreading or reflexed, linear-lanceolate, typically surpassing the disk, the inner ones erect, narrowly ovate, mostly 6-8 mm long, greenish-brown; ray flowers 6-8, or occasionally absent, yellow, about 1.5 cm long; disk flowers yellow.

Summary_Public: The Columbia tiger lily (Lilium columbianum) is a perennial herb arising from an egg-shaped, fleshy-scaled, white bulb 3-5 cm long, featuring sturdy, smooth stems 40-120 cm tall (reaching 0.6–1.2 m or 60-120 cm in height) that produce bright orange, downward-facing, nodding flowers with dark spots. Inhabiting mesic open forests, roadsides, clearings, thickets, and meadows across lowland, steppe, and alpine zones; common throughout southern British Columbia south of 54°N; extending south to Idaho and northern California; also found in forests, meadows, and clearings from low to subalpine elevations, as well as in cultivated gardens in the San Juan and Gulf Islands.
Description_Botanical: The Columbia tiger lily, Lilium columbianum, is a distinctive BC native lily that resembles turk’s cap and martagon lilies. Native lily (0.6–1.2 m) with slender stems producing small downward-facing light orange flowers with dark spots and reflexed petals. Mature bulbs can produce candelabras of up to 20 blooms. Tall perennial lily with nodding, spotted orange flowers and edible scaly white bulbs.

Summary_Public: Shrub growing up to 4 m tall; produces small bright red, plump, sweet-tart berries (up to 1 cm). Inhabits dry to moist forests and decaying wood across lowland and montane zones; common in western British Columbia, mainly west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, and infrequent in southeastern British Columbia.
Description_Botanical: Red huckleberry is an erect deciduous shrub (Ericaceae) growing 1-4 m tall (up to 4 m tall), featuring bright green, very prominently angled stems that are glabrous or minutely hairy when young, with strongly angled twigs. Leaves are alternate, deciduous (though often some are persistent), oval to oblong-elliptic (elliptic to ovate), 0.9-3 cm long, 0.4-1.6 cm wide, thin, with entire margins (the juvenile leaves persistent, dark green, and finely toothed), glabrous to minutely hairy, and tips usually rounded (with a sharp point at the tip). Flowers are greenish to pinkish, with blossoms solitary in the axils of the lowest leaves of the youngest shoots. Shrub growing up to 4 m tall; produces small bright red, plump, sweet-tart berries (up to 1 cm).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Red huckleberry is an erect deciduous shrub (Ericaceae) growing 1-4 m tall (up to 4 m tall), featuring bright green, very prominently angled stems that are glabrous or minutely hairy when young, with strongly angled twigs.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous (often some persistent), oval to oblong-elliptic, 0.9-3 cm long, 0.4-1.6 cm wide, entire, glabrous to minutely hairy, tips usually rounded; juvenile leaves persistent, dark green, finely toothed. Litter indicator for mesic sites.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Solitary in leaf axils; flower stalks 2-8 mm long; corollas yellowish-pink, waxy, broadly bell- to urn-shaped, 4-5 mm long; calyces shallowly lobed, the lobes persistent in fruit; filaments glabrous; anthers with prominent spreading awns, the apical pore-bearing tubes short.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berries are globe-shaped, 6-10 mm wide, and bright red.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Red huckleberries grow from moist to dry forests at a range of elevations. The small, red fruits are a traditional food. They may be eaten fresh o r cooked and made into jam.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Forms tight ericaceous root mats and phenolic leaf litter that gradually acidifies surface humus and slows annual weed invasion; compatible with acid-tolerant woodland companions.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: It requires excessive drainage and acidic soils to become established.

Its distribution extends northward to southeastern Alaska and southward to California, including Saltspring, Matia, Decatur, Cypress, Patos, and Lopez Islands, with common occurrence in Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia. It occurs across a range of elevations in moist to dry forests, open woodlands, and on rotten logs, frequently growing on old stumps and within the shrub layer of Littlewood Forest. It does best in full or partial shade.

Blossoms are white to greenish white, drooping, single or in small grapelike clusters.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Erect perennial shrub 1 to 2 m high; biennial upright spiny/bristly canes with shredding bark. Medium shrub, 0.5-2 m tall, perennial with biennial stems (canes); stems erect to ascending, almost unarmed to prickly and bristly, often glandular-hairy, sometimes smooth and glaucous beneath the prickles; bark yellow to cinnamon-brown, shredding.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, pinnately compound, 5-20 cm long; leaflets 3 to 5 on first-year canes, mostly 3 on flowering canes, egg-shaped to broadly lanceolate, 3-10 cm long, double-saw-toothed and sharply long-pointed at the tip, greenish and smooth to sparsely hairy above, paler and greyish-woolly to nearly smooth beneath, the veins and leaf-stalks often glandular-prickly; stipules linear-awl-shaped, 4-10 mm long.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurs in mesic to moist thickets, rocky slopes, clearings, burns, old fields, and open forests in the lowland and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia, mostly in and east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains; ranging east to Newfoundland and south to California, northern Mexico, and North Carolina. It occupies open woods, thickets, clearings, burned areas, riverbanks, roadsides, and trails on fine to coarse soils; it is drought-tolerant, adapted to nutrient-rich conditions, and tolerates a wide pH range. A circumpolar species distributed from Alberta across Canada, the United States, and Eurasia, the American red raspberry is native to North America and also grows from northern Europe to northwestern Asia.

Antelope bitterbrush is a slow growing shrub that is moderate to very deep rooted with wide ecotypic variations. It is normally 0.6–1.8 m in height and up to 2.4 m in width with wedge shaped, three lobed leaves (some are persistent in winter).

Stratification_Dormancy: Germination is improved with a cold treatment and seed should be broadcast or planted shallowly ( 3 mm deep).
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Consult your local nurseries to choose the right cultivar for your specific landscape. Artemisia species can be propagated by seeds, by division of the rootstock, or by cuttings taken in the early summer.
Nursery_Availability: Artemisia frigida is available through your local native plant nursery within its range.
Nursery_Stock_Format: Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS)
Ethno_Medicinal: The Blackfeet chewed the leaves of prairie sagewort for heartburn, and applied the leaves to wounds to reduce swelling. Medicine, fragrant grass. The roots and tops were boiled and drank as a tea for “mountain fever.” Other tribes, who used this species of sage include the Arapaho, Comanche, Gros Ventre, Cree, Navaho, Tewa, and Ute (Nickerson 1966, Carlson and, Denig 1855, Elmore 1944), Robbins et al. 1916, Cheyenne women used prairie sagewort to correct menstrual irregularity. Root or leaf tea taken by women during menstrual periods.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Leaves used for dye.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: The Cheyenne used prairie sagewort ceremonially as a smudge for purification in the Sun Dance. The Delaware-Okl chewed the leaves as a ceremonial medicine.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Contains volatile oils classified by the FDA as hazardous in concentrated internal doses.

Summary_Public: Perennial forb with hairy stems, 0.6–1.5 m tall; velvety opposite leaves to 15.2 cm; rose-colored star-shaped flowers in fuzzy umbel; horn-shaped fruits with silky seeds; sticky sap. Moist to mesic roadsides, ditches, streamsides, meadows, and grasslands in the steppe and montane zones; common in south-central and southeastern British Columbia; east to Manitoba and south to Missouri, Texas, and California; tolerant of moist soils in prairies, meadows, roadsides, streams, and ditches; drought-tolerant; western United States and Canada.
Description_Botanical: A member of the Milkweed Family (Asclepiadaceae), showy milkweed (Asclepias speciosa) is a hairy perennial forb and herb arising from a rhizome, reaching 0.6–1.5 m tall with erect to ascending stems 0.4-1.2 m tall that are woolly, greyish, or glabrous below, yielding sticky sap and milky juice. The velvety opposite leaves measure to 6 in (10-20 cm long), being simple, fleshy, persistent, and short-petioled with oblong or oval to elliptic or ovate blades, rounded or heart-shaped at the base (rarely cordate and clasping). Asclepias flowers resemble crowns arranged in fuzzy umbels, displaying rose-colored, star-shaped petals with a rose-purple reflexed corolla and hoods elevated above the corolla in pink, aging yellow, with horns exerted beyond the hoods. Perennial forb with hairy stems, 0.6–1.5 m tall; velvety opposite leaves to 15.2 cm; rose-colored star-shaped flowers in fuzzy umbel; horn-shaped fruits with silky seeds; sticky sap.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Perennial forb with hairy stems, 0.6–1.5 m tall; sticky sap. A member of the Milkweed Family (Asclepiadaceae), showy milkweed (Asclepias speciosa) is a hairy perennial forb and herb arising from a rhizome, reaching 0.6–1.5 m tall with erect to ascending stems 0.4-1.2 m tall that are woolly, greyish, or glabrous below, yielding sticky sap and milky juice.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, simple, 10-20 cm long, fleshy, oblong or oval, rounded or heart-shaped at the base, stalked.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence an umbrella-like cluster; flowers pink to reddish-purple; sepals greenish-tinged with red.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Pods cylindric, bearing soft tubercles, 7-11 cm long, many-seeded, containing seeds with tufts of white cottony hairs; seeds flattened, wrinkled.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Adapted to well-drained winter-wet soils with prolonged summer dry periods.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Prairies, meadows, roadsides, stream banks, and ditches; prefers moist soil, highly drought-tolerant. Dry to moist loamy soils.
Summer_Watering: Minimal to zero summer water once established; occasional deep soak only in extreme drought during year one.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Moist to mesic roadsides, ditches, streamsides, meadows, and grasslands in the steppe and montane zones; common in south-central and southeastern British Columbia; east to Manitoba and south to Missouri, Texas, and California; tolerant of moist soils in prairies, meadows, roadsides, streams, and ditches; drought-tolerant; western United States and Canada.

Fire_Ecology: Both milkweed and dogbane were burned in the fall by California Indian tribes to eliminate dead stalks and stimulate new growth. Burning causes new growth to have taller, straighter stems with longer fibers.

Stratification_Dormancy: Collect seeds after pods have ripened, but before they have split open. The seeds are wind dispersed, so be careful when gathering to place in a paper or burlap bag to avoid seed lost.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Seeds can be directly sewn into the ground in the fall.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Seeds and plants of selected Asclepias cultivars are available from many nurseries. It is best to plant species from your local area, adapted to the specific site conditions where the plants are to be grown.
Pruning_Management: When used for fiber, milkweed is collected in the autumn after the leaves have begun to senesce or dry up. Plants grow in places that have been disturbed such as road grading, construction sites, logging landing fills, and etc. Pete Bunting (pers. Comm. 2-9-1999) says, "In the fall when the milkweed has dried I check to see if they will break off at the ground line. The plants are usually a yellow tan to gray depending on how long they have dried."
Nursery_Stock_Format: Nursery Plugs (2-inch / 50-cell); 4-inch to 1-gal Container; Restoration Seed (PLS); Rooted Divisions
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Edible shoots, buds, flowers, young seed pods, ground seeds. Pueblo people ate green milkweed pods and uncooked roots from one of the species that forms fleshy tubers underground. The young shoots, stems, flower buds, immature fruits, and roots of showy milkweed were boiled and eaten as a vegetable by various indigenous groups of eastern and mid-western America. In some areas the young leaves and stems were used as greens.
Ethno_Medicinal: People have used milkweed for fiber, food, and medicine all over the United States and southern Canada. Sap used as antiseptic for cuts, ringworm, corns, calluses (Cheyenne). Seed decoction for snakebite (Paiute).
Ethno_Material_Tech: Stems used as cordage. Fibers from the stems of milkweed have been identified in prehistoric textiles in the Pueblo region. Tewa-speaking people of the Rio Grande still make string and rope from these fibers.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Summary_Public: Occurs in dry grasslands, shrublands, and forest openings in the steppe and lower montane zones; frequent in south-central British Columbia, becoming less frequent eastward in southern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Manitoba and south to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Purple threeawn is commonly found on dry plains with gravelly or sandy soils, though occasionally on clay soils, and often associates with sand dropseed and grama species across its native range in western North America from Canada into Mexico.
Description_Botanical: A perennial, strongly tufted grass from fibrous roots with hollow, minutely rough stems mostly (15) 20-40 cm tall (ranging from 24.1–90.2 cm / 25 to 90 cm in length); open sheaths; mostly basal blades 1-2 mm wide, 7-25 cm long (2.5–24.1 cm / 3.0 to 25 cm long, 1–2 mm / 0.07-0.2 cm wide), typically involute with flat bases, and minutely rough; and ligules scarcely 0.5 mm long, membranous, with frontal margins bearing hairs 2-3 mm long. Purple threeawn is a slender, densely cespitose perennial bunchgrass featuring a sparingly branched panicle inflorescence. Glumes are unequal with the lower glume shorter than the upper, colored light to dark brown or purple. Awns range from 6.1–14 cm (6.0 to 14 cm) in length, with the central awn thicker than the lateral awns.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A perennial, strongly tufted grass from fibrous roots with hollow, minutely rough stems mostly (15) 20-40 cm tall (ranging from 24.1–90.2 cm / 25 to 90 cm in length). Purple threeawn is a slender, densely cespitose perennial bunchgrass featuring a sparingly branched panicle inflorescence.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Sheaths open; blades 1-2 mm wide, 7-25 cm long, in-rolled, minutely rough; ligules scarcely 0.5 mm long, membranous, the frontal margins with hairs 2-3 mm long.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 1-2 mm wide; 7-25 cm long; 0.5 mm long; 2-3 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a narrow panicle, 5-10 cm long, the branches mostly loosely ascending; lower glumes 7-13 mm long, about 1/2 the length of the upper ones, awn-tipped; florets 10-15 mm long, the calluses flattened, about 1 mm long; lemma awns (4) 5-8 cm long, 3-branched, the lateral branches divergent; paleas 2-2.5 mm long, slightly surpassed by the lodicules.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 5-10 cm long; 7-13 mm long; 10-15 mm long; 1 mm long; 5-8 cm long
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Seedlings grow and mature quickly and produce a marketable crop in the year of planting. Because seed ripens indeterminately, a Flail-Vac harvester collects the ripe seed crop without damaging or eliminating the ability to make subsequent harvests as later flowering florets mature.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Fibrous); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Purple threeawn is adapted to dry, recently disturbed sites.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurs in dry grasslands, shrublands, and forest openings in the steppe and lower montane zones; frequent in south-central British Columbia, becoming less frequent eastward in southern British Columbia; extending east to southwestern Manitoba and south to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California. Purple threeawn is commonly found on dry plains with gravelly or sandy soils, though occasionally on clay soils, and often associates with sand dropseed and grama species across its native range in western North America from Canada into Mexico. However, it occasionally occurs on clay soils as well (Hatch and Pluhar 1993). This colonizer species is often associated with sand dropseed [Sporobolus virginicus (L.) Kunth] and grama (Boutelous spp.) species.
