Sowing_Protocol_Time: Begin seedbed preparation well in advance of planting. Establish a clean, weed-free seedbed by either tillage or herbicides. Prior to planting, the site should be firm and have accumulated soil moisture.

Purple threeawn is best started using greenhouse grown transplants and planted into bedded rows.
Pruning_Management: Avoid grazing of new plantings for 90 days to allow plants to become established. Purple threeawn readily reseeds itself with minimal soil disturbance. Allow plants to produce seed annually to maintain stand health.

Description_Botanical: Coniferous tree with soft, fine, wooly inner bark and easy-to-carve wood, typically 20-40 m tall at maturity; branches and branchlets drooping strongly; bark ridged and fissured, not tearing off in long thin strips; wood aromatic with a potato-like smell; growing tip (leader) drooping. Description_Botanical: An evergreen shrub or small tree 2-15 m tall with a fluted or twisted trunk, papery reddish scaly bark, and branches spreading to drooping in flat sprays. Small tree 2-15 m tall, often shrubby; bark thin, with outer purplish scales over reddish to reddish-purple inner bark; male and female plants separate. Needles are 2-ranked, flattened, pointed at the tip, (12) 14-18 mm long, 1-2 mm broad, yellow-green and paler on the lower surface. Fruits develop as a round, red, fleshy aril 5-6 mm long borne on the underside of the branches; pollen cones are yellow, globe-shaped, and 3 mm long.

Summary_Public: Large coniferous tree with shallow roots, short feathery needles, very small cones, and flexible wood. Inhabits moist to dry slopes, river terraces, and flats in lowland and montane zones; common in and west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains in western British Columbia and in southeastern British Columbia; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to northern California, northern Idaho, and northwestern Montana.
Description_Botanical: A large coniferous tree reaching up to 50 (60) m tall, characterized by shallow roots, flexible wood, a narrow crown with a noticeably drooping leader, and young twigs covered with a mix of short and longer hairs. The bark is rough, scaly, and strongly furrowed and ridged in older trees, transitioning from smooth and reddish-brown when young to darker brown or reddish-brown. Needles are somewhat flattened, rounded at the tip, 8-20 (25) mm long, characteristically unequal in length, short-stalked, finely toothed, irregularly spaced, and spread unevenly at right angles to form feathery, flat sprays; they are glossy yellow-green above and almost entirely white-stomatiferous below. Seed cones mature from green to brown, are ovoid to oblong-egg-shaped, 1.5-2.5 cm long, stalkless, and hang down at the end of the twigs with many thin papery scales.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A large coniferous tree reaching up to 50 (60) m tall, characterized by shallow roots, flexible wood, a narrow crown with a noticeably drooping leader, and young twigs covered with a mix of short and longer hairs. Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Needles somewhat flattened, rounded at tip, 8-20 (25) mm long and characteristically unequal in length, spread unevenly at right angles to the branches to form feathery, flat sprays; glossy and yellow-green on upper surface, almost entirely white-stomatiferous on the lower.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Pollen cones yellow, 3-4 mm long.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Seed cones maturing from green to brown, 1.5-2.5 cm long, oblong-egg-shaped.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Thq’iinlhp tolerates shade and grows abundantly underneath mature trees, where it provides an important source of food for deer and elk. Their shallow root system makes them susceptible to blowing over. They are often found growing out of old tree stumps or decaying logs.

Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Western hemlock occurs on a variety of soil types. This plant is well adapted to grow on humus and decaying wood, and is also found on mineral soil MacKinnon 1994.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabits moist to dry slopes, river terraces, and flats in lowland and montane zones; common in and west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains in western British Columbia and in southeastern British Columbia; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to northern California, northern Idaho, and northwestern Montana. In coastal British Columbia, it inhabits the understory of mature forests on old stumps and nurse logs. Western hemlock is native in northwestern California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia, Alaska, Idaho, and Montana (McMinn & Maino 1963). In California, western hemlock occurs near the coast in scattered localities from Del Norte County southward to the vicinity of Elk Creek, Mendocino County.

Stratification_Dormancy: Seed is best sown in a cold frame in the autumn or late winter. Dormancy is variable with some seed lots requiring cold stratification (Dirr & Heuser 1987). Stratification accelerates and improves total germination and, unless seeds are known not to require pretreatment, cold stratification at 5°C from three weeks to three months is recommended.
Pruning_Management: Seedlings transplant well when they are 20.3–91.4 cm tall. The best survival rate can be achieved if seedlings are transplanted between 8 and 50.8 cm, this is usually when they are about five to eight years old. Transplanting larger seedlings will check badly and hardly put on any growth for several years. This slow growth predisposes the seedling to pest, poor root development and wind throws, and related damage.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: New leaves useful as tea. Large boughs tied in bundles and submerged to collect spawning herring eggs for food. Dried cambium inner bark eaten fresh or dried into square cakes.
Ethno_Medicinal: Western hemlock was commonly employed medicinally by several native North American Indian tribes who used it to treat a variety of complaints. Hemlock pitch was applied for a variety of purposes, including poultices or poultice coverings, linaments rubbed on the chest for colds and when mixed with deer tallow as a salve to prevent sunburn. A decoction of the pounded bark has been used in the treatment of hemorrhages, diaphoretic, and diuretic.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Bark used for reddish-brown dye. Western hemlock bark has high tannin content and was used as a tanning agent, pigment and cleansing solution. Some Coast Salish people used a red dye made from hemlock bark to color mountain goat wool and basket materials and as a facial cosmetic and hair remover.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Traditionally utilized for ceremonial headdresses and spiritual bathing.

Summary_Public: Fast-growing deciduous tree up to 50 m height; sweet-smelling resinous buds, white seed fluff; soft, heavy outer bark without slivers. Inhabiting floodplains, forests, streambanks, and woodlands, the range of black cottonwood extends from Alaska, including various islands, through the coastal regions of western Canada (Yukon, British Columbia, and Alberta) into the northwestern United States (Washington, Oregon, Montana, Idaho, and Nevada; rare in North Dakota, Wyoming, Utah, and California), reaching as far south as Baja California Norte.
Description_Botanical: Fast-growing deciduous tree up to 50 m with fragrant resinous buds in spring. Clouds of white fluff fall from the tree when the seed is distributed later in the season. Belonging to the Willow Family (Salicaceae), these native trees reach 30-60 m in tallness, typically with a straight, branch-free trunk for over half their length, forming a broad, open crown in open sites; bark is gray to gray-brown on mature trees, deeply furrowed into flat ridges on older portions. Leaves are deciduous, simple, alternate, ovate-lanceolate to deltate, variable in size and shape on the same tree, rounded or cordate at the base, 7-12 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide, hairless or nearly so, with finely toothed margins, dark green above and slightly paler beneath, commonly with whitish or brownish resin blotches, turning yellow in autumn, on round petioles 3-4 mm long.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Fast-growing deciduous tree up to 50 m height; soft, heavy outer bark without slivers. Fast-growing deciduous tree up to 50 m with fragrant resinous buds in spring.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, simple, narrowly to broadly egg-shaped or lanceolate, 5-20 cm long, 3-12 cm wide, the bases tapered to heart-shaped or squared-off smooth, finely toothed and hairy on the margins, the teeth often tipped with a callous gland, lower side whitish or pale green and brownish; leaf stalks 2-10 cm long, often with a pair of glands near the blade; buds finely hairy with fringed scales.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 5-20 cm long; 3-12 cm wide; 2-10 cm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Borne in catkins; male catkins 2-3 (5) cm long, soon deciduous, with 8-60 stamens; female catkins 8-20 cm long.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules, broadly egg-shaped, carpels 2-3, smooth or hairy, nearly unstalked.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Black cottonwood begins producing seed at about 8-10 years – abundant seed is usually produced every year. High germination rates and seedling survival depend on continuously moist conditions, such as in fresh alluvium, during the first month.
Spread_Behavior: Woody crown and lateral root system
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Deep lateral / Taproot / Woody burl); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Texture_Tags: Sandy / Gravelly; Loam; Clay; Rich / Organic
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Black cottonwood grows on alluvial sites, riparian habitats, and moist woods on mountain slopes, at elevations of 0–2100(–2750) meters. In eastern Washington and other dry areas, it is restricted to protected valleys and canyon bottoms, along streambanks, and edges of ponds and meadows.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.

Stratification_Dormancy: Black cottonwood begins producing seed at about 8- 10 years – abundant seed is usually produced every year. Seeds under natural conditions are short-lived, usually for less than a month.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Seed will readily germinate on a variety of favorable sites, particularly where mineral soil has been exposed or new soil deposited.
Pruning_Management: Root suckers and profuse cottony seed from female trees require urban site maintenance planning; keep clear of underground drainage lines and building foundations.

Ethno_Medicinal: Buds used as a topical pain reliever and antimicrobial. Disinfectant properties of resin from buds were discovered by Native Americans, who used the resin to treat sore throats, coughs, lung pain, and rheumatism. Medicine.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Leaf buds used for dye. Soft outer bark carved into soft figures/toys.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: In urban sites, the aggressive root systems of black cottonwood can invade and damage drainage systems and also may heavily draw available moisture from gardens and building foundations, especially in clay soil. Root suckers also may be considered a maintenance problem, and the profuse production of cottony seed from female plants can be a minor nuisance. The shallow root system of black cottonwood, especially on wet soils, make the species susceptible to damage from ice storms, heavy snow, and wind. Unseasonably early or late frosts may damage saplings, but in dormancy, it is one of the most frost-resistant trees in the northwestern USA.

Summary_Public: Massive evergreen coniferous tree (46–61 m / up to 60 m tall) with durable, clear-grained wood and fibrous reddish-brown bark; scale-like leaves with white markings underneath; small wooden seed cones. Forests, Riparian Areas, Woodlands.
Description_Botanical: An evergreen coniferous tree of the cypress family (Cupressaceae) thriving in moist and nutrient-rich soils, reaching 50 (-75) meters tall (historically cited up to 46–61 m / 60 m), often buttressed at the base with a conical to irregular crown; older individuals frequently exhibit multiple leaders and dead spike tops. Branches are arching with pendent, flattened branchlets arranged in fan-shaped sprays, while the aromatic wood features durable, clear grain and a drooping growing tip (leader). Bark is gray to reddish-brown, 10-25 mm thick, ridged and fissured, readily tearing off in long, thin strips. Leaves are evergreen, scale-like, sharply pointed, (1-) 3-6 mm long, somewhat overlapping and closely pressed to the stem in opposite alternating pairs (4 rows), glossy green above with white stripes on the lower surface, turning brown and shedding with age, and emit a spicy fragrance when crushed.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Massive evergreen coniferous tree (46–61 m / up to 60 m tall) with durable, clear-grained wood and fibrous reddish-brown bark. An evergreen coniferous tree of the cypress family (Cupressaceae) thriving in moist and nutrient-rich soils, reaching 50 (-75) meters tall (historically cited up to 46–61 m / 60 m), often buttressed at the base with a conical to irregular crown.

Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: In clearcuts and other disturbed areas, seedlings account for most of the western red-cedar regeneration, but seedlings in mature stands may be less abundant than individuals produced by vegetative reproduction from layering, rooting of fallen branches, and branch development on fallen trees.
Discovered_Drive_Details: The red cedar is a tremendously important species. Its wood and inner bark have been especially prized for making numerous items. Red cedar wood has been used for various items including houses, canoes, and spreaders used when barbecuing salmon.

Pruning_Management: In mixed-species and uneven-aged stands, western red cedars tolerate shady understory conditions and can maintain slow but acceptable growth rates over long periods. In timber harvest of these mixed-species stands, most of these trees are taken by clearcutting. Because of steep terrain, decay, and breakage, harvesting costs are high and lumber recovery is low. Because of its high susceptibility to windthrow in wet environments and in the moist sites where growth and yield are highest, western red cedars should not be left as scattered seed trees.

Description_Botanical: A deciduous shrub or small tree growing 1-8(-15) meters tall, rhizomatous and forming colonial thickets with smooth mottled brown/grey bark and straight main stems with spreading, ascending branches. Twigs are light brown, sparsely to moderately hairy, and sometimes glandular. Leaves are alternate, deciduous, nearly round to narrowly ovate or ovate-oblong, 4-10 cm long, with a heart-shaped or rounded base, blunt to broadly acute apex, often nearly angular and slightly lobed near the tip, and doubly serrate margins, usually pubescent on major veins and vein axils; petioles may bear glandular hairs. Male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers are separate, but both types present on each plant (the species monoecious); male flowers numerous in long, pendulous stalks (catkins) 4-6 cm long, in clusters of 2-3 near branch tips, appearing in the fall but opening the following spring; female flowers: several in a scaly bud, tiny and inconspicuous with only bright red stigma and styles protruding from the otherwise gray-brown buds, almost completely enclosed by bracts, near the end of the twigs.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Shrub up to 3 m tall with smooth mottled brown/grey bark.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Alternate, deciduous, elliptic to oval, leaf blades heart-shaped with a sharp-pointed tip, doubly saw-toothed, paler below than above, 4-10 cm long, turning yellow in the fall.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Male flowers arranged in catkins, appearing before the leaves in spring; female flowers borne in very small catkins featuring protruding red stigmas.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Nuts are hard-shelled, completely enclosed by bristly bractlets, occurring in 2's or 3's at the end of branches, measuring barely 1.5 cm long, and being thinly hairy or glabrous.

Summary_Public: Herbaceous aquatic perennial geophyte, 20-90 cm tall with distinctive waxy arrowhead-shaped leaves and starchy submerged tubers/bulbs. Inhabiting wet ditches, ponds, lakeshores, and marshes across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; infrequent in British Columbia south of 56°N, absent from the Queen Charlotte Islands, northern Vancouver Island, and the adjacent coast; extending east to Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia, and south to Maine, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Florida, Mississippi, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California; also found in northern South America and Hawaii.
Description_Botanical: An herbaceous aquatic perennial geophyte, 20-90 cm tall, characterized by waxy arrowhead-shaped leaves and starchy submerged tubers/bulbs. It arises as a perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herb from a tuber-producing rhizome with stems 20-50 (90) cm tall. All leaves are basal; emergent leaf blades are arrowhead-shaped, 5-25 cm long, long-stalked and sheathed at the base, and submerged leaf blades are lanceolate or linear and essentially bladeless, up to 80 cm long. Representing the Arrowhead Family (Alismataceae), both Sagittaria latifolia and Sagittaria cuneata grow in swampy ground or standing water in ponds, lakes, stream edges, and ditches (Hickman 1993), producing edible white or bluish tubers.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: An herbaceous aquatic perennial geophyte, 20-90 cm tall, characterized by waxy arrowhead-shaped leaves and starchy submerged tubers/bulbs. It arises as a perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herb from a tuber-producing rhizome with stems 20-50 (90) cm tall.

Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Sagittaria species may be planted from bare root stock, by transplanting the tubers, and by seeding directly into wetland soil. Live plant transplants or transplanting tubers are preferred revegetation methods where there is moving water.
Pruning_Management: Hydrology is the most important factor in determining wetland type, revegetation success, and wetland function and value. Changes in water levels influence species composition, structure, and distribution of plant communities. Water management is absolutely critical during plant establishment, and remains crucial through the life of the wetland for proper community management. Sagittaria species require moist soils to standing water for successful revegetation.
Nursery_Availability: Available from native plant nurseries specializing in aquatic plants.
Nursery_Stock_Format: Dormant Bulbs / Corms (Fall Planting); 4-inch Container; Stratifiable Seed
Edible_Parts_Flavor: Starchy tubers roasted, eaten raw, or milled into flour (tasting like potatoes).
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Edible bulb. Sagittaria is an aquatic plant with tuberous roots that can be eaten like potatoes. Edible wetland root/tuber vegetable harvested in river bays and deltas.
Ethno_Medicinal: Root tea used for digestive tract issues. Root poultice used to heal cuts and infections. Leaf/root teas for lactation, digestion, cuts. Leaf and root teas prepared for lactation, digestion, and cuts.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Indian women collected it in shallow water from a canoe, or waded into ponds or marshes in the late summer and loosened the roots with their toes. Tubers harvested from mud in fall/winter by wading or using canoes. The roots would rise to the top of the water where they were gathered and tossed into floating baskets.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: The Iroquois used it as a ceremonial blessing when they began planting corn.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.

Cones are 1-4 cm long, with solid centres and rounded tops.

Summary_Public: A nitrogen-fixing deciduous shrub with russet-scaled leaves and bitter red berries. Found on mesic to dry sites in the lowland and steppe to subalpine zones; common throughout British Columbia except absent on the Queen Charlotte Islands, northern Vancouver Island, and the adjacent northern coast; extending north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Ohio, Minnesota, South Dakota, New Mexico, and Oregon.
Description_Botanical: A nitrogen-fixing deciduous shrub of the Elaeagnaceae family, featuring erect to spreading stems 1-2 m tall (or 0.9–4 m) with young brownish-scaled stems and older brownish, scaly branches. Leaves are opposite, entire, elliptic to narrowly egg-shaped (or oval), 1.5-6 cm long and 1-3 cm wide, greenish on the upper surface with whitish-silvery hairs, and white-scaly and brownish-scaly with rusty brown spots beneath. Flowers are small, yellowish or brownish, with male and female flowers borne on separate shrubs. The fruits are drupelike, red or yellowish, ovoid achenes, that are fleshy and edible but almost tasteless or bitter (Viereck & Little 1972).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A nitrogen-fixing deciduous shrub of the Elaeagnaceae family, featuring erect to spreading stems 1-2 m tall (or 0.9–4 m) with young brownish-scaled stems and older brownish, scaly branches.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Opposite, entire, elliptic to narrowly egg-shaped, 1.5-6 cm long, 1-3 cm wide, greenish on the upper surface, white-scaly and brownish-scaly beneath.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of 1 to several inconspicuous axillary flowers clustered on short branches; male and female flowers on separate plants, the male flowers brownish; petals lacking; sepals spreading to reflexed, 4-lobed, the lobes 1-2 mm long; stamens 8. Male and female flowers are borne on separate plants, with the male flowers exhibiting a brownish coloration.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Berries, bright red, oval, 6-8 mm long, fleshy, saponin-rich (soapy when crushed).
Discovered_Drive_Details: Soapberries contain a natural detergent - like substance that makes them soapy and bitter. Because of this, they can be whipped into a frothy mass, something like whipped cream. Soapberries may be gathered on southern Vancouver Island or obtained through trade then whipped with sugar and eaten.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Symbiotic nitrogen-fixer that elevates site fertility and accelerates canopy closure; in low-nutrient Garry oak or alpine meadows, space carefully so vigorous nitrogen responders do not crowd slow forbs.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Shepherdia canadensis occurs in dry to moist open woods and thickets, from lowlands to middle elevation forests MacKinnon 1994. It prefers moist to wet soil and is generally found on rocky, sandy, or gravelly soils and is able to survive on nutrient poor soils because of its nitrogen fixing ability.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Arbuscular Mycorrhizal (AM) & Actinorhizal Nitrogen-Fixing (Frankia root nodules)
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found on mesic to dry sites in the lowland and steppe to subalpine zones; common throughout British Columbia except absent on the Queen Charlotte Islands, northern Vancouver Island, and the adjacent northern coast; extending north to Alaska, Yukon Territory, and Northwest Territories, east to Newfoundland, and south to Ohio, Minnesota, South Dakota, New Mexico, and Oregon. Also inhabits dry to moist open forests, gravelly riverbanks, and alluvial flats such as the Salmon River delta (Switzmalph); dry open areas, rocky oak meadows, and sunny thickets. Lopez Island, San Juan Island, and the Saanich Peninsula.

Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Grizzly Bears, Black Bears, Small Mammals. Soapberries are a keystone late-summer caloric food source for grizzly and black bears.
Stratification_Dormancy: Seeds have a hard seed coat and scarification with sulfuric acid for twenty to thirty minutes followed by two to three months of cold stratification will help the embryo to develop (Dirr & Heuser 1987).
Sowing_Protocol_Time: The seeds must not be allowed to dry out.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Buffaloberry seeds should be harvested in the autumn and sown immediately in a cold frame.
Nursery_Availability: Somewhat available from native plant nurseries within its range.
Nursery_Stock_Format: 4-inch to 2-gal Container; Bare-root; Forestry Plugs; Seed
Edible_Parts_Flavor: Berries whipped with water and sweeteners into a frothy dessert called 'Indian Ice Cream' (sxúse); highly valued for trade.
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Edible fruit. Buffaloberry berries were used to make “Indian ice cream” which has a bitter taste but was often sweetened with salal berries, camas bulbs, or hemlock cambium. The berries were also eaten fresh or dried.
Ethno_Medicinal: The Wet’suwet’en used the twigs, leaves, berries, and juice medicinally for everything from heart attacks to indigestion. Consumed as a festive food, health food, and tonic for influenza, indigestion, and various ailments. Berry whip eaten as health food, for colds and flu.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Berries harvested by beating branches over a basket, then whipped with water (and traditionally cedar root egg beaters) to make a frothy confection ("Indian Ice Cream" / sxúse). Whipped with special whippers in baskets into 'soapberry whip' feast confection.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Traditionally utilized for ritual purification by hunters and young men at puberty. Spiritual.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Saponin is much more toxic to some creatures, such as fish, if eaten in large quantities. Shepherdia canadensis fruit contain low concentrations of a bitter principle, saponin, which foams in water. It is very poorly absorbed by the body and can be broken down by thoroughly cooking the fruit.

Summary_Public: Spiny shrub (1-10 m tall), sticky ('gummy') leaves, fuchsia-like flowers, sticky hairy berries. Description_Botanical: A loosely branched deciduous shrub, 0.5-1 m tall, with spreading stems that are finely hairy and usually bear 3 slender, 7-12 mm long nodal spines, and bark that is brownish at first, turning deep greyish-red. Leaves are alternate, egg-shaped, shallowly heart-shaped at the base, 1.5-2.5 cm wide, 3-5-lobed less than half their length, the lobes rounded, shallowly cleft and deeply toothed, sparsely hairy or glabrous on the upper surface, and more or less hairy and glandular below, with stalks equal to or slightly shorter than the blades and glabrous. Red fruit. Spiny shrub (1-10 m tall), sticky ('gummy') leaves, fuchsia-like flowers, sticky hairy berries. Height 1-10m (or small shrub).

Summary_Public: Inhabits marshes, lakeshores, and streams in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia south of 56°N, becoming less frequent northward; ranging north to Alaska and Yukon Territory, east to Newfoundland, and south to Tennessee, Georgia, Texas, New Mexico, and California. Hardstem bulrush is found at low to mid elevations, generally below 2,300 m, in inundated to periodically wet areas of marshes, swamps, and meadows and along lake, reservoir, and pond shorelines.
Description_Botanical: Hardstem bulrush is a robust perennial rhizomatous wetland obligate species belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), forming dense colonies and reaching up to 3-5 m (typically 100-300, up to 500 cm or 3 m) in height. Stems are circular in cross-section, tapered, firm, and not easily crushed between the fingers, measuring 1-2 cm thick and 1-3 m tall, in upright gray-green to dark-green stands. Leaves are few and short, borne mainly or entirely toward the bases, featuring prominent, well-developed sheaths and poorly developed or absent blades. The inflorescence is a terminal panicle of 3 to 10 spikes comprising up to 50 or more spikelets, each sessile or on a short pedicel, and exceeded by a 2.5 to 10 cm lateral bract.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Hardstem bulrush is a robust perennial rhizomatous wetland obligate species belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), forming dense colonies and reaching up to 3-5 m (typically 100-300, up to 500 cm or 3 m) in height. Stems are circular in cross-section, tapered, firm, and not easily crushed between the fingers, measuring 1-2 cm thick and 1-3 m tall, in upright gray-green to dark-green stands.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Few, borne mainly or entirely toward the bases of the stems; sheaths prominent, well-developed; blades short, poorly-developed, or bladeless.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Scales are pale grey-white, measuring mostly (3) 3.5-4 mm long, broadly egg-shaped, and marked with numerous short, linear, reddish-brown dashes; they are more or less sticky short-hairy, with margins somewhat irregularly jagged or fringed with cobwebby, soft, long-tangled hairs, and feature a midrib.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: If less than 4 dm² is removed from any 1-m² area (1 ft² in 1 yd²), the hole will fill in within one growing season.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: It is generally found in areas of standing water ranging from 10 cm to more than 1.5 m (4 in to 1.5 m) in depth. It will not tolerate long periods of very deep water.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Typically Non-Mycorrhizal or facultatively weakly AM (specialized root hairs or wetland nutrient uptake)
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabits marshes, lakeshores, and streams in the lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common throughout British Columbia south of 56°N, becoming less frequent northward; ranging north to Alaska and Yukon Territory, east to Newfoundland, and south to Tennessee, Georgia, Texas, New Mexico, and California. Hardstem bulrush is found at low to mid elevations, generally below 2,300 m, in inundated to periodically wet areas of marshes, swamps, and meadows and along lake, reservoir, and pond shorelines. Hardstem bulrush occurs throughout North America except for the southeastern states from Louisiana east to Florida and north to Tennessee (USDA-NRCS, 2011).

Fire_Ecology: Hardstem bulrush re-establish from seed and rhizomes following fires (Smith and Kadlec, 1985). Fire is used to manage tule wetlands to remove old stems and restore open water to the wetland.
Companion_Plants: Cattail; Sitka Sedge; Wapato

Erosion_Slope_Control: Water Treatment/Erosion Control: Hardstem bulrush’s dense root mass makes this species an excellent choice for soil stabilization. Its above ground biomass provides protection from erosive wave action and stream currents that erode shorelines or stream banks. The rhizomatous root system also forms a matrix for many beneficial bacteria, making this plant an excellent choice for wastewater treatment (Hurd et al., 1994).
Foot_Traffic_Lawn_Use: Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.
Common_Bee_Visitors: Wind-pollinated / Spore-bearing (no floral nectar; provides overwintering stems, duff, or bare mineral soil habitat for cavity- & ground-nesting bees)
Host_Butterflies_Common: Common Alpine; Dun Skipper; Western Branded Skipper
Host_Butterflies_Scientific: Erebia epipsodea; Euphyes vestris; Hesperia colorado oregonia
Host_Moths_Common: Yellow-collared Scape Moth
Host_Moths_Scientific: Cisseps fulvicollis; Amphipoea americana; Ctenucha rubroscapus; Hypocoena rufostrigata; Mythimna oxygala; Plusia putnami; Xylomoia indirecta
Birds_Interactions: Waterfowl will feed on the seed; The dense tules provide excellent nesting cover for numerous waterfowl and wetland birds. Seeds feed waterfowl.
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Muskrats, Beavers, Avoided by Ungulates. Rootstock eaten by muskrats.
Seed_Collection_Harvest: Seeds ripen in late August to September. Seeds are not held tightly in the seed head, and high winds, frost, and brushing against the seed head will cause the seeds to dislodge.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: There are no cultivars, improved, or selected materials of hardstem bulrush. Planting plugs (either from the greenhouse or wild transplants) is the surest way to establish a new stand of this species. Care should be taken not to collect plants from weedy areas as weeds can be relocated to the transplant site. Wild plants can be collected and transplanted directly into the desired site. If less than 4 dm² is removed from any 1 m² area (1 ft² in 1 yd²), the hole will fill in within one growing season. Hardstem bulrush reproduces sexually by seed and asexually through vegetative spread via rhizomes.
Pruning_Management: Water level in a wetland should be fluctuated from saturated conditions up to a maximum depth of 30 cm of standing water for establishing plants. The young plants can handle deeper water, but not for an extended period of time. This species can tolerate periods of drought and total inundation. It will spread into water depths of 1 to 1.5 m.
Nursery_Availability: Common wildland collected seed is available from commercial sources (Native Seed Network).
Nursery_Stock_Format: Restoration Plugs (77-cell / 45-cell); 4-inch Container; Pure Live Seed (PLS); Root Division
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Seed and young seeds edible. The young sprouts and shoots of hardstem bulrush can be eaten raw or cooked, and the rhizomes and unripe flower heads can be boiled as a vegetable. Hardstem bulrush rhizomes were also sundried and pounded into a kind of flour.
Ethno_Medicinal: Hardstem bulrush has also been used by Native American tribes medicinally. The Cree used a poultice of stem pith to stop bleeding.
Ethno_Material_Tech: Stems used in basketry. Mat weaving (tule mats, bedding, wall partitions). Gathered stems woven into mats, widely traded among Coast Salish, Interior Salish, and Nuu-chah-nulth.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Navajo and Ramah tribes used the plant as a ceremonial emetic, and the Nlaka'pamux (Thompson) tribe placed ashes from burned stems on a newborn’s bleeding navel.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Pests are generally not a problem. Aphids will feed on the stems, but generally will not kill the plant.

Summary_Public: A low herb featuring broad leaves and erect flower spikes, growing as a perennial from a fibrous root with several erect, simple, smooth or stiff-hairy stems 5-50 cm tall. Found in mesic to dry lawns, fields, roadsides, and waste places across lowland, steppe, and montane zones; common in southwestern British Columbia and less frequent elsewhere, introduced from Eurasia and frequently occupying moist to dry low-grass areas along trails and roadsides as a non-native taxon.
Description_Botanical: A low herb featuring broad leaves and erect flower spikes, growing as a perennial from a fibrous root with several erect, simple, smooth or stiff-hairy stems 5-50 cm tall. Basal leaves are broadly elliptic to lanceolate or egg-shaped, tapered into a long stalk, entire or irregularly toothed, 4-18 cm long, 2.5-11 cm wide, and strongly parallel-veined; stem leaves are lacking. Low-growing annual or perennial herb with a rosette of broad, strongly-veined basal leaves and erect green flower spikes. Common non-native low leafy plant.

Summary_Public: Dioecious Deciduous Tree/tall spindly shrub up to 15 m height with velvety young leaves/twigs and large catkins. Description_Botanical: This native willow stands alone as being the most drought-tolerant willow of our region. Small deciduous tree up to 15 m with attractive foliage and large catkins. Males and female flowers are on different plants (dioecious). Shrubs or trees dioecious, 3-20 m tall, not colonial; branches erect, flexible at base; twigs yellow-green to yellow-brown, sparsely to densely velvety-hairy.

Summary_Public: Occurring in mesic to dry roadsides, fields, and waste places across lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this species is frequent in British Columbia south of 56°N and was introduced from Eurasia. Field mustard typically inhabits disturbed areas, including roadsides, ditches, cultivated fields, orchards, and gardens.
Description_Botanical: An annual herb arising from a taproot, producing glabrous or sparsely hairy, glaucous stems 20–40 cm tall that range from simple to freely branched. Basal leaves are slender-stalked and pinnately cleft with 2–4 lateral lobes and an egg-shaped, wavy-toothed terminal lobe that is the largest. Lowermost stem leaves resemble the basal leaves but feature ear-like, clasping or unstalked bases, while the upper leaves are oblong, narrowly egg-shaped or lanceolate, and subentire. Field mustard is an upright winter annual or biennial that is a member of the mustard family (Brassicaceae).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: An annual herb arising from a taproot, producing glabrous or sparsely hairy, glaucous stems 20–40 cm tall that range from simple to freely branched.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves slender-stalked, pinnately cleft with the terminal lobe the largest, 2-4 lateral lobes, the terminal lobe egg-shaped, wavy-toothed; lowermost stem leaves similar to the basal but ear-like at the bases and clasping or unstalked, upper oblong, narrowly egg-shaped or lanceolate, subentire.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescences arranged in terminal clusters, borne on stout, ascending flower stalks 7-25 mm long; petals are yellow and measure 6-8 mm long, subtended by sepals 3-4 mm long.
Flower_Measurements_mm_cm: 7-25 mm long; 6-8 mm long; 3-4 mm long
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Siliques are ascending to spreading, straight, 3-7 cm long, and 2.5-3.5 mm wide; styles are beaked, measuring 10-15 mm long; seeds are 1.5 mm long and minutely honeycombed.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Annual completing its full lifecycle from germination to seed within one growing season.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Field mustard is an extremely adaptable plant that grows in sandy to heavy clay soils and tolerates a pH range from 4.8 to 8.5 (Hannaway and Larson, 2004). It grows best in well-drained, moist soil, but may also grow in droughty conditions, moderate heat, and soils with low fertility (Clark, 2007).
Mycorrhizal_Association: Typically Non-Mycorrhizal or facultatively weakly AM (specialized root hairs or wetland nutrient uptake)
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Occurring in mesic to dry roadsides, fields, and waste places across lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this species is frequent in British Columbia south of 56°N and was introduced from Eurasia. Field mustard typically inhabits disturbed areas, including roadsides, ditches, cultivated fields, orchards, and gardens. This plant is native to Eurasia, but has spread all over the world and is now naturalized throughout much of North America. It grows from sea level to 1524 m.
Habitat_Tags: Prairies; Wetlands & Marshes; Thickets & Clearings
Biogeoclimatic_Zone: Bunchgrass (BG); Ponderosa Pine (PP); Interior Douglas-fir (IDF)
BC_Regional_Range: Southern Interior; East of Cascade Crest
Elevation_Belts_Range: Lowland to Steppe to Montane (0–1200 m)
Key_Features_Tags: Pollinator Magnet; Erosion Control; Cover Crop / Green Manure; Deer Resistant; Edible
Garden_Use_Tags: Meadow; Hedgerow / Thicket
Foot_Traffic_Lawn_Use: Not suited for heavy foot traffic; best planted in restoration beds, meadows, or borders.
Bloom_Months: Jan; Feb; Mar; Apr; May; Jun; Jul; Aug; Sep
Common_Bee_Visitors: Bumblebees (Bombus occidentalis, B. vosnesenskii, B. mixtus); Mason & Orchard Bees (Osmia lignaria, Osmia spp.); Mining & Digger Bees (Andrena spp., Colletes spp.); Leafcutter & Resin Bees (Megachile spp.); Sweat Bees (Halictus & Lasioglossum spp.)
Mammals_Browse_Wildlife: Cultivars with larger roots, commonly called forage turnip, have been a popular forage crop for livestock in Europe and Asia for at least 600 years (Undersander et al., 1991). Forage turnip is a useful crop for extending the fall grazing season for dairy cows and other livestock (Thomet and Kohler, 2003).
Seed_Collection_Harvest: Good seed production requires cross pollination by various insects. One or two hives per acre can ensure good seed set (Duke, 1983). Seed production fields need to have proper isolation distances among varieties and all other forms of B. juncea, B. campestris, and B. napus.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Drill seed in the spring, late summer, or fall at a rate of 1.7–11.2 kg/ha and a depth of ½ to ¾ inch in rows 10.2–30.5 cm apart; alternately, broadcast at 9–15.7 kg/ha followed by cultipacking (Clark, 2007; Knodel and Olson, 2002). Field mustard has approximately 150,000 to 200,000 seeds per pound, so a seeding rate of one pound per acre will result in approximately 3 to 5 seeds per square foot.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Field mustard seed is generally available from commercial cover-crop suppliers, though quantities may be limited.
Pruning_Management: Soils should be tested prior to planting to determine fertilizer and lime requirements. When planted as a fall catch crop following a cash crop that has been well fertilized, additional fertilizer may not be needed. Lime should be added to correct pH to 5.5 to 6.8. Fertilizer applications, if required, should be banded at least 5.1 cm to the side and below the seed.
Nursery_Stock_Format: Direct-Sow Seed Packet; Bulk Restoration Seed (PLS); Nursery Cell Plugs
Ethno_Culinary_Food: Widely adopted and grown in gardens as food. Field mustard roots and leaves were used as food by many Native American tribes following introduction of the plant by white settlers.
Ethno_Medicinal: Various parts of the plant have been used as a folk remedy for different types of cancer, either by boiling the mashed stems and leaves, powdering the seeds, or making a salve from the flowers.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: The roots, leaves, and especially seeds of Brassica rapa and related species contain sulfur compounds. This plant may become weedy or invasive, primarily in cultivated fields and disturbed or waste areas, and may displace desirable vegetation if not properly managed. Brassica rapa is listed as an invasive weed in Weeds of the West and Weeds of the United States and Canada.

Summary_Public: Shrub layer wetland species; strongly odorous flowers on a stalk hooded by a bright yellow bract; very large elongated leaves. Inhabiting swamps, wet ditches, and moist forests across lowland and montane zones; common in southern British Columbia west of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, and less frequent elsewhere in the province south of 56°N; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to Montana, Idaho, and California, typically found in swamps, bogs, and moist low-lying wetland sites.
Description_Botanical: Perennial semi-aquatic or terrestrial herb of the shrub wetland layer, arising from a short, thick rhizome and fibrous roots, featuring strongly odorous flowers on a stalk hooded by a bright yellow bract. Perennial semi-aquatic or terrestrial herb from a short, thick rhizome and fibrous roots; stems several, 30-70 cm tall. Leaves all basal, with blades egg-shaped to broadly lanceolate, entire, 30-150 cm long and 10-70 cm wide, short-stalked. Fragrant.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Perennial semi-aquatic or terrestrial herb of the shrub wetland layer, arising from a short, thick rhizome and fibrous roots, featuring strongly odorous flowers on a stalk hooded by a bright yellow bract. Found along shorelines and in wetlands, including swamps, lakeshores, and moist interdunal depressions, this plant is common in coastal southwestern British Columbia and the Queen Charlotte Islands, ranging northward to southern Alaska and southward to northern California.
Description_Botanical: A deciduous dioecious shrub or tree, 0.6-8 m tall, not colonial, producing beautifully large catkins (pussywillows) in early spring followed by soft, silvery leaves. Male and female flowers are on different plants (dioecious). On the east side of Vancouver Island, this functions as a wetland plant, whereas on the outer coast it frequently forms thickets just above the driftwood line. Dioecious shrubs or trees, 0.6-8 m tall, not colonial; branches erect, flexible at base; twigs yellow- to red-brown, smooth or densely hairy.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: A deciduous dioecious shrub or tree, 0.6-8 m tall, not colonial, producing beautifully large catkins (pussywillows) in early spring followed by soft, silvery leaves.

Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Flowers are unisexual, lacking sepals and petals, and are borne in stout, unstalked catkins which flower as leaves emerge or before them; floral bracts are dark with straight or wavy hairs, possessing 2 stamens and 1 smooth or hairy ovary with styles measuring 0.6-2.3 mm long.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules which split open to release the seeds, each of which is surrounded by a tuft of hairs; stalks 0.5-2 mm long.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.

Summary_Public: Large coniferous tree with sharp needles; light and exceptionally strong wood. Inhabiting moist to mesic slopes and river terraces in lowland and montane zones; common in extreme western British Columbia; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to northern California.
Description_Botanical: Large coniferous tree reaching up to 90 m tall (up to two hundred feet) with a crown of noticeably long, horizontal main branches and drooping branchlets. Bark is gray and smooth on small trunks, becoming dark grayish-brown to purplish and thin-scaly on older trunks; young twigs are glabrous. Needles are flattened, stiff, very sharp, yellowish-green to bluish-green, 2.5-3.8 cm (1 to 1½ inches) long, standing out in all directions, pungent, with white lines of stomata on the upper surface. Seed cones are 5-9 cm (one to four inches) long, hanging down, reddish-brown to yellowish-brown, with very thin, rounded scales featuring finely irregularly toothed tips.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Large coniferous tree reaching up to 90 m tall (up to two hundred feet) with a crown of noticeably long, horizontal main branches and drooping branchlets. Bark is gray and smooth on small trunks, becoming dark grayish-brown to purplish and thin-scaly on older trunks; young twigs are glabrous.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Needles sharp, flattened; standing out in all directions; pungent.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Pollen cones red.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Seed cones 5-9 cm long, reddish-brown to yellowish-brown, scales rounded and finely irregularly toothed at tip.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Tth’qw’ulhp is most commonly found in areas that are moist but well-drained. It grows in the coastal forest with thq’iinlhp, xpey’ and pashuluqw, with a forest floor often covered with mosses, horsetails and blueberries. It feels like you will be poked or punctured after you grab a branch with needles on it, hence the name tth’qw’ulhp.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Year-round evergreen foliage anchors winter garden structure.
Spread_Behavior: Woody crown and lateral root system
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Acidic needle duff, dense feeder-root competition, and year-round canopy shade out sun-loving meadow herbs; underplant with adapted acidophilic woodland understory flora.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Picea sitchensis is often found on moist well-drained sites such as alluvial floodplains, marine terraces, and headlands MacKinnon 1994.
Mycorrhizal_Association: Ectomycorrhizal (EcM; Suillus, Russula, Lactarius, Amanita & forest truffle symbionts)
Summer_Watering: Keep consistently moist; do not allow soil to dry out during growing season.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting moist to mesic slopes and river terraces in lowland and montane zones; common in extreme western British Columbia; ranging north to southeastern Alaska and south to northern California. Flourishing in moist, well-drained coastal forests, Sitka spruce is native to the Pacific Coast region from Alaska to western British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, and northwestern California.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: New leaves useful as tea. The inner bark was eaten fresh, or dried into cakes and eaten with berries. It was also dried and ground into a powder and used as a thickener in soups or added to cereals when making bread.
Ethno_Medicinal: Sitka spruce was widely employed medicinally by several native North American Indian tribes who used it especially for its antiseptic qualities in the treatment of lung complaints, sores and wounds. It has been chewed in the treatment of throat problems, coughs, and colds. Sitka spruce pitch was also used as a medicine for gonorrhea, syphilis, internal swelling, and toothaches.

Description_Botanical: A spore-bearing segmented wetland plant forming dense patches; perennial arising from a felty-hairy, blackish, tuber-bearing rhizome. Sterile stems 15-150 cm tall, 5-20 mm thick, their central cavity more than 2/3 the stem diameter, regularly and abundantly branched, the sheaths with 15-30 teeth, the teeth with dark tips; branches in regular whorls; fertile stems appearing in spring before sterile stems, 10-40 cm tall, pale brown, unbranched, dying when the spores are shed, the sheaths 4-8, pale brown with 20-40 darker teeth. Fertile stems appear in spring prior to the sterile stems, measuring 10-40 cm tall, pale brown, unbranched, and dying upon spore release, with 4-8 pale brown sheaths bearing 20-40 darker teeth. Cones measure 4-8 cm long, are hollow, and rounded at the tip.

Search_Keywords_Index: Amsinckia menziesii; Small-flowered Fiddleneck; Menzies' Fiddleneck; Devil’s Lettuce; Rough Fiddleneck; Harvest Fiddleneck
Summary_Public: Annual Forb, 15-50 cm height with helicoid cymes and orange-yellow flowers. Inhabiting meadows, shorelines, and moist to dry disturbed areas in steppe and montane zones, this taxon is common in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, rare northward, and introduced in Vancouver, ranging north to Alaska and the Yukon and south to California.
Description_Botanical: Common Fiddleneck is an annual forb and a member of the borage family (Boraginaceae), known for its distinctive helicoid cymes—coiled inflorescences, which are clusters of flowers arranged on a stem. With its vibrant orange-yellow blooms, it is both visually striking and pollinator-friendly. A slender, bristly-hairy native annual forb standing 15–80 cm tall from a taproot, bearing simple to branched stems. Alternate, lance-oblong to linear leaves (2–12 cm long, 0.5–2.5 cm wide) lead up to characteristic coiled scorpioid cymes of small, pale yellow tubular flowers (4–7 mm long) that uncurl as they bloom, yielding bumpy keeled nutlets.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Common Fiddleneck is an annual forb and a member of the borage family (Boraginaceae), known for its distinctive helicoid cymes—coiled inflorescences, which are clusters of flowers arranged on a stem.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves not forming a persistent tuft; stem leaves lance-oblong, elliptic, or linear, 2-12 cm long and 0.5-2.5 cm wide, alternate, entire.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence a coiled cluster; petals yellow, fused into a tube 4-7 mm long that spreads (2-4 mm wide) at top to 5 shallow lobes, the throat open; calyx lobes 5, with both silky and longer, stiff hairs. Helicoid Cymes.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Nutlets 4, clustered together, 2-3.5 mm long, egg-shaped, warty or pimply and often wrinkled, greenish or grey to brownish-black.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Annual reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Fall_Winter_Interest: Persistent fruit, hips, cones, or dried seedheads add late-season visual interest and winter wildlife forage.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic and non-aggressive (Taproot); low root competition makes it safe for intimate mixed borders and diverse polyculture interplanting.
Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: In drier areas, they are more commonly found occupying depressions and low areas that accumulate additional soil moisture. Dry open meadows, bluffs, and disturbed sunny grounds.
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting meadows, shorelines, and moist to dry disturbed areas in steppe and montane zones, this taxon is common in southern British Columbia east of the Coast-Cascade Mountains, rare northward, and introduced in Vancouver, ranging north to Alaska and the Yukon and south to California. Both species are associated with mixed warm desert shrub, creosote bush, sagebrush steppe, and pinyon-juniper communities in low valleys and foothills. Menzies’ fiddleneck has also been collected in higher-elevation plant communities including mountain brush and aspen-fir communities (Welsh et al., 2003). Bristly fiddleneck is widespread, occurring in all western states from New Mexico north to Idaho and into British Columbia (USDA NRCS, 2023).

Seed_Collection_Harvest: Tilley et al. (2023) recommend wearing protective gear to minimize or prevent eye, skin, and inhalation hazards from fiddleneck bristles. Seed can be collected by clipping stems just below the inflorescence or using a racquet and hopper. Raquet and hopper methods allow for multiple harvests and require less hands-on removal of stems.
Sowing_Protocol_Time: Tilley et al. (2023) found no significant difference in germination in three different soil types (fine sandy loam, loam, and clay loam). They did find significantly fewer seeds emerged from depths of 1 and 2 cm compared to surface sown seeds. This may indicate a possible light requirement for germination agreeing with Forbis (2010), or it may be the result of low seedling vigor.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Fiddleneck seed is currently difficult to obtain on the commercial market and wildland collection is often the only means of obtaining seed. Seed should be selected based on the local climate, resistance to local pests, and intended use.
Pruning_Management: Bristly and Menzies’ fiddleneck are early seral colonizers. They are typically abundant on disturbed sites for the first few years following disturbance and then reduce in density making way for later seral, longer-lived species. Occasionally these species can form persistent stands, especially under management where succession is interrupted.

Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: Seeds and foliage contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can cause hepatic fibrosis in livestock if grazed in quantity; bristly hairs may irritate skin.

Summary_Public: Rhizomatous Perennial Sedge up to 2 m height. Inhabiting lakeshores, wetlands, marshes, and streams across lowland, steppe, and montane zones, this taxon is frequent throughout British Columbia, ranging north to Alaska and the Yukon, east to Newfoundland, and south to Maine, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, as well as Central America.
Description_Botanical: Soft-stem bulrush (Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani) is a large, wetland-inhabiting perennial sedge belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), sometimes growing in water up to 2 m deep and reaching up to 2-3 m (50-200 cm or more, up to ten feet) in height. Perennial herb from long rhizomes; stems nearly round in cross-section, tapered, smooth, easily crushed between the fingers, 50-200 cm tall or more. Leaves are few, restricted to the base (reaching about 1/2 the length of the stems); sheaths are brown to straw-coloured or mottled brownish, and reddish near the base; blades are usually lacking or numbering 1 or 2, when present C-shaped to flattened top to bottom, much shorter than the sheaths, with margins often minutely rough. Blossoms are borne in an open inflorescence of many stalked, budlike spikelets, covered by reddish brown scales below the top of the stem (Tiner 1987).
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Soft-stem bulrush (Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani) is a large, wetland-inhabiting perennial sedge belonging to the Sedge Family (Cyperaceae), sometimes growing in water up to 2 m deep and reaching up to 2-3 m (50-200 cm or more, up to ten feet) in height. The plant arises from long rhizomes with nearly round, tapered, smooth stems that are easily crushed between the fingers.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: All near the base of the stems, few, to about 1/2 the length of the stems; sheaths brown to straw-coloured or mottled brownish, reddish near the base; blades usually lacking or 1 or 2, if present, C-shaped to flattened top to bottom, much shorter than the sheaths, the margins often minutely rough.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Spikes are several to numerous, terminal, reddish-brown, 5-12 mm long, arranged in unstalked clusters within a branching inflorescence, or some borne singly in compound, compact to open clusters, with lax and sometimes drooping inflorescence branches; involucral bracts are solitary, rarely more, erect, reduced, not leaflike, thickly C-shaped to nearly circular in cross-section, tapered, sometimes featuring minutely rough margins, measuring up to 7 cm long, and appearing like an extension of the stem.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Scales brown to purplish-brown, with numerous, short, red-brown linear marks, (2) 2.5-3 (3.5) mm long, smooth, egg-shaped, the margins entire to somewhat irregular or jagged or short-fringed and short-awned; perianth bristles 6, brown, about equalling to surpassing the achenes; achenes plano-convex, mostly 2-2.3 mm long, not completely concealed by the scales at maturity, abruptly sharp-pointed. Perianth bristles number 6, are brown, and approximately equal to surpassing the achenes.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Perennial reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.
Allelopathy_Competition_Notes: Non-allelopathic moderate clonal spreader (Rhizomatous); weaves steadily through mixed groundcover matrices without harsh chemical inhibition.
Moisture_Notes: Thrives in seasonally saturated soils, riparian benches, or poorly drained depressions.
Soil_Preferences_Narrative: Soft-stem bulrush occurs in deep or shallow water, or in muddy or marshy ground around lakes, ponds, streams, and wooded wetlands (Guard 1995). This species usually occurs in poorly drained soil. It grows better in saline conditions than in fresh water, and it tolerates a wide range of salinity.

Summary_Public: An annual forb growing 40-80 cm in height with yellow flowers and a fragrance resembling tea tree oil mixed with grapefruit, frequently inhabiting clay soils on bare ground between perennials with seasonal inundation and summer drying. Inhabiting meadows, moist to dry roadsides, open slopes, and forest openings in lowland and montane zones, mountain tarweed occurs infrequently and is scattered throughout southern British Columbia, extending east to Saskatchewan and south to Colorado, Arizona, and California.
Description_Botanical: This annual often grows in clay soils on the bare ground between perennial plants. It is well-adapted to having water sit on the surface in the winter and drying completely in the summer. It has a fragrance that has been described as tea tree oil mixed with grapefruit. An annual forb growing 40-80 cm in height with yellow flowers and a fragrance resembling tea tree oil mixed with grapefruit, frequently inhabiting clay soils on bare ground between perennials with seasonal inundation and summer drying.

Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Inhabiting meadows, moist to dry roadsides, open slopes, and forest openings in lowland and montane zones, mountain tarweed occurs infrequently and is scattered throughout southern British Columbia, extending east to Saskatchewan and south to Colorado, Arizona, and California. As the most widely distributed Madia species, its native range spans western and northern North America from British Columbia to the Southwestern United States, across southwestern Canada, and into the Rocky Mountains, with naturalized populations in Alaska, eastern Canada, and the north-central and northeastern United States. It predominantly occupies disturbed sites—including grassland openings, meadows, swales, shrublands, woodlands, forests, marsh and lake edges, and roadsides—at elevations of 0–3658 m.

Summary_Public: An annual forb growing 20-80 cm in height with yellow flowers, part of the suite of annual plants inhabiting mossy rocks, capable of long blooming in gardens, with edible roasted seeds. Found in meadows and rocky slopes, grassy tarweed inhabits dry roadsides, open slopes, and forest openings within lowland, steppe, and montane zones.
Description_Botanical: Part of the suite of annual plants that make their living on mossy rocks. An annual forb growing 20-80 cm in height with yellow flowers, part of the suite of annual plants inhabiting mossy rocks.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves lacking; stem leaves alternate, linear to lance-linear, 2-11 cm long, 1-10 mm wide, stiff-hairy and often densely glandular upwards.
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Heads with ray and disk flowers, numerous in an elongate inflorescence; involucres urn-shaped, 6-11 mm tall; involucral bracts linear dorsally, crescent-shaped laterally, glandular; ray flowers yellow, 3-9, 1.5-2 mm long; disk flowers 13-15, fertile, with black anthers.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Achenes flattened, hairless, often mottled, 2.8-5 mm long; pappus lacking.
Maturity_Timeline_Lifespan: Annual reaching mature stature within 1–2 growing seasons under suitable site conditions.

Soil_Preferences_Narrative: It often grows in coarse, sandy or gravelly soils, but is also found on silty/clayey soils, and sometimes on serpentine soils. It prefers full sun, but can tolerate light shade (Cronquist, 1961).
Summer_Watering: Occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat; avoid waterlogging.
Natural_Habitat_Narrative: Found in meadows and rocky slopes, grassy tarweed inhabits dry roadsides, open slopes, and forest openings within lowland, steppe, and montane zones. It is infrequent in extreme southern British Columbia, ranging south to Utah, Nevada, California, and Mexico, with a disjunct distribution in Chile. Grassy tarweed grows on open or partially shaded slopes or in flats in grasslands, meadows, shrublands, woodlands, forests, disturbed sites, stream banks, and roadsides (Jepson Flora Project, 2012). Grassy tarweed is native to western North America from southern British Columbia to northern Baja California and east to Utah and Montana, at elevations from sea level to 2377 m (Cronquist, 1961).

Summary_Public: Occurring in dry to moist open woods, meadows, and roadsides, this species is common throughout British Columbia across all vegetation zones, extending north to southern Alaska, the Yukon Territory, and the Northwest Territories, east to Quebec and Nova Scotia, and south to Maine, New York, Michigan, Minnesota, Iowa, South Dakota, New Mexico, Utah, Nevada, and California. Hookedspur violet inhabits varied environments including dry to moist meadows, coastal areas, open woods, grasslands, and open, disturbed ground from lowlands to near timberline, and is found extensively in the western half of the United States to New England and northward throughout Canada.
Description_Botanical: Hookedspur violet is a common native perennial forb of the violet family (Violaceae) featuring short to elongate, slender rhizomes and growing to approximately 10.2 cm in height. Perennial herb arising from a rhizome, lacking stolons, with stems absent in spring but developing ascending, usually hairy aerial stems 2-10 cm tall as the season progresses. Basal leaves are egg-shaped to heart-shaped with blunt-toothed margins, blades 0.5-4 cm long that are smooth or hairy, and stalks 5-7 cm long. Plants typically produce round to oval 5.1 cm leaves from branched, hairy stems.
Stems_Bark_Morphology: Hookedspur violet is a common native perennial forb of the violet family (Violaceae) featuring short to elongate, slender rhizomes and growing to approximately 10.2 cm in height. Perennial herb arising from a rhizome, lacking stolons, with stems absent in spring but developing ascending, usually hairy aerial stems 2-10 cm tall as the season progresses.
Leaf_Type_Arrangement: Basal leaves egg-shaped to heart-shaped, the margins blunt-toothed, the blades 0.5-4 cm long, smooth or hairy, the stalks 5-7 cm long; stem leaves similar, sometimes few; stipules jagged or sharp-toothed (at least basally), reddish-brown or greenish, often with reddish-brown flecks, 3-10 mm long.
Leaf_Dimensions_cm_mm: 0.5-4 cm long; 5-7 cm long; 3-10 mm long
Flower_Inflorescence_Type: Inflorescence of single, axillary flowers; petals 5, blue to deep violet, lower petal 8-16 mm long including the 4- to 8-mm long spur, the spur not pouched, lowest 3 petals often whitish with purple markings, lateral pair white-bearded; sepals 5, lanceolate, 1/3 to 1/2 as long as the petals; style heads bearded with short to long hairs. There are 5 petals colored blue to deep violet; the lower petal measures 8-16 mm long, including the 4- to 8-mm long spur, which is not pouched.
Fruit_Seed_Type_Dimensions: Capsules are smooth and 6-11 mm long, containing dark brown seeds.
Discovered_Drive_Details: Habitat Restoration: Hookedspur violet is used for coastal butterfly habitat restoration in the Pacific Northwest, and is established by either seed or as plugs.

Moisture_Notes: Prefers evenly moist, well-drained soils without standing winter water.

Stratification_Dormancy: Seeds should be sown less than 3 mm deep and covered lightly with soil or vermiculite. Seeds experience dormancy and need up to 120 days of wet, cool conditions (stratification) to trigger germination in the spring. Seeds experience dormancy and need up to 120 days of wet, cool conditions to trigger germination in the spring.
Propagation_Methods_Cultivars: Seeds can be sown on restoration sites in the fall at a rate of 1.1 kg/ha, or 50 seeds per square foot. For best establishment of seed production fields, stratify seeds in a cooler, sow into plugs in a greenhouse in late winter, and transplant out in spring. Transplanting into fields covered in weed fabric containing holes on a 0.3 m by 0.3 m spacing is most efficient for weed control and ease of seed harvest. Established by seed or as plugs.
Pruning_Management: Hookedspur violet prefers recently disturbed sites, and is easily outcompeted by taller or more vigorous plants. Management to control competition and prevent encroachment of trees may be necessary to ensure survival of this species on restoration sites.
Nursery_Availability: None, but containerized plants are sometimes available from commercial sources in the Pacific Northwest.

Ethno_Culinary_Food: The leaves and flowers of all violets are edible, and can be eaten in salads, used as potherbs, or brewed as tea.
Ethno_Medicinal: Hookedspur violet was used in traditional medicine by the Blackfoot, Nuxalk (Bella Coola) and Tolowa tribes. Leaves and roots were used to treat stomach problems and asthma in children, and as a cataplasm to treat soreness and swelling. In addition, the Southern Dakelh (Carrier), and S'Klallam (Klallam) used the plant as an analgesic and gastrointestinal aid, and the Makah tribe used it as a gynecological aid.
Ethno_Material_Tech: The Blackfoot Indians used a blue dye obtained from hookedspur violet to dye arrows.
Ethno_Ceremonial_Spiritual: Flowers eaten or used as ornamental charms.
Pet_Child_Livestock_Safety: Generally non-toxic; harvest away from roadsides and pesticides, and confirm species ID before consumption.
Warnings_Toxicity_Pests: This plant is covered with many types of insects, but no damage has been observed to established plants. Developing seed is highly predated by both birds and mice, and control measures are necessary to avoid loss of large amounts of seed in seed production fields.

Inhabiting wet to dry meadows, grassy slopes, fens, shrub-carrs, tidal marshes, clearings, roadsides, thickets and open forests from the lowland to subalpine zones; common throughout BC south of 57°N, infrequent northward and rare on the Queen Charlotte Islands.
Description_Botanical: Castilleja miniata is a species of Indian paintbrush known by the common name giant red Indian paintbrush. Castilleja miniata, commonly known as giant red Indian paintbrush, is a wildflower native to western North America from Alaska to Ontario to California to New Mexico, where it usually grows in moist places across a wide variety of habitat types. This perennial forb herb grows up to about 80 centimeters (80 cm / 0.9 m) tall with slender, green to dark purple herbage. Foliage consists of alternate, lance-shaped to lance-linear or lanceolate leaves that are 3 to 6 centimeters (3-10 cm) long, pointed to long-tapering to a sharp-pointed tip, entire, and coated in thin hairs to appressed-rough-hairy or nearly smooth.
